News.title: We are going to be outnumbered TWO TO ONE by UK’s ‘Guantanamo Bay’ – we won’t feel safe to walk our village streets
News.content:
Next

IN a sleepy North Yorkshire village – where the biggest excitement is a particularly lively bingo night – residents fear their peaceful existence will soon be shattered.

The tranquil village of Linton-on-Ouse faces an influx of migrants with plans to turn its former RAF base into a sprawling asylum processing centre.



Linton-on-Ouse sits amid rolling farmland, boasting a solitary pub among a scattering of quiet residential streets.

Its village shop has closed, the nearest manned police station is 12 miles away and the small number of residents who live there are served by one infrequent bus service.



But villagers are set to be dwarfed by the prospect of up to 1,200 migrants accommodated on their doorstep – potentially leaving the existing population outnumbered almost two to one.

Residents previously branded the plan’s the UK’s answer to “Guantanamo Bay” – dubbing it “Guantanamo-on-Ouse”.

Locals – many of whom live just a handful of metres from the perimeter of the proposed camp at RAF Linton – are furious and fearful.

Placards, banners and posters can be found between the village’s stone cottages and neat hedgerows, displaying a simple message: “Wrong plan. Wrong place.”



Home Office officials have however previously insisted the site will have permanent security and appropriate accommodation.

Lyn Wilson, 69, who has lived in Linton-on-Ouse for a decade, said she would fear for the safety of herself and her four grandchildren, branding the proposals as “absolutely ridiculous”

She said: “What are 1,200 young men going to do around here? Come to the craft group on a Tuesday afternoon?

“We’re tiny village of 600 adults and 100 children. We’d be absolutely dwarfed by young men.”

Lyn says she’d “no longer walk up and down the street” and fears many families – who moved into Linton after Covid – will no longer use the village playground.



RAF Linton opened in 1937 and became an important bomber station during the Second World War, when British and Canadian airmen flew dangerous missions against the Nazis.

The base closed in 2020 and was subsequently proposed as an asylum reception centre by the Tories in 2022.

Those plans were eventually shelved after furious opposition – only for Labour to announce this year they were once again looking at housing asylum seekers.

Under the controversial scheme, 1,200 migrants at a time would live on the base while having their claims processed, free to come and go as they please.

The plans were grimly dubbed “Guantánamo-on-Ouse” by a Lib Dem councillor – in reference to the US military immigration detention site in Cuba.



Retired IT support manager Phil Banks, 72, said the prospect of turning RAF Linton into an asylum centre was unworkable.

He said: “We got told we’re middle class, that we should take our fair share. A lot of people in the village would agree – a fair share.

“Going by government figures, that would be one asylum seeker per 200 residents. So our fair share would be three. Not 1,200.”



Mr Banks added: “It’s the wrong place for them, and it’s the wrong place for us.

“It’s nowt to do with race. If it were 1,200 young men from around the UK – Newcastle, Glasgow, London – it wouldn’t work. What are they going to do?”

The Linton Action Group has calculated that converting and operating the former RAF base could cost taxpayers £270million.

The group said each occupied bed per night could cost up to £853 – more than the cost of keeping asylum seekers in hotels.

But the Home Office says its plans to close asylum hotels will save money – and said they do not “recognise” the figure touted by the group.



The action team has written to the Chancellor John Healy demanding a full financial review ahead of work to convert the base.

And they claim the site may only be able to operate it for three years before being returned to the Ministry of Defence.

Group chairwoman Prof Olga Matthias described Labour’s plan as “impractical’ and ‘ridiculous”.



She said: “You only have to look for two seconds to see that it doesn’t work. It can’t possibly work.

“I’m just gobsmacked at the utter sheer, complete stupidity of persisting with this plan.”

Prof Matthias, who moved from Leeds during lockdown in search of peaceful country life, warned residents could be left trapped in homes they cannot sell.

She added: “Life circumstances happen. People need to move for a job, for children, to downsize. And if this centre happens, people can’t go.

“About a third of the village are rental properties – people have already handed in their notices.



“I don’t think I would be able to sell, even if I wanted to. Would you buy my house – however beautiful it is – when there are these plans afoot?”

Lyn also fears that people who bought homes after the previous asylum plans were abandoned could find themselves exposed.

She said: “Some of the families who have moved in since 2022 thinking the worry is gone, they could effectively end up in negative equity if they did want to move, because they’ve bought more recently.”

Unlike other isolated military camps dotted around the country earmarked for asylum processing, RAF Linton is embedded within residential streets and cul-de-sacs.



On the other side of the metal fence which once separated the base from civilian streets are a clutch of renovated former military homes.

The properties were promoted to families and professionals seeking peaceful country living within commuting distance of York.

But at The Paddocks, the show home is surrounded by empty properties with stark “TO LET” signs displayed in windows.

Some tenants have already handed in their notice, according to local residents.



Dean Bovington, 56, was a security officer at RAF Linton during his 28 year career in the Armed Forces, relocating back to the village a decade ago with his now 17-year-old son.

Dean said: “I’m a bit worried for him. He’s quite naive because we are in a small village. So, even if he is taller than me, he’s not quite as worldly-wise.

“My predominant concern is my son and I know lots of people in the village have similar fears for their children, especially teenage girls and younger.”

Under the latest proposals, the former airfield would house single adult male asylum seekers aged between 18 and 65, with CCTV and 24-hour security in place.



People accommodated there would be free to come and go, although they would be required to sign in and out.

Labour says the scheme would operate for a minimum of three year and cut Britain’s reliance on expensive asylum hotels.

But critics say the former RAF base should instead be redeveloped to provide desperately needed homes.

Farmer Chris Kirby, 75, grows crops on the land surrounding RAF Linton and for more than three decades has mown the air strip’s grass.



He said: “They need to do something with the site because it’s not been used for anything for more than five years. But an asylum processing centre is not the answer.

“We all thought we had heard the last of this in 2022, when they realised just how unworkable this was.

“The buildings have deteriorated even more since then, there’s still very little power and the sewage is already overloaded.”

The Home Office says no final decision has been taken, with feasibility assessments still outstanding and locals left in limbo.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A Home Office spokesperson said: “We do not recognise this figure. We are working to fairly house asylum seekers across the country, engaging with local authorities to reduce the impact on communities.



“This includes closing every asylum hotel and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites, saving taxpayers over £1bn on asylum support since the election.”

News.title: ‘His country is in shambles’: Trump blasts Zelensky AGAIN saying he ‘doesn’t care’ about ending war after depot attacks
News.content:
Next

DONALD Trump has lashed out at Volodymyr Zelensky saying he “doesn’t care” about ending the war in Ukraine.

The US president accused Ukraine of being in “shambles” as he said Washington was doing all it can to not “drive Russia away from the bargaining table”.



Relations between the world leaders have deteriorated rapidly in recent days with Trump.

On Friday Trump blocked numerous sanctions against Russia and earlier this month struck a diesel deal with Vladimir Putin.





A furious Zelensky said Trump had “rewarded” the Russian tyrant and said he felt “betrayed” by the White House.

Now Trump has said: “Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past, he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.

“He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now.

“His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead.”



Trump again slammed the Ukrainian army over its attacks on Russian oil hubs for “seriously hurting the world diesel markets“.

The US president has been trying to push down the soaring costs of petrol ahead of the November mid term elections.

In his post to TruthSocial he said: “I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.”



Earlier this month Trump purchased millions of barrels of oil from Russia – a decision many have criticised for feeding money into Putin’s war machine.

Zelensky has blasted the move as a “happy birthday present for Putin.”

He further criticised the US president as “not fair and not honest” adding that the agreement will bring further bloodshed to his country.

Trump had previously begged Zelensky to stop bombing Russian oil and gas facilities.

In a snub to the world leader, Ukraine recently resumed its ferocious attacks on Russia’s oil refineries and terminals – sending a huge swarm of drones into St Petersburg last night.



Powerful explosions ripped through Putin’s hometown as towering flames and massive plumes of smoke filled the night sky.

One target was a major data centre linked to VK – Russia’s Facebook with reports of critical disruption to services, including cloud platforms.

Data centres have become the new frontier in Ukraine’s war against the Russian tyrant.

Last week Ukraine crippled Russia’s “Google” with a wave of drone strikes on internet hubs – sparking huge blazes and wiping out critical services.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Banking services, apps and AI chatbots were all wiped out after the huge blitz on multiple Yandex sites across Russia.



The strike marked Ukraine’s third attack in three days.

News.title: Flight from Israel forced into emergency landing after bomb threat on board just weeks after plane ‘hijacking’ terror
News.content:
FLIGHT CHAOS Flight from Israel forced into emergency landing after bomb threat on board just weeks after plane ‘hijacking’ terror







Next

A FLIGHT from Israel has been forced into an emergency landing after a bomb threat on board.

The A320 aircraft was flying from Tel Aviv to Vienna as it was suddenly diverted to land in Sofia, Bulgaria, over a “bomb threat signal”.



The bomb threat that prompted the Austrian Airlines emergency landing stemmed from an anonymous tip, according to The Times of Israel.

According to reports, Austrian authorities received a phone call from Vienna about a suspicious object aboard the plane.



Passengers on board the threatened flight were reportedly a delegation of young people who were due to speak at the United Nations.

The Austrian citizen who reported the bomb was not on the plane, and at this stage it appears that it was a false alarm, YNET reports.

Bulgaria’s Ministry of Transport and Communications said: “According to initial information, there are six crew members and 51 passengers on board.

“During the flight, on the border with Romania, the crew reported a bomb threat signal and decided to land in Sofia extraordinarily.

“According to the procedures, an Air Force fighter took off and accompanied the plane until it landed at the airport in Sofia.

“A working headquarters has been formed and the responsible institutions have started an inspection.



“Passengers were taken off board the aircraft.”

According to FlightRadar24 information, the flight landed at 9:08pm in universal coordinated time or 10:08pm GMT.

The Lufthansa Group who own the airline, said: “We confirm that a threat was received regarding Austrian Airlines flight OS82 from Tel Aviv to Vienna, as a result of which the flight was diverted to land in Sofia, Bulgaria.”

They say the affected passengers will be re-assigned to an alternative flight as soon as possible.

This incident comes just weeks after an Israel-bound Flydubai plane was diverted to Saudi Arabia following a suspected terror plot.



The plane plummeted 17,400 feet in 90 seconds after a pilot knifed his fellow pilot with an axe in an attempt to allegedly take control of the passenger plane.

Hamam al-Hammami, 29, allegedly attacked captain Smit Machchhar with the reported plan of crashing into Tel Aviv airport in the hope of causing mass casualties.

It is understood the alleged hijacker planned it to be a 9/11-style attack.

Although badly hurt, Captain Smit was able to unlock the cockpit door, allowing for heroic passengers to take down the alleged hijacker.

Once inside, the brave passengers and crew grappled with the Omani co-pilot to regain control of the plane.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailed the “heroes” on board the flydubai plane for their intervention.

Last week, two anonymous reports of bombs on Delta Airlines flights from New York to Israel were received, but both proved to be false.

News.title: Leaked Green Party checklist urges members to avoid ‘exclusionary’ pubs and declare pronouns at meetings
News.content:
Next

GREEN Party meetings must avoid “exclusionary” pubs and should start with each member revealing their pronouns, a woke checklist declares.

The Sun has been passed internal party guidance for how Zack Polanski’s environmental activists ought to conduct “inclusive” events.



Boozers are off-limits because they “may feel uncomfortable or exclusionary” for those who do not drink alcohol.

At the start of the meeting organisers should “ask attendees how they would like to be addressed, including their name and pronouns”.



Tory Party chairman Kevin ­Hollinrake said: “First, a Labour MP suggested that black labradors and pints of warm ale were a far-right fantasy of Britain.

“Now the Greens think pubs are too ‘exclusionary’.



“Left to this lot, the Great ­British pub would soon be a thing of the past.

“Pubs are the heart of our ­communities and bring people together from all walks of life.

“This is peak political madness from left-wingers who have completely lost touch with ­ordinary Britain.”

Green Party members have been instructed to think twice before daring to hold meetings in bars.



Late meetings should be avoided “wherever possible” to accommodate people’s caring responsibilities, health needs and long journeys home.

Those chairing each meeting will be told to police the conversation so it is not “dominated by one or two voices,” nudging ­quieter members into speaking.

Regular breaks must be built in to the meetings for “accessibility and comfort” — which critics say would turn robust political debates into carefully managed sensitivity sessions.



Mr Polanski courted fresh ­outrage yesterday after refusing to overturn a controversial Green Party motion that declared ­“Zionism is racism”.

He told the BBC: “I’m not going to try to overturn it.

“At the first available opportunity, I do want to amend it.

“I want to move away from ‘one state’ towards saying that Israelis and Palestinians should decide that future for themselves.”

The Green leader said he could not scrap the policy before 2028, adding: “I’m not an out-of-control autocrat like some of the leaders of the Labour Party.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Mr Polanski also refused to say that Israel has a right to exist.

He said: “There is no right to exist for any country. People have a right to exist.”

News.title: Shocking moment man grabs rabbit by the ears and carries him away from family home before dumping poor pet in car park
News.content:
Next

THIS is the horrifying moment a man grabs a rabbit by its ears after “stealing it” from a family home.

Shocking footage shows two people laughing as one holds the writhing bunny while his friend films the ordeal before they dump the poor pet in a car park.



Rabbit owner Amy Grace was shocked to discover footage of her beloved pet being whisked away from her property in St Pauls Street, Hull.

The mum-of-two had nipped out to the shops, only to find that little Peter had vanished when she came back – sparking a frantic search.



Not long after he was reported missing, her furry companion was returned to her after being found abandoned in a car park.

A horrified Amy said: “Somebody had picked him up last night. He’d been dumped on Temple Street, in a car park.



“Thankfully they picked him up and took him inside and then saw my posts this morning and contacted me to come and get him.”

Peter wasn’t badly hurt during the ordeal.



But his gut stasis, a condition he has had for a long time, had worsened.

The illness causes the intestines to slow down or stop digesting food completely.

“His belly was massive and really inflamed so we’ve got him home and given him his medication in time,” Amy added.

“He’s had kisses and cuddles and the cat and dog have been all over him.”

Commenting on the video shared to a Hull community group, one user wrote: “What kind of society are we living in?”



Another wrote: “Poor baby, look how they are swinging him around, they clearly have no respect for animals.”

One shocked user said: “You should not ever carry rabbits by their ears!”

It is alleged that the two unknown men who yanked Peter from the garden tried to sell him to a neighbour.

The local initially had no idea he was a pet, thinking the men were simply trying to sell him a wild rabbit.

Amy contacted Humberside Police about the incident, thanking everyone who shared her posts.



She condemned the cruelty, saying: “It was just so wrong what they did and it could have been so much worse.”

News.title: I dodged Gaddafi’s deadly bombs and came face to face with his bloodied body – but his death was no victory for Libya
News.content:
Next

THE Kalashnikov-toting Libyan rebels beckoned me inside the giant deep-freeze and gestured at the corpse sprawled beneath a flowery blanket.

It took a few moments for my eyes to adjust from the African sunshine to the gloom inside — but the prone figure was as ­recognisable in death as in life.



Lying at my feet on a blood-sodden mattress was one of history’s most ruthless and unhinged tyrants — Colonel Muammar Gaddafi.

The Butcher of Lockerbie, known globally as Mad Dog, had met the grisly fate every despot most fears.



Hauled from a roadside storm drain, the self-styled African King of Kings was executed by a mob of his own people 15 years ago tomorrow.

It seemed to herald a new dawn for Libya, a land rich with vast oil and gas reserves.

Britain, which had skin in the game, had been instrumental in toppling Gaddafi’s brutal regime, which had long been a sponsor of terrorism.

Mad Dog had gifted tonnes of ­Semtex high explosive, AK-47s and rocket-propelled grenades to the IRA, and his government later accepted responsibility for the December 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, which killed 270.

During the 2011 Libya uprising, RAF fighter jets had targeted the ­Colonel’s forces and helped establish a no-fly zone to protect civilians.

Libya’s ragtag rebel forces did the hard yards on the ground.



Yet today Libya is a basket case ruled by two rival governments and has become a key waystation for migrants crossing the Mediterranean to Britain and Europe.

After Gaddafi was overthrown, this blighted land lapsed into years of civil war before an uneasy ceasefire was declared in 2020.

Now UN-backed Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh governs western Libya from the capital, Tripoli, while military strongman Khalifa Haftar controls the south and east.

In the west, rival tribal militias battle for control of smuggling routes and territory, unleashing sporadic bouts of violence with innocents caught in the crossfire.

Philip Ingram, 61, a former British military intelligence officer, told me: “Libya is now being exploited by organised crime gangs who are making a fortune from people smuggling. That’s feeding the warlords who are fighting each other.”



So what happened to the flames of revolution that swept through north Africa promising democracy, justice and prosperity?

At the start of the eight-month conflict, I had hitched a ride with a rebel leader heading into Libya from Egypt.

He proudly told me his car was loaded with copies of the Magna Carta and the US Declaration of Independence to help spread democracy.



The revolution was sparked in ­February 2011 when Gaddafi violently put down peaceful Arab Spring ­demonstrations.

It was par for the course for the murderous tyrant.

After seizing power in a 1969 coup, he had banned independent political parties, trade unions and a Free Press.

Inside that deep-freeze in the Libyan port of Misrata, I saw the extent of the trauma local people ­suffered under Gaddafi’s 42-year rule.

A burly man with a long beard was in the queue behind me for a glimpse of his former ruler’s cadaver. As he passed the remains, he screamed: “You’re a criminal, murderer!”



Guards were forced to pull the angry man away as he aimed a kick at the Colonel’s body.

I had my own reasons for despising Mad Dog’s regime. In March 2011, Sun photographer Dan Charity and I were forced to pull over just 650ft from the giant Ras Lanuf oil refinery after one of Gaddafi’s warplanes swooped low towards us.

That morning, a TV reporter had warned me that if the refinery was hit, everything within five square miles would be “vapourised”.

When the jet got close enough to see the sun glinting on the deadly missiles strapped to its underbelly, I knew it was time to take cover.

But my scrambled mind refused to allow my body to function and I remained rooted to the spot. Surely even Mad Dog wouldn’t blow up an oil refinery that funnelled cash into his war machine?



Then I heard Dan swearing loudly and yelling, “It’s a bomb”. A ­mushroom cloud of sand and debris began billowing just 300ft away.

I hadn’t heard a thing. I later learnt that at times of extreme fear, the brain can filter out noise and cause temporary deafness.

Wide-eyed and frantic rebel soldiers who had been even nearer the blast began bolting towards us.



One frantically screamed in broken English: “Gaddafi mad. Gaddafi murderer.” The warplane disappeared over the horizon, but its payload has left the constant shrill ringing of tinnitus in my ear to this day.

Later, we arrived at Ras Lanuf’s ramshackle hospital as a rebel fighter was bundled screaming from a battered car into the emergency ward.

Suddenly, there was a loud whistling sound followed by a huge bang. A rocket had struck just 100ft away.

Dan and I ran outside and a second missile passed over our heads and exploded into houses a stone’s throw away.

Then, a third rocket smashed into the rear of the hospital as medical staff ran for cover. Our driver, Saleh, beckoned us to our car and we sped off, dodging rebels firing anti-aircraft guns from the back of 4×4 Toyotas.



Another shell thumped into the road beside us. Speeding 90 miles along the desert highway to the oil town, Brega, rebels showed us a huge crater from an earlier Gaddafi ­air strike. Rebel Ali Ahmed, 64, told me the shellhole — which still stank of ammonia-like explosive — was just 200ft from a gas pipeline.

The fighter added: “We have to destroy this crazy man Gaddafi or he will destroy this whole country.”

Libya, population 7.5million, is a vast nation with a highway running for 1,000 miles along its Mediterranean shore that connects most of its major cities, where much of the fighting took place.

One side would claim dozens of miles of territory before their supply lines were so stretched that they were rolled back by their enemies. It went back and forth for months, leaving as many as 30,000 dead and 50,000 wounded.

The same desert battlefields saw allied forces under British General Bernard Montgomery eventually defeat the Germans ­commanded by “Desert Fox” Erwin Rommel in WWII.



The anti-Gaddafi volunteer militia comprised shopkeepers, farm labourers and office workers who rode Mad Max-style, machine-gun-decked pickups into battle.

A fellow journalist said: “To call them a rabble would be unfair on rabbles.”

Yet, I witnessed this brave civilian force — armed with a hotch-potch of AK-47s and rocket-propelled grenades — stand firm against a much better-equipped and trained army. As Gaddafi’s rockets rained down, they were willing to die to free their homeland from tyranny.



With the aid of Nato airpower, the rebels slowly began to prise apart the dictator’s vice-like grip on power. Dan and I later toured Gaddafi’s 40-room palace near Al Bayda, east of Benghazi, which had been liberated by rebels.

It was a monument to tacky dictator chic, with huge glass chandeliers, ornate wooden fireplaces and a ­luxury indoor swimming pool.

I lowered myself slowly on to one of the Colonel’s plastic-seated toilets as watching rebels looked on, smirking. Beneath the Bond villain-like lair was a cavernous bunker, reached through a 9in-thick blast door, where Gaddafi could make a last stand.

On the toilet wall of his master bedroom’s en suite was a special button above the toilet roll holder. Depicting a servant offering drinks, it appeared Mad Dog liked to summon refreshments while seated on his loo.

Nearby, I found a baggy pair of gold-braided knickerbockers that might once have been part of Gaddafi’s odd personal wardrobe.



The Colonel liked to strut around in safari suits or grandiose military outfits while attended by his 40-strong Amazonian guard of female security personnel.

Unsurprisingly, the mansion was looted from top to bottom, with farmer Bashir Sharif, 36, telling me: “Gaddafi is a vampire who sucked the blood from our country. Why shouldn’t we get something back?”

Finally, the rebels fought Mad Dog to a standstill. After a Nato air strike on his 75-vehicle convoy near his hometown of Sirte in central Libya, the King of Kings cowered in a storm drain like a rat in a sewer. Dripping blood and begging for his life, Gaddafi was dragged out by a frenzied and vengeful mob.



Beaten savagely and “sodomised with a bayonet” Libya’s supreme ruler was eventually shot dead.

Rebel Mansol Salah Hamden, 32, told me: “People were pulling and hitting him and screaming abuse. His trousers kept falling down and he kept trying to pull them up. Then a man I recognised from Benghazi shot him.”

Later, rebel fighters allowed me to hold Gaddafi’s famed golden gun and examine his leather Cuban-heeled boots, handmade in London.

In the euphoria in the days after his blood-soaked downfall, I had imagined that oil-rich Libya might become another Dubai.

Yet Britain, then led by David Cameron, and the West soon forgot about their rebel allies. Philip Ingram said: “There wasn’t a clear political end state.”



And as soon as rival rebel factions began fighting each other, the West decided, “This is getting too difficult, we’ll let them get on with it”.

Ingram explained: “Western leaders had thought, ‘We get rid of Gaddafi and we’ll get this free democratic country that will sell us lots of oil’.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“It was based on political fantasy.”

Mad Dog is long gone, but the brave rebels I watched fight for their freedom haven’t got the country they deserved.

News.title: Bake Off star arrested on child abuse charges after cops ‘find sickest indecent images on devices’
News.content:
Next

A FORMER contestant on The Great British Bake Off appeared in court charged with making indecent images of a child rated in the most serious category, The Sun can reveal.

John Mincher, who was named as the “star baker” by judge Paul Hollywood in one episode of the 2024 series, was arrested in August.



Police allegedly found two ­indecent images of a child on the 39-year-old’s devices.

Mincher appeared before a judge at Wolverhampton magistrates’ court last Friday afternoon.

He entered a not guilty plea to a single charge of making two ­indecent images of a child.



The court heard both images were classed by investigators as Category A — the most serious.

Mincher, wearing a white shirt and dark green tie, opted to stand trial before a jury.

He is to appear at Wolverhampton crown court next month.

Deputy District Judge Kate Harney told him he was accused of “incredibly serious offences”.

Mincher, of Wolverhampton, was released on conditional bail. He became a household name in the early stages of series 15 of the Channel 4 show.



The NHS worker wept with delight when celebrity chef ­Hollywood enthusiastically shook his hand and crowned him as the star baker in the first episode.

Viewers took Mincher to their hearts as he said: “I don’t want to cry, but I’m so proud of myself and they are good tears.”

Margarita-loving Mincher, who joked with Brummie show presenter Alison Hammond, bragged of attending gigs by Beyoncé and Britney Spears, posting a picture with the Toxic singer.



From loaf cakes to Viennese sandwiches, viewers watched him make a range of creations on the popular programme.

But he failed to impress the judges during bread week in ­episode three and became the third contestant to leave the show.

He said: “It’s just how it is. Because everyone is so talented, you drop the ball and then it is your time to go.”

He later boasted how being on GBBO changed his life forever.

He said: “It has given me the confidence to believe in myself and to know that I am good enough to achieve whatever I want in life.”



After Bake Off, Mincher told how he became famous and was stopped by starstruck shoppers in his local Morrisons.

He said he was going to write a book, and had become matey on GBBO with fellow West Midlander Alison.

He recalled: “I’d say there was definitely a little bond between us.



“The accent was an immediate connection and we just had a sort of shorthand. She was really supportive.”

News.title: Gypsy Rose Blanchard, 35, involved in ‘sideswipe’ car crash just weeks after death of partner Ken Urker
News.content:
ROAD CRASH Gypsy Rose Blanchard, 35, involved in ‘sideswipe’ car crash just weeks after death of partner Ken Urker







Next

GYPSY Rose Blanchard has been involved in a car crash just weeks after the death of her partner and father of her baby.

The grieving convicted murderer was involved in a collision with a male driver as she was driving home from a hair salon appointment to remove her extensions ahead of Ken Urker’s funeral.



The state police department confirmed the crash in Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana.

A Facebook user posted about the accident, writing: “2026 is wild. Just got sideswiped by Gypsy Rose.”



No one was injured in the collision and no arrests have been made.

The user continued in the comments: “She was coming back from getting her hair done in Kenner.”

In a surprising reply in the comments section, Gypsy said: “I was getting my extensions taken out because I have a funeral to go to in the coming weeks.

“Again have a blessed day.”



Accompanying the caption, the Facebook post featured images of the white car’s damage – most notably a heavily dented driver’s side door and widespread scuff marks.

The user also attached a photo of the police report arising from the crash.

No injuries were reported with the collision resulting in minor property damage, according to the cops.

According to TMZ, Gypsy was temporarily blinded by the sun at an intersection where the accident occurred.

The crash comes amid a heartbreaking period for Gypsy.



Just three weeks ago Gypsy’s partner, Ken Urker, died on October 1 — his 34th birthday.

Ken was found at his home in Raceland, Louisiana, with his final text from Gypsy left unanswered.

The Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Office report lists the incident as an “overdose,” although an official cause and manner of death have not yet been released.

The police command log says the caller reported that Ken had been “in a dark place,” failed to show up for work and had previously made threats to take his own life.

Cops found Ken lying on a bed, reportedly finding syringes and a spoon in the bathroom next to a “brown powdery substance.”



Gypsy reportedly sent Ken a happy birthday text on the day of his tragic death.

The pair shared daughter Aurora Raina Urker, who was born in December 2024.

A heartbroken Gypsy said, “Ken was an amazing father and a man who was deeply loved.”

Ken and Gypsy first connected while she was serving a prison sentence for her role in the murder of her mother, Clauddine “Dee Dee” Blanchard.

Ken wrote to Gypsy after watching the HBO documentary Mommy Dead and Dearest and later proposed during a prison visit in 2018.



Gypsy later married Ryan Anderson while still behind bars, before the couple separated following her release.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

She was released from prison in December 2023 after serving more than seven years.

Gypsy later rekindled her relationship with Ken and announced her pregnancy with Aurora.

News.title: Tel Aviv flight makes emergency landing after 'bomb threat'
News.content:
Tel Aviv flight makes emergency landing after 'bomb threat'

The plane reportedly landed in Bulgaria after an emergency was declared on board

View Image The jet was forced to make an emergency landing (Image: YAHYA ARHAB/EPA/Shutterstock)

A flight has made an emergency landing and was escorted by a fighter jet after an alleged bomb threat was reported by a crew member.

‌



‌



According to AP, the flight, which departed Tel Aviv, Israel, heading for Vienna on Sunday, was forced to land in the Bulgarian capital of Sofia after cabin crew said they received a threat.

‌



Bulgarian state television reported, citing a statement from the transportation ministry, the flight was carrying 51 passengers and six crew members at the time. It said the crew member reported the threat and an air force fighter jet escorted the plane to safety.

Article continues below

BNT reported the incident was being investigated. The airline has not been identified.

News.title: Priest dies after giant crucifix crushes him during mass
News.content:
Priest dies after giant crucifix crushes him during mass

There were audible gasps after the large wooden cross fell onto Father Sánchez Molinari as he gave a sermon inside the church - the archdiocese later confirmed he died

View 3 Images Father Sánchez Molinari was delivering a sermon when he was hit by the falling cross

A priest has died after a giant crucifix fell onto his head during a livestreamed mass.

‌



‌



Father Sánchez Molinari was crushed to death when the giant cross was fell while he delivered a sermon in Guayaquil, Ecuador, on Saturday. Tragically, the incident was being recorded and went out to those watching online.

‌



The large wooden cross mounted on the wall behind Father Molinari somehow detached and swiftly fell on him. Father Molinari collapsed onto the floor the instant the cross made contact with his head.

‌



There were audible gasps as it dawned on those present that the priest had been seriously injured. "Father, father...call an ambulance," one female member of the congregation was heard screaming.

View 3 Images The priest tragically died after being struck by the falling cross

Others present were also heard screaming as the video continued to be sent out via a livestream. It is unclear what caused the crucifix to fall from the wall.

‌



"We inform you that our brother, Father Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari, who served as parish priest of the Perpetual Help Church, central vicariate, has departed to the House of the Father to enjoy His presence and His glory," said Cardinal Archbishop Luis Cabrera Herrera.

"The Archdiocese of Guayaquil joins in prayer for the eternal rest of his soul and expresses its solidarity, affection, and love to the Redemptorist family, his relatives, and friends. May he rest in peace."

View 3 Images Father Molinari was praised by other religious leaders in Ecuador

Article continues below

The San Lorenzo parish in Vinces in the region of Los Rios, also paid respect to the late priest. A message posted on social media said: "With hope placed in God’s love and mercy, we share the news of the passing of Father Patricio Sánchez Molinari, who served with dedication and pastoral love for several years as parish priest of our Vinces community."

Father Molinari was a member of the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, founded in 1732. His duties included carrying out pastoral and missionary work in the area, reports La Prensa Grafica.

According to local outlets, the Archdiocese of Guayaquil lost two priests last year. Alfonso Aviles and Pedro Anzoategui both drowned while attempting to rescue an altar boy.

News.title: CFB Wainwright fire - latest: Four dead and dozens injured in Alberta military base disaster
News.content:
At least seven people are dead and dozens more have been left injured after an explosion and fire at CFB Wainwright, after what sources have said was an accident during a live-fire training exercise

Major fire at Canada military base: What we know so far

Four service members have been killed with dozens more seriously injured following a major fire at the Alberta military base, the Prime Minister Mark Carney has confirmed

Speaking from Ottowa on Sunday night, he said the situation is "evolving rapidly" with a formal briefing scheduled later today.

"The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," he said and confirmed flags will be flown at half-mast.

The blaze started near the CFB Wainwright Canadian Forces Base in Alberta at around 4pm local time yesterday (Saturday) and "spread rapidly due to high winds".

Canadian TV network Global News reported that the incident happened when a gas line or gas well was hit during a live-fire training exercise, citing unnamed military sources.

Dr Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton, said: "This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton and that is why we are clearing our decks and mobilizing to respond as if it was our own city.

"It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It’s a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."

Prime Minister of Canada Mark Carney said in a post on X: "Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected.

"We are working closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities. Premier Smith and I are in close contact as are our relevant ministers and officials."

News.title: Inside 'boulder-house' with huge windows and natural outdoor pool after owner finally wins planning row
News.content:
Inside 'boulder-house' with huge windows and natural outdoor pool after owner finally wins planning row

The eco-friendly property, designed to resemble natural rock formations, will feature irregularly-shaped windows, a courtyard and a natural outdoor pool

View 5 Images The 'boulder-house' will be built on Ilkley Moor

A contentious contemporary home designed to resemble stone boulders has been granted planning permission to be constructed on a nature reserve on moorland, despite facing significant opposition.

‌



‌



Plans for the eco-friendly property, set to be built on Heber's Ghyll Drive in Ilkley, near Bradford, had previously been rejected before an appeal was lodged with the Planning Inspectorate.

‌



The dwelling, designed to mimic large, irregular natural rock formations, will feature uniquely shaped windows, a courtyard and a natural outdoor pool.

‌



Ilkley Town Council recommended rejecting the planning application, submitted by businessman David Rasche, arguing it would be a "visual anomaly to the moorland".

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 5 Images Plans for the eco-friendly property had previously been rejected

‌



Ibiza airport flooded as mum found dead and torrential rain batters holiday hotspot READ MORE :

Britain's biggest warship HMS Prince of Wales sets sail for the North Atlantic READ MORE :

Councillors contended that the land formed part of several protected areas of interest, including the South Pennine Moors Site of Special Scientific Interest and the South Pennine Moors Special Protection Area and Special Area of Conservation.

Ilkley Moor also forms part of the Bradford Pennine Gateway National Nature Reserve, which is backed by Natural England.

The council further highlighted that the proposed development sat in close proximity to the Swastika Stone, a prehistoric rock carving and one of hundreds of Scheduled Ancient Monuments found on Ilkley Moor.

‌



View 5 Images The home will feature uniquely shaped windows, a courtyard and a natural outdoor pool

However, architects Shaw and Jagger maintained that the property, which will be built on green belt land, takes "cues from the surrounding rocks and escarpments synonymous with the landscape."

They added: "The building depicts a series of monolithic elements embedded in the earth as the wild, dramatic environment looms around, attempting to overcome them."

‌



The original application was turned down by Bradford Council planners on grounds of 'non-determination', meaning a verdict wasn't reached within the stipulated timeframe.

View 5 Images The building has been at the centre of a planning row

However, the decision was challenged and the developers secured approval from the Planning Inspectorate in August via the country house clause.

‌



The country house clause demands an isolated design of "exceptional quality" in that it "is truly outstanding", would "significantly enhance its immediate setting and be sensitive to the defining characteristics of the local area".

View 5 Images The property has been christened Fomorian

Neighbouring Ilkley Quarry is home to the renowned rock formation "Cow and Calf" which takes its name from its resemblance to the animals.

Article continues below

The property has been christened Fomorian - referring to a mythical race of giants in Irish folklore - and takes its inspiration from a creature called Rombald who is believed to have inhabited the moor.

News.title: Two teenagers die after crash in Suffolk with others injured
News.content:
Two teenagers die after crash in Suffolk with others injured

Emergency services including police and the East of England ambulance service attended Debenham Road, Little Stonham, to reports of a collision involving two cars

View Image Debenham Road Suffolk

Two teenagers have died after a crash in Suffolk. Emergency services including police and the East of England ambulance service raced to Debenham Road, Little Stonham, to reports of a collision involving two cars at around 10.15am today (Sunday).

‌



‌



Suffolk Constabulary said a red Peugeot 107 and a silver Volkswagen Passat were involved in the crash.

‌



A man in his late teens, who was a passenger in the Peugeot, died at the scene.

‌



The driver of the same car, a woman in her late teens, was taken to Addenbrooke’s Hospital where she died from her injuries.

The occupants of the Passat suffered minor injuries. Police, ambulance, air ambulance and fire crew all attended the scene.

Article continues below

In a statement, the Suffolk force said: “Two people have died following a serious road traffic collision in Little Stonham.

“Police are appealing for witnesses to the collision and would like to hear from motorists driving in the area who may have dash cam footage prior to the incident.”

Anyone with information is asked to contact the Joint Norfolk and Suffolk Serious Collision Investigation Unit, quoting 37/61603/26.

News.title: Three officers injured after 'lorry on wrong side of the road hits police car'
News.content:
Three officers injured after 'lorry on wrong side of the road hits police car'

The lorry was seen swerving on the wrong side of the road and failed to stop for police

View Image The force said three officers were injured (Image: PAUL GILLIS / Reach Plc)

Police officers have been injured in a horror lorry incident after the force was pursuing an alleged intoxicated driver.

The vehicle was spotted swerving on the Moygannon Road in Warrenpoint, Northern Ireland, which prompted officers to pursue the vehicle on Saturday at around 11.25pm.

The force said the report of the lorry matched that to a description of a lorry driving dangerously on the Derryleckagh Road in Newry.

The vehicle failed to stop for police and proceeded at speed on the wrong side of the road, striking a police car before continuing towards Rostrevor, Belfast Live reports.

The vehicle eventually came to a stop, and the driver made off on foot before being apprehended by police.

Chief Inspector Will Brown said in a statement: “At approximately 11.25 pm on Saturday, 17th October, police received a report of a blue articulated lorry swerving on Moygannon Road in the Warrenpoint area.

“Officers responded and located a lorry matching the description on the Derryleckagh Road, Newry.

“When signalled to stop by a police patrol vehicle, it failed to do so and a short pursuit ensued.

“The lorry was driven at speed and on the wrong side of the road before it struck a police vehicle and continued towards Rostrevor.

“Three officers inside the police vehicle sustained injuries, which are not believed to be serious at this time. The patrol car was extensively damaged.

“The lorry later came to a stop in the Water Street area of Rostrevor, where the driver, aged 36, made off on foot but was detained by officers following a short foot chase.

“He was arrested on suspicion of a number of motoring offences, including driving while disqualified, driving while unfit through drink or drugs, and dangerous driving. He remains in custody at this time as enquiries continue.

“Our officers put themselves on the front line to help keep people safe. Thankfully, no one sustained more serious injuries during this incident, including officers and other road users.

“Our investigation is underway and we are appealing to anyone who saw the lorry, or who has dash-cam footage of its movements, to contact police on 101, quoting reference number 1770 of 17/10/26.”

A report can also be submitted online using the non-emergency reporting form via https://reporting.psni.police.uk/appeals

Article continues below

Alternatively, contact Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111 or online at: http://crimestoppers-uk.org/

News.title: Hardest places for kids to grow up in England revealed as Children's Commissioner warns of 'state of emergency'
News.content:
Hardest places for kids to grow up in England revealed as Children's Commissioner warns of 'state of emergency'

A landmark Children's Commissioner report, The Childhood Lottery, uses more than 160 measures to highlight the greatest challenges faced by children across every local authority in England — and which child poverty hotspots face a 'state of emergency'

View 2 Images Middlesbrough has been one of the most challenging places to grow up in England (Image: In Pictures via Getty Images)

Middlesbrough, Hounslow and Bradford have been identified as the toughest places in England for children to grow up, according to a groundbreaking report by the Children's Commissioner.

‌



‌



The Childhood Lottery, set to be published on Monday, scrutinises the obstacles facing youngsters across every local authority in the country.

‌



Nottingham, Halton in Cheshire and Peterborough are amongst other areas where childhood is particularly challenging, while Cheshire East, Merton and Surrey have been pinpointed as the most favourable places to grow up.

‌



On Monday, Dame Rachel de Souza, England's Children's Commissioner, is expected to deliver a speech in which she will warn of a "state of emergency" in certain communities.

The Childhood Lottery, a brand new dataset and interactive map, draws together more than 160 measures to assess the greatest difficulties encountered by children.

View 2 Images England's Children's Commissioner Dame Rachel de Souza (Image: PA)

‌



60 years on from Aberfan tragedy - one in 10 families in Wales still live near high risk coal tips READ MORE :

Each area has been assigned an overall score, with rankings built upon nearly 100 metrics covering access to health and social care, education and housing, safety, opportunities for play and whether children have a say in decisions taken by local leaders.

The most challenging places to grow up have been identified as Middlesbrough, Hounslow, Bradford, Nottingham, Halton, Peterborough, Leicester, Liverpool, Sunderland and Medway.

Cheshire East, Merton, Surrey, Richmond upon Thames, Hertfordshire, Cheshire West and Chester, Haringey, Leicestershire, Central Bedfordshire and Wokingham are identified as the least challenging areas for young people.

‌



The report concludes "the postcode lottery is real" and highlights stark differences in children's experiences based on where they grow up.

It finds there are "unacceptable outcomes and levels of service delivery for children in too many parts of the country", representing a "state of emergency" in certain regions.

For instance, of the more than one million youngsters who had active referrals to children and young people's mental health services in 2024-25, the median number of days from referral to second contact in Leicester was six, compared with 118 in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight.

‌



The report revealed that all regions feature in the 25 locations where the data indicates childhood is most difficult, including Somerset in the South West, Birmingham in the West Midlands, and Hounslow in London.

In a speech on Monday, Dame Rachel is expected to urge Andy Burnham's Government to guarantee children's outcomes and life chances are not dictated by their postcode.

The commissioner is expected to say that "every single local area in England has work to do to make lives better for their children".

‌



"In some communities, these challenges amount to nothing less than a state of emergency. Not for every child. Not everywhere," she will say. "But what we see here is a litany of failure. In so many areas of the country, children are being radically failed."

Dame Rachel is anticipated to state that devolution presents "an opportunity" and is a "unique chance to remove the extreme inequality and unfairness" highlighted in the report.

She is set to say: "New powers will mean new structures, and therefore new opportunities to think about, listen to, and deliver for children.

‌



"Local areas must be provided with support from central government to raise standards for children across health, social care, housing and communities, with urgent action where it falls beyond a set level.

"This needs to be our response to the emergency."

Dame Rachel is additionally expected to put forward a series of recommendations, amongst them the appointment of a deputy mayor for children in every strategic authority.

‌



The Childhood Lottery draws on data compiled by the Children's Commissioner, together with figures from the Department for Education and 10 other public bodies.

The report is due to be launched at an event in Westminster on Monday.

Police swarm Farmfoods after woman 'loses control' and crashes into supermarket

Dramatic photographs show a car smashed through a supermarket window in Liverpool.

Police and emergency services raced to the scene of the Farmfoods supermarket on Green Lane, Stoneycroft, to reports of a crash at around 3.22pm today (Sunday, October 18).

News.title: Polanski says he will not overturn Green Party's 'Zionism is racism' motion
News.content:
Zack Polanski has said he will not overturn a motion passed by Green Party members that declared Zionism a form of racism.

The Green leader told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments, it would be party policy until 2028.

The motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month, described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".

It divided the party and sparked a major backlash from MPs, Jewish campaigners, the government and the European Green movement, with the equality watchdog writing to the party for more information on it.

The fallout from the motion overshadowed the final days of Polanski's campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, in which he came second to Labour, and threatened his leadership.

He came under criticism for not voting on the motion which was passed by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the party's 230,000 members - in Brighton earlier this month.

The motion also asserted the party's backing for "a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine", a full arms embargo on Israel and a commitment to Palestinian liberation.

Asked if he would now step in as leader to overturn it, Polanski said: "I'm not going to try to overturn it.

"At the first available opportunity, I do want to amend it - I want to move away from one state, towards saying that Israelis and Palestinians should decide that future for themselves."

He said this would not be until 2028 as "you can't [amend it] within the rules, so when you vote on something in our party conference that's then policy for two years".

Kuenssberg asked if he would therefore change the rules as leader, but Polanski said: "I think if members have made a decision, then I respect the democratic will of our members."

Former Green Party co-leader and current MP Adrian Ramsay responded by calling for action to be taken sooner.

"I don't think it's tenable for us to continue the next two years with this policy that's been adopted given the huge political distraction that it's been for our councillors across the country," he told the BBC News Channel.

"One way forward could be to have a ballot of all party members to establish very clearly where does the party as a whole stand - my view is we would see a different answer."

Polanski had previously said he would not have voted for the motion without two amendments.

The first of these would have avoided "determining there was a single democratic state", and the other would have specified that the motion should not be used to discipline Jewish Green members who attend synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.

Both of these amendments were voted down by members at the party's conference.

Green MPs, including Ellie Chowns, have called for the party's member-led decision-making procedures to be reviewed given how few people took part in the vote.

News.title: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
News.content:
Warning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicide

The few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood.

"This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says.

The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars.

"You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says.

He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune.

We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction.

Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape.

Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs.

News.title: Ending corridor care in hospitals for children a priority, says health secretary
News.content:
The health secretary has asked the NHS to draw up urgent plans to speed up ending hospital "corridor care" for children.

Yvette Cooper told the BBC there would be new standards for caring for children in A&E in England, with figures collected on corridor care by age for the first time.

She was speaking on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg where the programme highlighted the case of two-year-old Finlay Roberts who died in 2024 after spending hours in a hospital corridor before being discharged.

The health secretary has announced Â£140m to improve urgent care in England ahead of what she said would be a "more difficult" winter than usual.

The government has already pledged to end corridor care for all patients by the end of this parliament, and now Cooper has said eradicating it for children would be prioritised.

Corridor care refers to patients receiving treatment or waiting in corridors, waiting rooms or other hospital areas due to a lack of appropriate space.

The health secretary was also asked if the government would meet a key manifesto pledge that 92% of patients would start treatment within 18 weeks of booking a hospital appointment by 2029.

"That remains our manifesto commitment and of course we're going to keep working towards it," Cooper said.

Pushed further on whether the target was achievable, she replied: "The whole point about having the targets is about having something stretching that we work towards."

The 18-week target has consistently not been met for more than a decade.

Cooper said that the NHS was dealing with a number of challenges after record A&E admissions following heatwaves over the summer.

According to the latest figures for England, an estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.

On the programme the story of Finlay Roberts, was highlighted. He died after being discharged from hospital in 2024 following hours spent in an A&E corridor in north London.

Finlay's father David told the BBC the situation was a "terrible mess", with the family moved into a room with a bed before being moved back into the corridor.

"He just clung to me, as we now know, slowly dying," he said.

Liz Roberts, Finlay's mother, said corridor care "robs people of their dignity when they are at their most vulnerable". She recalled being told to administer a suppository to her son in the corridor.

Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS, saying: "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor."

News.title: Suspects hunted after police officer injured in shooting
News.content:
Detectives are searching for two suspects who fled after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre.

Nottinghamshire Police said the officer had approached two suspects in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday.

The officer is in a stable condition in hospital, where he is receiving treatment for a wound to his foot, the force added.

Detectives said a man and a woman had fled the scene and that a firearm, which could be seen within the cordon, had been found.

Angel Row remained closed by a large police scene until Sunday evening.

Police cars were parked along the road, which is lined by fast food stores and shops, and orange traffic cones had been laid out alongside items left on the road.

The cordon had also been extended to St James's Street, where an officer is standing guard.

The force said there would be a heightened police presence as the investigation continued.

News.title: Man, 80, who died in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond named
News.content:
An 80-year-old man who died in a light aircraft crash is understood to be flying instructor Ian Haggis.

He and a 16-year-old boy died when their plane came down near Loch Lomond. The teenager's identity has not been released.

The pair had flown out from Glasgow Airport at 16:17 and stopped transmitting at 16:37, a few miles north east of the village of Drymen near Stirling.

Emergency services were called to the crash at about 16:45 on Friday.

Both of them were pronounced dead at the scene.

Temporary airspace restrictions are currently in place over the area while the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) carries out its inquiries.

Old Drymen Road, near the scene of the crash, remains closed with vehicles being turned around and hillwalkers rerouted.

News.title: Search for Amelia Earhart's plane resumes after stormy weather
News.content:
A search for the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote island in the Pacific Ocean has resumed after severe weather caused researchers to stop for several days.

A team has travelled to Nikumaroro Island, part of Kiribati, hoping to solve the mystery of the famed aviator's disappearance by investigating the so-called Taraia Object, spotted in the atoll's lagoon in aerial imagery.

The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937, spawning decades of speculation about her fate.

Rough seas and strong winds forced the team to remain on their research vessel for three days, until the weather cleared on Sunday.

"We are finally getting off the ship and able to land on Nikumaroro," Sirisha Bandla, a technology specialist who is part of the expedition, said in a video update from the deck of the Marin Mainiku.

The researchers arrived at the uninhabited atoll last week and began an underwater survey of the area of interest.

But the weather - powered by strong El NiÃ±o conditions in the Pacific - has so far prevented them from beginning a second of three phases, in which underwater objects will be probed to determine their depth and sediment will be dredged.

News.title: Photos show luxury boat with 50m pool and water slides near Kim Jong Un's summer retreat
News.content:
An 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year.

What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end.

After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula.

This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family.

It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC.

The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size.

News.title: There's a crackdown on sports piracy but is it already out of control?
News.content:
"Football's Gone Round the Spend!" screamed The People newspaper one Sunday in July 1995. It reported breathlessly that three clubs between them were set to pay out more than Â£20m on new players.

The highlight that summer was the transfer of Stan Collymore from Nottingham Forest to Liverpool for a British record fee of Â£8.5m.

That number might not seem too impressive today, in an age when Â£100m transfers are almost commonplace. But at the time it was seismic stuff, and it symbolised the conversion of football from sport into big business.

All of this had been made possible in the early 1990s by the creation of the Premier League, and its initial TV deal with the broadcaster Sky, which paid more than Â£300m for five years of rights. The agreement put live top-tier football behind a TV paywall for the first time.

It was a lucrative model, one that other leading championships in motorsport, rugby, golf and cricket would later seek to replicate.

But now, that model is coming under pressure. Piracy has become endemic in British sports: around half of sports fans now admit to using what they might euphemistically call "alternative" means to watch paywalled material, according to the consultancy Ampere Analysis.

News.title: NHS data breaches a disgrace, health secretary says
News.content:
NHS staff accessing the medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims and possible breaches over a man killed by a tiger is a "disgrace", the health secretary has said.

Speaking to the BBC, Yvette Cooper said she expected action to be taken against staff who had breached NHS data and privacy standards.

Her comments came after Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust confirmed it had sacked a total of 15 members of staff and Yorkshire Ambulance Service said William Chapman's medical records may have been accessed illegitimately.

Dr Manjeet Shehmar, NUH medical director, previously said there was "simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason".

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Cooper said "there's got to be proper respect for patients" from NHS staff.

"Let me be really clear about this," she said. "There are proper data and privacy standards across the NHS."

Students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

NUH said in May that it had sacked 11 members of staff for inappropriately accessing the victims' medical records, and had informed the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and Nottinghamshire Police of the investigation.

At the time, the ICO told the BBC it would "assess any evidence provided by the trust in due course and consider our next steps", while police said there was "no criminal investigation".

In its update about further dismissals on Friday, NUH said it had taken action against "doctors, nurses, registered healthcare professionals and other staff", and that independent regulators such as the Nursing and Midwifery Council and General Medical Council, the ICO and Nottinghamshire Police had been informed.

NUH added a new system, currently under testing, was being implemented to protect patient records in future and alert the trust to potential breaches.

News.title: Man and woman in their late teens die in collision
News.content:
Two people in their late teens died in a collision involving two cars, Suffolk Police said.

Officers were first called by the ambulance service to Debenham Road near Little Stonham at 10:15 BST.

Fire crews and the air ambulance were also called to the incident that involved a red Peugeot 107 and a silver Volkswagen Passat.

Police said a male passenger in the Peugeot died at the scene. The female driver was taken to Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge by land ambulance, but has since died as a result of her injuries.

The occupants of the Passat suffered minor injuries, the police spokesperson added.

The road was expected to reopen later in the evening.
