Sports.title: Fabio Wardley reveals why he wanted to get straight back into the ring with Daniel Dubois as he defends his team after they came under fire for not pulling him out earlier in first defeat
Sports.content:
Fabio Wardley reveals why he wanted to get straight back into the ring with Daniel Dubois as he defends his team after they came under fire for not pulling him out earlier in first defeat

Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon.

Not, at least, according to those who watched him endure 11 gruelling rounds against Daniel Dubois in Manchester in May. Not according to those who questioned whether his corner should have pulled him out earlier, as his face became increasingly battered and his right eye swelled shut. And certainly not according to those who believe the punishment he absorbed makes a rematch a risk too far.

But Wardley has never been one to follow the script.

When the 31-year-old first faced Dubois, 29, he did so as the WBO heavyweight champion. He dropped his opponent twice in the opening three rounds, threatening to produce one of the biggest victories of his career before Dubois fought his way back into the contest and eventually stopped him in the 11th.

Now, with the WBO title back on the line, Wardley finds himself in more familiar territory in one respect: he is the challenger, the underdog and the man many expect to lose again.

And, as he explains when we sit down ahead of the rematch, he rather likes it that way.

Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon but he's never one to follow the script

Dubois (right) and Wardley (left) will go toe-to-toe for a second time on Saturday evening

'It's been the staple of my career for as long as I can remember, well, since I started. It has been the main focal point. After the first five or six fights, when I started to step up the level, even incrementally, even slightly, people were saying I was going to lose, that it was a step too far, and all the rest of it. It's all the stuff everyone's heard before,' he says.

'It's a side of the coin I'm very much used to, and the pressure's off. I'm the challenger here. I'm expected to lose and expected to go even quicker, and Daniel's supposed to put on a better performance, and all the rest of it. So there's no pressure on me. There's nothing on my shoulders.'

It is a strikingly relaxed assessment from a fighter preparing to walk back into the ring with the man who inflicted the first defeat of his professional career.

Wardley, however, insists that defeat has done little to change him. He is not pretending that losing a world title is enjoyable, but nor does he regard it as a defining moment in his life.

'Not a lot has changed. I'm not that different. Don't get me wrong, a loss is never fun. It's never nice, it's never enjoyable. But for me, at least, it wasn't soul-crushing or devastating, and it hasn't had any effect on me as a person, my character or anything else.

'The job’s the job, the game’s the game. From the very beginning, I’ve accepted that getting through heavyweight boxing unscathed isn’t guaranteed, especially given the way I compete at the highest level and my desire to take on the biggest challengers out there.

'I think people forget that the first time around, I picked Daniel. I asked for that fight because I looked at the crop of heavyweights and thought, "That's the best one to challenge myself against."

'Knowing that about myself, and knowing that's my angle, was I ever going to get through this undefeated like Floyd Mayweather? Probably not. So, look, it comes how it comes. But as long as I'm happy with myself in terms of the performances, that I've given my all and all the rest of it, I can sleep at night.'

Their first fight in May was a brutal affair, with the contest being stopped in the 11th round

Wardley took a lot of punishment in the latter rounds of their first encounter in May (above)

It is that willingness to put himself in the firing line which has made Wardley such a compelling heavyweight. His fights are rarely short on drama, and the first meeting with Dubois was no exception. He started at a blistering pace, dropping DDD in the opening 10 seconds, only for the momentum to swing as the punishment began to accumulate.

By the later rounds, Wardley was absorbing heavy shots and fighting through considerable damage. His condition between rounds prompted questions about whether the contest should have been stopped sooner, with particular scrutiny falling on his corner for allowing him out ahead of the 10th.

Wardley disagrees with the suggestion that his team failed him. He regards the people around him as family and trusts them to put his welfare first, even when the decisions they make are questioned from the outside.

He is equally dismissive of the noise surrounding the timing of the rematch, arguing that those watching from the outside cannot know the full picture of his recovery. His position is that he and his team are best placed to judge the damage he sustained and whether he is ready to fight again.

For Wardley, the prospect of another brutal encounter is not something he has brushed aside or refused to think about. It is a reality he has had to confront with himself, knowing that by stepping back into the ring with Dubois, he is willingly putting himself in a position where he could once again withstand a frightening amount of punishment.

It is a remarkable thought process: to acknowledge the possibility of enduring the same damage all over again, to ask himself whether he is prepared to go through it, and then to make peace with the answer before he has even thrown a punch.

'It's a level of early acceptance. The second I triggered the rematch clause, even before that, I had to have a conversation with myself and ask, "This could go the exact same way. Are you ready for that? Are you OK with that?"

'As long as the answer is yes from me to me, then cool, let's go. But by now, it's nowhere near my brain as a question mark or something I'm having to deal with, battle with or anything else. It's already been ticked off, boxed and put away. It is what it is.'

Wardley was checked by the doctor and spoken to by the referee multiple times in the fight

As a result, Dubois became a two-time heavyweight champion and will now defend his belt

There is little melodrama in his delivery. When the possibility of going through the same ordeal again is put to him, Wardley does not attempt to dress it up as fearlessness or pretend that the risks do not exist.

'It's an acceptance of the game and the sport we got into, and especially the way I fight as well,' he says.

That approach is perhaps best illustrated by what goes through his mind when he is taking punishment in the ring. Wardley is not a heavyweight who is inclined to retreat quietly after being caught cleanly. His instinct is to make sure his opponent knows there will be a response.

'Especially in those moments, it's about getting back at them. All right, you took one… let your hands go. Don't just let them get away with it for free. At least let them know. Let them have it in their brain that if they get off a few shots, I'm not just going to take them, run away and roll over.'

It is a mindset that makes for spectacular viewing, but one which also places enormous demands on a fighter's corner.

Wardley describes those 60 seconds between rounds as almost too precious to waste on anything other than the information he needs to continue. With the clock ticking and another round approaching, he wants tactical instruction rather than an emotional check-in.

'No, I think it's 90 per cent tactical, 10 per cent everything else, because in those moments, compassion doesn't need to come into it. That's not where the compassion needs to be.

'Those 60 seconds are so precious, such a small moment. It feels like a click. It feels like nothing. It feels like it's done and gone so quickly that you're on your stool, you're off your stool and the next round has started.

'In that time, you need to get the information. It's not time for, "Oh, a little rub on the shoulder. Are you doing OK, Fab? Is everything alright? Are you going to be alright, mate? Do you want me to dab your face a bit?" No. Let me know what I need to know. Let's get this going again.'

Wardley knows that the rematch will be gruelling. He knows his durability will continue to be questioned. But he also knows why he wanted the first fight in the first place.

For Wardley, the pursuit of the biggest challenges has always mattered more than protecting an unbeaten record. Defeat by Dubois has not changed that. He is back because in his mind, the possibility of the same ending has already been accepted and because it’s a risk worth taking.

Sports.title: Daniel Dubois' second clash with Fabio Wardley promises to be even MORE brutal than their first, writes JEFF POWELL MBE - as May's champion vows to 'bash and smash' his rival
Sports.content:
Even the most hardened boxing fans can be taken aback by the depths of brutality which two men are capable of inflicting on each other. Especially the heavyweights.

So it was on the Saturday night this May when Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley battered hell's bells out of each other in Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena. Wardley dropped his world title challenger twice in the first three rounds. Just 28 seconds into the 11th, Dubois had to be pulled off the champion he had reduced to a bleeding and battered but still-standing wreck.

We mere mortals can only ask: How on earth do they do it? ‘We’re fighters,’ says Dubois. ‘Honoured to share a ring with him.’

‘Born to do it,’ says Wardley, who found out that truth of himself when he tried white collar boxing. ‘Love being in with such a great fighter.’

What in heaven goes through their minds at the prospect of doing it again, as they are on Saturday night at the O2? Do they not realise the danger this sledgehammer head-banging presents to their health?

Prepare yourselves, dear gentle readers, for this stunning answer from Dubois: ‘Dementia? If you’re talking about dementia, no point worrying. We’ve probably got it already.’

Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley have both spoken of their love for stepping into the ring with one another ahead of their rematch on Saturday

But as brutal as their meeting in May was, tomorrow night's clash at the O2 has been teased as even bloodier

A chilling insight, this, into the mentality of men who fight not only for a living but for the lust for glory, the thrill of battle, the roar of the crowd, the smell of the greasepaint, the glare of the lights and not least their manly pride.

And on nights like this, for a world championship. This time the WBO belt which Dubois ripped from Wardley’s fairy-tale grasp five months ago.

What, no nerves? ‘I live with the chaos,’ says Dubois. ‘Chaos all day every day and specially on the night. I love the fear. It gives me the power. I hold the chaos in until it’s at its peak when the first bell goes. Then it explodes as I let it out. Which brings power and clarity.’

Wardley comes not only from his different background in commerce but also with an opposite mindset. He says: ‘No one wants to lose a world title but if it has to be, then what really matters is how it happens.

‘I feel more relaxed and confident having proved I can engage a top-level fighter in a great fight, which everyone expected me to lose easily. Calm makes me better.’

That and the lessons he learned in the five months since his gladiatorial — and only — defeat thus far. ‘We’ve studied every critical moment of the first fight,’ he says. ‘And I’ve adapted where necessary. Had to because I have more to work on than Daniel with all his experience.

‘But we’ve not only looked at me. We’ve looked at him. He’s not as adaptable as me. He’s not suddenly going to become light-footed and free moving. I’ll give him something different.’

To which Dubois says: ‘I’ll give him another beating. Bash him up. Smash him worse than before. And quicker. We didn’t know quite what he might do in the first fight. Now I know what to expect.

‘I also know that he’s not good enough to adapt. I’m his daddy now.’ That is clarity, Dubois style. He also discounts those two knock-downs. As a man who has been a slow starter at times — although not when he demolished Anthony Joshua from the get-go — he says: ‘Things happen in boxing. You can get caught. But I also know now that he doesn’t have the power. No real power.’

Wardley, for his part, denies that he was as badly hurt as it appeared in fight one. Their respective trainers have disagreed about the 11th-hour stoppage. Dubois’ coach Don Charles says the towel should have been thrown in earlier.

Wardley supports his man Ben Davison’s assertion that he was still in the fight throwing punches, saying: ‘The optics looked bad, what with the blood and the bruising and the punches. But I trust my team to take care of me. Trust them with my life.

‘A lot of the punches were glancing and in the 10th round I shook him with an uppercut. If the big right that followed had connected cleanly we might have had a different ending.’

This man who escaped office drudgery to chase his dream hopes to go on to meet the December winner of Joshua v Tyson Fury. Dubois fancies some of that big money but is also looking beyond, to unifying all the other world titles vacated by Oleksandr Usyk.

Will the ending on Saturday be different from Wardley v Dubois One? Probably not. Dynamite Dan likely added the more valuable knowledge to his wider experience and has never looked this bullish before a fight.

What we do know for sure is that this pair will give us another thriller.

Sports.title: Following decades of US domination, British heavyweight boxing is on top - after Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley and Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua, there are Brit-bashes galore waiting to be made, writes JEFF POWELL MBE
Sports.content:
In the small hours of May 16, 1955 my father woke me in the darkness, lit a candle in the scullery, plugged in his old crystal radio set and told me to listen to a world heavyweight title fight taking place in San Francisco.

Don Cockell of Balham, south London, was challenging Rocky Marciano of Brockton, Massachusetts, for the world heavyweight championship. Most of the sound which came whistling through the static was that of Marciano’s eight-ounce gloves thudding into Cockell’s head and body.

Marciano kept knocking down Cockell, who kept getting up. Until the ninth round, when Rocky nailed him to the canvas for good with a booming right which seemingly connected while he was on his knees.

When the BBC radio commentator put that question to the champ, Marciano replied: ‘Britain can be proud of her boy Don Cockell.’

Jack Powell, whose toughness had carried him through the landings and trenches of the Second World War as well as countless fights inside and outside the ring, slammed his fist on the kitchen table and said: ‘As if keeping beating us ain’t enough, they have to bloody patronise us.’

I was 13. Not until I was 50 – and Marciano had long since become the only heavyweight champ to retire undefeated – would Lennox Lewis end our century-long wait for a successor to Bob Fitzsimmons.

Lennox Lewis (pictured) ended Great Britain's wait for a successor to Bob Fitzsimmons as the United States dominated the heavyweight scene

American stars such as George Foreman (left) and Muhammad Ali (right) dominated the previous era

That eternity was flooded with such revered Americans as Jack Johnson, Jack Dempsey, Joe Louis, Floyd Patterson, Sonny Liston, Muhammad Ali, Joe Frazier, George Foreman, Mike Tyson, Larry Holmes and Evander Holyfield.

The golden age of heavyweight boxing gave us the Fight of the Century and the Thrilla in Manila – both between Ali and Frazier – the Rumble in the Jungle with Ali and Foreman, the Upset of the Century by Buster Douglas over Tyson, Dempsey v Gene Tunney, Louis v both Max Schmeling and Jersey Joe Walcott and Ali’s slaying of the Liston monster. That was the time when the Star Spangled Banner flew over America’s mocking of ‘Britain’s Horizontal Heavyweights.’

Henry Cooper remained perpendicular against The Greatest of them all but there was scant recognition over the water of how he knocked Ali down and almost out with the left hook renowned as ‘Enery’s ‘Ammer’ in the first of two stadium fights he lost to his propensity to suffer cuts.

So, oh, how we gloated when we watched Riddick Bowe dump his WBC belt in a London dustbin rather than fight Lewis, who was thereby elevated to his first title by decree. Rejoiced when Lennox validated his title by beating Oliver McCall in September 1995. Acclaimed Lenny the Lion when he became our only three-time world heavyweight champion.

We breathed a huge sigh of relief when Frank Bruno beat McCall at an emotional Wembley, finally to become world champion. Just as we fretted for him when he genuflected umpteen times on his way to the Las Vegas ring for a second crushing by Tyson and the loss of his crown.

Even so, British heavyweight boxing was transitioning from famine to feast. The US can boast 53 champions all time in the prize-ring’s marquee division. All the way back to the immortal John L Sullivan in the late 1880s. But the UK has accelerated from one active heavyweight champion in 2003 – Lewis when he bloodied and defeated Vitali Kliltschko – to a running total of 11 today if you delete the asterisks against Michael Bent, Herbie Hide and Henry Akinwande who wore the WBO belt before that organisation was fully recognised.

David Haye built on the Lewis legacy when he bamboozled Russia’s 7ft giant Nikolai Valuev and thereby emulated Holyfield’s feat of an undisputed cruiserweight king becoming world heavyweight champion.

The Russo-Ukraine brothers Klitschko broke the US domination but then both Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua followed that Lewis victory over Vitali by vanquishing Wladimir.

British heavyweight boxing was transitioning from famine to feast, which has included the likes of Tyson Fury (left) and Anthony Joshua (right)

Britannia’s Rule was stunningly interrupted by Oleksandr Usyk’s revival of the Kyiv Conspiracy with two dazzling victories apiece over the Gypsy King and AJ, followed by another double over their heir apparent Daniel Dubois.

Oleksandr The Great’s abrupt relinquishing of all the belts opened the gateway to an immediate UK renaissance. One in which it is not Americans but Brits fighting each other for the glittering prizes.

This Saturday at the O2, Dubois and the amazingly reconstructed white-collar boxer Fabio Wardley reprise their blood and thunder war for the now-respected WBO title. This time with Dynamite Daniel as the champion.

The winner is likely to go on to meet in the not-too-distant future whoever prevails in the over-long awaited settlement between Fury and Joshua - which, belatedly though it comes in December, is so full of fascination that it has sold ticket at prices higher than the gross national product of some third-world countries.

By then Moses Itauma should have recovered from the drastic loss of stamina – and a blown IBF title shot against Croatia’s Filip Hrgovic – to resume leadership of the next generation. German WBC champion Agit Kabayel will soon be in all those crosshairs.

With all the above except Joshua in Frank Warren’s stable there are more Brit-bashes galore waiting to be made. With only one big guy of promise, Jared Anderson, to be seen on the western horizon.

And to think Americans used to belittle their last heavyweight champion of note Deontay Wilder as ‘just a puncher’.

The biggest puncher since Iron Mike, as it happens. How they must be wishing over there that Fury had not ended the Bronze Bomber’s five-year run of knockouts in the murderous final act of their epic trilogy.

Daniel Dubois (left) and Fabio Wardley (right) will face off this weekend with more Brit-bashes galore waiting to be made

Throughout America’s glorious boxing history the world heavyweight champion was the symbol of their national manhood. Today they lay no claim to any of the alphabelts.

There are extraneous factors at work. The majority of strapping young American athletes - be they graduating from college or seeking ways out of the projects - are taking to basketball, their version of football and baseball, rather than take a headbashing in the ring on the off-chance of making their fortunes.

US boxing is down to pinning its hopes on a brash young Mexican-American welterweight Ryan Garcia - on the back of his destruction of a humiliated Conor Benn. All while the Blue Riband of the ring is hoisted this side of the pond.

Not so Yankee-Doodle-Dandy now, gentlemen.

Sports.title: 'You cannot keep fighting gung-ho like that': Daniel Dubois' trainer warns Fabio Wardley is risking his boxing future - and says team put his health at risk by letting him battle on in first bout
Sports.content:
Daniel Dubois' trainer Don Charles believes Fabio Wardley is already feeling the effects of the punishment he absorbed in their brutal first encounter, as he suggested the former heavyweight champion's corner did him a 'disservice' by allowing their fight to continue for so long.

Wardley and Dubois produced a gruelling contest in Manchester last May, with the fight eventually stopped in the 11th round after the former world champion had subjected his opponent to a sustained assault in the latter rounds.

Wardley's remarkable resilience was a defining feature of the contest, but Charles believes the damage he endured could already be catching up with him ahead of their highly anticipated rematch this Saturday.

The veteran trainer also questioned whether Wardley's team should have intervened sooner, suggesting that their hope of seeing the champion produce another fight-changing punch may have come at a cost to his health.

'They let Fabio down a little bit, in my opinion, for his health,' Charles said.

'Being the champion, being a guy who has done it previously and is able to pull out a shot at any point during the fight, whether early or late, he has got that in him.

Daniel Dubois' trainer Don Charles believes Fabio Wardley is already feeling the effects of the punishment he absorbed in their brutal first encounter

Dubois (right) and Wardley (left) will go toe-to-toe for a second time on Saturday evening

Their first fight in May was a brutal affair, with the contest being stopped in the 11th round

'So perhaps the team were thinking, 'Maybe he just needs that one punch', because he has done it in the past. But there comes a point where you have to do the sensible thing.

'A couple of days after the fight, I relaxed and watched it back. Oh my God, it was really bad, in my opinion.

'Again, it is their decision. There is the referee there and there are the doctors. But I think they let Fabio down a little bit, in my opinion, for his health.'

Charles stressed that his focus during the fight had been entirely on Dubois, meaning he had not fully appreciated the extent of Wardley's punishment until he watched the contest back afterwards.

His comments come amid renewed scrutiny of the first fight and the decision to allow Wardley to continue into the championship rounds, although the man from Ipswich has defended his corner against suggestions they got it wrong.

Wardley regards the people around him as family and trusts them to put his welfare first, even when the decisions they make are questioned from the outside.

Charles believes the physical demands of Wardley's all-action style could have consequences beyond a single night in the ring, arguing that the damage accumulated in such gruelling contests can gradually take its toll.

'I think he is already noticing the wear and tear, from an observational point of view,' Charles said.

Charles suggested the former heavyweight champion's corner did him a 'disservice' by allowing their fight to continue for so long

Dubois has just signed a six-figure deal brokered by NVA SEG Talent Group to become the global ambassador for British performance and lifestyle brand Resonance Energy Wear

'It is entertaining for the public, granted, but you cannot have a very long career fighting like that. It catches up with you. It really does, and it chips away at you.

'You cannot keep fighting gung-ho like that. It is very entertaining, like I said, but you really have to look at the bigger picture.'

Charles believes Dubois will approach the return bout with greater discipline after being caught off guard in their initial meeting and warns the rematch could end early despite preparing for the possibility of another prolonged battle.

'What you are going to see is a more disciplined display and more alertness,' he said.

'Obviously, we got caught off guard last time, so we have rectified that. This time, it is going to be a more disciplined, more dynamic and more technical performance.

'We have trained as if this were the olden days, when you boxed up to 15 rounds. If this fight has to go 15 rounds to get a victory, 15 rounds it is.

'This fight could end in round one, or it could end in round 12 or 15. It needs to be.'

One of Charles's biggest questions ahead of the rematch concerns how Wardley will respond when Dubois lands cleanly, particularly if DDD can recreate some of the punishing moments from their first encounter.

Charles believes Dubois will approach the return bout with greater discipline after being caught off guard in their initial meeting and warns the rematch could end early

Charles believes the physical demands of Wardley's all-action style could have consequences beyond a single night, arguing that the damage accumulated can gradually take its toll

The expert trainer suggested that the memories of that night could return once Wardley begins absorbing shots again, although he acknowledged the 31-year-old's extraordinary toughness.

'Fabio is made of something else. He is made of steel, that man, the amount of punishment he took and kept taking,' Charles said.

'But it is our duty to recall those entries, to remind him of the pain he felt last May in Manchester.

'As soon as that bell rings, our duty is to recall that pain. If he has forgotten it, Daniel will remind him in that ring: 'This is what you were feeling.'

'He is a human being like you and I. Once he starts feeling that unbearable pain, the rest is up to him and his team, and what they do under the referee's supervision.'

Sports.title: Floyd Mayweather gushes over Donald Trump after President praises boxer's 'good looks' at Republican rally
Sports.content:
Floyd Mayweather gushed over Donald Trump on stage in Arizona - after the President praised the boxer's good looks.

Mayweather flew on Air Force One to Bullhead City, Arizona for a campaign rally held to support Republican candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

The undefeated fighter was the latest sports star to join Trump on the campaign trail and drew high praise as he was introduced.

'One of the greatest fighters in boxing history,' Trump said, calling Mayweather an 'unbelievable defensive fighter.'

'That's why he looks so good,' Trump continued, before adding as he walked up to the stage: 'Look at this guy, he looks so good. Who would believe he's a fighter? He looks so good! He doesn't have a mark!'

And the high praise was reciprocated, as Mayweather declared: 'We couldn't have chosen a better president twice than Donald Trump.'

Donald Trump welcomed boxer Floyd Mayweather to the stage in Bullhead City, Arizona

Trump praised Mayweather's good looks as he welcomed him to the stage at the rally

Mayweather delivered praise of Trump as he called America the 'greatest country in the world'

Mayweather had started his address by telling the crowd: 'America is the greatest country in the world. If I died and came back a million times, I would always choose America.

'It was great to represent this country in the 1996 Olympic Games,' Mayweather said. 'To go out there and represent the red, white, and blue.'

He then turned his praise to Trump before adding: 'So it's all about keeping this country strong, sticking together, and believing in one another. America is the greatest country in the world. Thank you.'

Mayweather, 49, a Vegas native, happens to have strong business ties in Arizona.

Dennis Rodman, Mike Tyson, Jake Paul, Roger Clemens and Jon Gruden have all made appearances at recent rallies in support of Trump.

Mayweather has long been an outspoken supporter of Trump, hailing him the 'best president in US history' last year.

He attended Trump's first inauguration as president and supported him throughout his first term in the Oval Office.

Policy-wise, Mayweather and Trump have been aligned on a few issues, including in the Middle East. Mayweather is a staunch supporter of Israel and donated $1million to the United Hatzalah of Israel in 2024.

Mayweather flew to the event on Air Force One earlier in the day to travel to the event

Mayweather has been aligned with Trump on several issues and been a public supporter

Mayweather is the latest sports star to be brought in by Trump on the midterms campaign trail

Join the discussion What do you think motivates celebrities like Mayweather to publicly align themselves with political figures?

'We had Trump before, we didn't appreciate him,' Mayweather told Fox Business in February of last year. 'I think Trump is a great president, actually he's the best president in my eyes, he's the best president we've ever had. Great business man and that's what it's about.'

'Trump has done an amazing job and a lot of people around America are upset. But no matter who goes into the White House, we're always upset. And I think Trump is the man for the job, he's the best president in my eyes.'

Mayweather's fellow boxing icon Tyson also joined Trump on the Presidential aircraft last week, making the journey from the White House to Syracuse, New York.

During his speech at the rally, Trump spotted Tyson in the crowd and invited the former boxing champion on stage.

'I think we have to call him up, Mike Tyson, will you get up here?' Trump said.

As the President's athletic guest of the day, Tyson praised Trump in front of the Syracuse crowd, thanking him during a brief moment on stage.

'Thank you, thank you very much. I'm just happy to be up here with my president, President Trump. There's no way in the world I would ever be here if it wasn't for a president like Donald Trump,' Tyson said.

Trump was also joined by NBA icon Rodman in Durant, Oklahoma, and former NFL coach Gruden and influencer-turned-boxer Paul in Youngstown, Ohio.

He announced his intention to award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to MLB legend Clemens when the former pitcher joined him at a rally in San Antonio, Texas.

Sports.title: Mercedes explains why its upgrade made its F1 car harder to drive
Sports.content:
If Mercedes left Sepang with more questions than answers, the Singapore Grand Prix weekend finally provided the engineering team with the first real clues to unlocking their new package. Although it was a sprint weekend, the reopening of parc ferme and the decision to split configurations between the two drivers offered a valuable opportunity to experiment and gather critical data.

The data will be analysed during the break ahead of Austin, with one key goal: understanding exactly why the package introduced in Malaysia hasn’t properly worked as expected, despite the potential to extract. Mercedes has now confirmed a crucial piece of the puzzle, explaining that the upgrades shifted the car's aerodynamic balance, making the W17 significantly more difficult to drive.

While the new package achieved its primary objective of increasing overall downforce, as shown through Malaysia’s high-speed sections, it also exposed an unexpected weakness. The upgrades shifted the W17’s aerodynamic balance too far forward, unsettling the car and significantly narrowing its operating window.

"I think, if you wanted to just take the first order of the problem, we wanted to deliver more performance with more downforce. And we have measured more downforce on the car," explained Mercedes deputy technical director Simone Resta on the team's Nu Silver Arrows Radio Show podcast.

"Unfortunately, it's not a black and white problem. It's not zero one. It's a very grey environment with multiple variables. And I think we delivered the downforce but perhaps we haven't delivered the same level of downforce in every single running point of the car on the track. And that is then starting to alter a little bit the balance of the car in the condition, and then the driver has to adapt."

The balance has shifted toward the front-end

To some extent, a shift in balance was to be expected given the extent of the floor and sidepod changes introduced in Sepang. The real issue, however, was that while Mercedes successfully unlocked the additional downforce it had been targeting, those gains were not delivered consistently across the full range of operating conditions, contrary to expectations. As a result, the engineers struggled more than usual to identify a set-up capable of extracting the full potential of the updated W17.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

“There are a few things we need to sort out, especially because we tend to see a car with more balance than before. Stronger front, even perhaps a bit more than we expected. So therefore, you need to re-centre the window we operate the car. And it's taking some time,” added Resta, emphasising that there is still untapped potential in the new specification.

This means Mercedes now has to approach both set-up and driving requirements differently to unlock the car's potential, while the W17 has become less forgiving and harder to drive when operating outside its ideal window. There is more performance to unlock, but accessing it consistently has become a far more complex task and the shift in balance has also made the car harder to drive.

During the first half of the season, one of the W17's strengths was its stable rear end, particularly in traction-limited situations. That strength often made Mercedes competitive and the benchmark at stop-and-go tracks, not only thanks to its power unit but also because of its ability to put power down effectively on corner exit from low-speed corners.

The rear is less stable under braking and this change the approach

However, the balance shift has also forced changes in driving technique. Antonelli, in particular, has always favoured an aggressive approach to corner entry, aiming to minimise the distance through the corner, gain time at the apex and getting back on the throttle as early as possible.

That approach worked brilliantly up to this point, partly because the previous specification provided a stable rear end that remained settled under braking, allowing him to attack corner entry. The new package, however, changed some of the W17's key characteristics and that stability.

As a result, the drivers have had to adapt their approach both at turn-in and through the mid-corner phase. Unsurprisingly, Antonelli reported persistent mid-corner understeer during both the Malaysia and Singapore weekends, stemming from an inability to rotate the car as cleanly as he would like on entry. That compromised his line through the apex and delayed throttle application on corner exit.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

A narrower window, but there is more potential to extract

To compensate for that understeer, drivers are left with two choices: increase steering input, which places additional load on the front tyres, or use the throttle to rotate the car at mid-corner, something that was frequently visible in Sepang. However, on a hot and abrasive track, however, the latter approach comes at a cost, as it accelerates rear tyre overheating and degradation. As a result, the updated W17 struggled considerably more than usual in Sepang's low-speed corners.

It therefore came as little surprise that, once parc ferme restrictions were lifted after the sprint race in Singapore, Mercedes shifted towards a significantly different set-up compared to the first part of the weekend. The direction chosen for qualifying and the race ultimately paid off, trying to find a more stable rear end.

Early indications of this had already emerged during the wet sprint: “The car was overbalanced initially, quite oversteer-y, difficult to drive. As the front tyres wore down, suddenly we found a much happier car balance. And then from there, Kimi suddenly was popping up with green and purple sectors and starting to match the pace of the leaders," said deputy team principal Bradley Lord.

The improvement was also evident on the timing sheets. Despite slower track conditions on Saturday, Antonelli was one of only two drivers in the top 10, alongside Hamilton, to improve on his Friday qualifying time. Most of that gain was found in sector two, the most technical part of the lap, where the set-up changes gave him the confidence to push harder and unlock more of the updated W17's potential.

For Austin, Mercedes will re-introduce the front wing tested during Singapore practice, aiming to recalibrate the package, widen the operating window, and extract the potential from the car the car: "We just have to re-centre the window. We just have to rework mechanically the car, trying to tweak a few of the characteristics that we're seeing with these packets on the car,” said Resta.

Sports.title: The maths behind when Mercedes could become F1 world champions in 2026
Sports.content:
The 2026 Formula 1 season has seen Mercedes return to its dominant past as it is on course to claim its first double championship victory since the COVID-struck 2020 campaign.

Kimi Antonelli and George Russell top the drivers’ standings with the former holding a 102-point advantage, while Mercedes leads second-placed Ferrari by 134 points in the constructors’ table.

It is thanks to 11 victories in 17 grands prix that the Silver Arrows is in this position at the start of the new regulations, most of those wins coming early on as rivals subsequently closed the gap.

Regardless, Mercedes is set for its first drivers’ title since 2020 after a period of Max Verstappen domination and a crown for Lando Norris, with it being a similar story in the constructors.

The Silver Arrows last won that championship in 2021 before Red Bull and McLaren overtook it during the ground-effect era, but with six rounds remaining in 2026, Mercedes is set for glory.

Antonelli can clinch his maiden world title next time out in Austin, though is most likely going to do it a week later in Mexico, whereas Mercedes may have to wait a little longer to win the teams’ crown.

How many teams can still win the F1 2026 world title?

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: James Sutton / LAT Images via Getty Images

There are 258 points left on offer in the 2026 F1 world constructors’ championship table, provided Qatar and Abu Dhabi go ahead amid the ongoing Middle Eastern conflict.

That means there are four teams left with a mathematical shot, as Mercedes leads Ferrari by 134 points, McLaren by 239 and Red Bull by 246 - fifth-placed Racing Bulls is 478 behind.

Position Team Points 1 Mercedes 578 2 Ferrari 444 3 McLaren 339 4 Red Bull 332 5 Racing Bulls 100 6 Alpine 68 7 Haas 30 8 Audi 23 9 Williams 12 10 Aston Martin 7 11 Cadillac 0

Can Mercedes win the F1 2026 world title at the US GP?

When F1 greets the chequered flag in Austin next weekend, there will be 215 points left available in the 2026 constructors’ championship.

That means the United States Grand Prix is likely to see McLaren and Red Bull drop out of contention, as they would need to be within 214 points post-Austin.

It is because Mercedes has nine more wins than both squads, so if McLaren and Red Bull cut it to 215 in Texas, they would still be eliminated from the fight due to countback of victories.

Given that would require the reigning champions and Red Bull outscoring Mercedes by at least 25 and 32 points respectively, Ferrari is realistically the only threat to the German marque.

And because the Scuderia will leave the United States still within 214 points of Mercedes regardless of what happens, the constructors’ title will not be decided next weekend.

When can Mercedes win the F1 2026 world title?

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

The worst-case scenario for Ferrari in Austin is that it experiences a double non-points score with Mercedes finishing 1-2, which would leave a 177-point gap between them.

If that unlikely scenario happens, the German marque heads to Mexico City with a chance of claiming its ninth constructors’ title - moving level with Williams on the all-time list behind Ferrari (16) and McLaren (10).

Again, provided Qatar and Abu Dhabi go ahead, there are 172 points available in the four grands prix after Mexico. So, if the above scenario in Austin happens, Mercedes would just need to make sure that Ferrari doesn’t outscore it by at least six points in Mexico.

Yet at no point this season has Mercedes taken a full score from a grand prix with Ferrari taking nothing, as the below table indicates - excluding sprint races as there are none left in 2026.

Grand Prix Mercedes points haul Ferrari points haul Australia 43 27 China 43 27 Japan 37 23 Miami 37 12 Canada 25 30 Monaco 25 18 Barcelona 18 25 Austria 40 14 United Kingdom 18 40 Belgium 25 30 Hungary 21 22 Netherlands 33 22 Italy 43 8 Spain 35 12 Azerbaijan 35 20 Malaysia 18 27 Singapore 17 26

Looking at that, Mercedes has outscored Ferrari by an average of 7.6 points across the 17 grands prix so if that were to happen across the next two, it leaves a gap of 149 points.

So even for Mercedes to clinch the title in Mexico is a tough ask. F1 is most likely looking at the grand prix afterwards, in Brazil, where the Silver Arrows could become world champions.

Sports.title: What drives Bortoleto as his junior rivals hit new heights in F1
Sports.content:
Gabriel Bortoleto has watched Kimi Antonelli and Isack Hadjar celebrate their first Formula 1 podiums. Both are from his generation of drivers, having competed against him throughout the junior categories.

So he knows them well, having raced against and beaten them - but their respective F1 careers have taken different paths so far. While Antonelli and Hadjar have already enjoyed podium success, Bortoleto is helping Audi build a team that hopes to challenge at the front in the coming years.

It would be understandable if Bortoleto felt impatient, but the 22-year-old has accepted that his opportunity may take longer to arrive.

“They're the two drivers from my generation who are getting podiums,” the Brazilian told Autosport. “I've raced against them all my life. The truth is that I did well against them in the junior categories, and I know what I'm capable of. But I have to be patient. Everyone has their own path. Let's see where we all end up in 20 years."

Bortoleto has already achieved his childhood dream of reaching F1, but the experience has also brought new challenges. After years of fighting for wins and championships in the junior categories, he now has to judge his progress by different standards.

"I'm very happy to be in Formula 1,” he added. “It's the first step towards a dream I've always had. At the same time, to be honest, it's also difficult when you come from the junior categories, where you've been winning, and then arrive in Formula 1 knowing you can't fight at the front. It's been almost two years now. Today, the goal is to score points, and that's not easy."

Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

What keeps Bortoleto motivated is his belief in Audi's future. He doesn't see the team as a stepping stone to a seat elsewhere, or his current situation as an opportunity to attract the attention of an established frontrunner. He wants to be part of the project when Audi itself becomes a winning team.

"What motivates me and keeps me going is the project I'm part of,” said the 2023 F3 and 2024 F2 champion. “I'm not in a team whose ambition is to stay where we are today. I'm in a team that's improving every year and has a clear long-term plan. I hope that one day I'll look back and see that everything we've been through helped us reach the top."

Bortoleto is also aware that, given his age and potential, he is expected to play an important role in Audi's future. But he sees that as a source of pride rather than pressure.

"Pride, yes. Pressure, no,” he said. “There will be difficult moments, there will be times when you're not winning, and I have to keep working on my mindset, on myself, and developing as a driver. Because the day Audi gives me the opportunity to win, with a winning car and a winning engine - and it will happen, I don't think it will take that long - I'll have to be ready to show what I can do."

Bortoleto is convinced that Audi will eventually give him the machinery to compete at the front. He understands that it may take time, but he also knows how quickly the competitive order in F1 can change.

"Right now, Hadjar and Kimi are definitely closer to the ultimate goal, which is winning a world championship. But everything could change in a year. You never know. I just have to keep doing my best,” said Bortoleto, who is 15th in the drivers’ standings, with Audi eighth in the constructors’ championship.

‘Mattia Binotto is much more than a boss’

Mattia Binotto, Audi F1 Team Photo by: Joe Portlock / LAT Images via Getty Images

One of the people Bortoleto regularly turns to for advice about his situation is Mattia Binotto. The man leading Audi's F1 project experienced Ferrari's successful years from within the team and has worked through very different periods in its history. He is now involved in building a new operation with ambitions of reaching the front, and Bortoleto values that experience.

"I talk to Mattia a lot,” he said. “I often ask him for help with this situation because I know he has a lot of experience and understands what I'm going through now. He's already been part of a winning team, and now he's in a team that wants to win. He helps me a lot."

Their relationship has also developed beyond what Bortoleto initially expected from the person running his team.

"He's a mentor, a friend, a boss, but he's also very different from what I imagined,” claimed Bortoleto. “Because normally, when you have a boss, the relationship is a bit formal. But he's different. I don't just see him as a boss, but also as someone I can go to for advice about my personal life. That's a really nice aspect of our relationship."

Another person Bortoleto turns to for advice is Max Verstappen. The two are friends and share an interest in sim racing, which gives the Brazilian plenty of opportunities to ask questions. Rather than focusing exclusively on driving techniques or preparing for qualifying, Bortoleto is particularly interested in Verstappen's experience of Red Bull's development into a championship-winning team.

"I talk to Max often,” revealed Bortoleto. “Obviously, the details stay between us, but we often talk about how I'm feeling, how I'm developing, what I want from Audi and how we're progressing as a team. I ask him questions about what he experienced at Red Bull before winning the world championship: what things were like, how the team worked."

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

And sometimes those conversations take place during a gaming session.

"These are things that sometimes come into my head while we're playing, so I ask him,” said Bortoleto.

Binotto and Verstappen can offer Bortoleto different perspectives on the same challenge. Binotto has experience of working within a successful organisation and helping develop a team with ambitions of winning, while Verstappen knows what it is like to spend years working towards a first world championship.

For Bortoleto, their advice is valuable as he tries to develop both as a driver and as part of a team that is not yet ready to fight for victories.

The boy who never wanted a Plan B

Bortoleto's willingness to be patient today contrasts with his attitude during his junior career, when he refused to consider any alternative to reaching F1.

"Never," he replied, when asked whether he ever had a Plan B.

"A lot of people told me it was wrong to think that way, and maybe it was, because there are many great categories in motorsport where you can become a professional and race at a high level. But I wanted to reach Formula 1 because that was what I'd dreamed of since I was a child."

As he progressed through the junior categories, people around him tried to make him consider the possibility that an F1 opportunity might never come. There were only so many seats available, driver turnover was limited and plenty of talented drivers had missed out.

Gabriel Bortoleto, Invicta Racing, Monza 2024 Photo by: Invicta Virtuosi Racing

"They would tell me, 'Even if you win Formula 3, and even if you're winning Formula 2, what are you going to do if it doesn't happen,” he said. "And I'd reply, 'I can't get that into my head. Don't even tell me that.' I'd get angry and walk away."

Bortoleto went on to win the F3 championship as a rookie before stepping up to F2 the following year. One of the defining moments of that campaign came at Monza in 2024.

He ended up in the gravel at the first Lesmo during qualifying, at a crucial stage of his championship battle. Title rival Hadjar was due to start third, while Bortoleto faced the prospect of starting from the back of the grid. For a few minutes, he feared the damage to his championship hopes could be considerable.

"I said to myself, 'I'm starting last, he's starting third. Even if I drive the race of my life, where can I finish? We all have the same cars, it's not as if one is much better than another. Even the engineers were saying it wouldn't be easy to overtake,” he said.

Bortoleto went on to win the race.

"With everything that happened during the race, winning was an incredible feeling for me. Something really special."

The result also came at a crucial point in his efforts to secure an F1 seat. Bortoleto had yet to sign a contract and knew that every opportunity to demonstrate his ability mattered.

"I had to show that I deserved an opportunity," he claimed.

Gabriel Bortoleto, Stake F1 Team KICK Sauber Photo by: Andy Hone / Motorsport Images

The phone call that made 20 years of work worthwhile

When confirmation of his F1 seat finally came, Bortoleto initially struggled to believe what he was hearing. Talks with Audi had been going on for some time, but he had not known whether the opportunity would be for 2025 or 2026. Then his manager called to tell him the date of the announcement.

"I said to him, 'What announcement? For 2026?' And he said, 'No, for 2025!' I replied, 'What are you talking about, 2025?' And he said, 'You'll be racing as a full-time driver in 2025.'"

Bortoleto was at his home in Milan with his girlfriend when he received the news. He immediately called his family in Brazil.

"I made a video call with my dad, my mum and my brother, and I said, 'I have something to tell you. Stop everything!' I remember my mum was crying, my brother was incredibly excited and my father didn't know what to say,” he said.

For Bortoleto, the moment was about more than securing an F1 contract. It was also an opportunity to reflect on the years of karting, travelling and sacrifices his parents had made to support his career - many of which he had been too young to fully appreciate at the time.

"It's impossible to explain what it means,” he said. “But it's the result of 20 years of work. I know how many days my father wasn't at home, how many races he couldn't come to watch when I was little because he had to work."

The Bortoleto family had no previous background in motorsport. His father worked in the internet and telecommunications industry before becoming involved in Brazilian motor racing, where he now runs the Stock Car series.

Rubens Barrichello in the Stock Car Pro Series Photo by: Duda Bairros

"They made so many sacrifices, including living away from me so they could keep working. And that day, when we had that video call, I think what went through my mind was that it was a huge achievement for me, but an even bigger one for my mum and dad. All those sacrifices had been worth it."

That family background also appears to have influenced Bortoleto's attitude towards money. Asked whether F1 drivers compare their salaries and compete over who earns the most, he smiles at the suggestion.

"I don't care how much other drivers earn,” he claimed. “What matters to me is having a winning car and a good project ahead of me. The money comes as a consequence. If you're a great champion, you'll never be short of money. If you're winning races, the last thing you should be worrying about is how much money you're making."

He also believes that earning a significant amount of money comes with responsibilities towards others: "If anything, the question is where to spend it or who to help. If you make all that money and don't help the people around you, you don't deserve it."

A mind that never switches off

Bortoleto admits that he finds it difficult to stop thinking about racing. Video games provide a way to relax, even when he is still spending his free time behind a virtual steering wheel.

"My mind is always on racing,” he said. “I need something that helps me switch off from what I do for the rest of the day. Sometimes it's still motorsport, but in a different way. I'm laughing, I'm having fun, it's not work. I don't have to chase perfection."

Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi F1 Team Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Perfection is something Bortoleto believes no human driver can truly achieve, however close they might come.

"The perfect lap? No, I don't think it exists, because perfection would mean being able to say, 'There was nothing more I could have done.' But you can have a lap that's very close to perfection. Perfection isn't human. For me, perfection is what you get in computer simulations."

That attitude also shapes how Bortoleto approaches his own development. Rather than judging himself solely by his current results, he wants to make sure he continues learning and improving throughout his career.

"I study, I try to understand,” he said. “In the end, when I look back at my career in 20 or 30 years, I don't want to think that I didn't do everything I could."

It is another reference to the long-term perspective that runs through Bortoleto's approach to F1. He is prepared to wait and see where he, Antonelli and Hadjar stand in 20 years, just as he wants to look back on his own career knowing he made the most of his opportunities.

For now, that means accepting that other drivers of his generation are fighting for podiums while he helps Audi develop into a team capable of challenging at the front. He sees those years as part of the process of reaching his ultimate goal, rather than time lost waiting for a competitive car.

Before the interview ends, there is one final question: where does Gabriel Bortoleto hope to be in five years?

"Hopefully winning world championships, obviously with Audi."

Sports.title: What Verstappen knew about Red Bull’s big upgrade when he signed his new F1 deal
Sports.content:
While Max Verstappen was still seriously considering the possibility of ending this Formula 1 season without winning a single race at Monza, things now look considerably different.

Verstappen came remarkably close to victory in Baku before actually coming out on top in the subsequent races of the triple-header in Malaysia and Singapore.

It marks a huge contrast with the beginning of this year, when Red Bull was a distant fourth in the pecking order and at times even found itself fighting Haas and Alpine.

Unsurprisingly, that sparked plenty of speculation about Verstappen's future again, although he revealed at Zandvoort that, in reality, he had come much closer to an early F1 retirement than to switching teams.

Ahead of Verstappen's home race, the news finally emerged: the Dutchman's already long-term deal with Red Bull had been renegotiated and extended by another two years.

Now that the Milton Keynes-based squad has made a huge step forward and is fighting for victories again, the question arises whether he might already have known more when he signed.

In other words, did Verstappen already know that Red Bull would become competitive again with its next upgrade package?

“No, not really, it was more just talking about the future, and of course the ideas about how the team is moving forward,” Verstappen replied. “And I liked those ideas. It’s also not that they really needed to convince me or whatever, it's just the general chat that you have with the team.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Jayce Illman / Getty Images

“And for me, it's been really enjoyable to work with this team. Naturally, yes, with the progress that we have had, it's a nice bonus, because fighting up front is a lot more satisfying, of course.”

Verstappen also added that the Baku upgrade is not just about outright performance. Perhaps even more important than the pure gains in load and lap time is the fact that the RB22 has become considerably more predictable again.

And that is precisely what allows the driver behind the wheel to make more of a difference again, at least as far as the limitations of the current power unit regulations allow him to do so.

“The big thing that has changed with our car is that has just become a lot more predictable and balanced, where in the beginning of the year many times I didn't know what was going to happen going into a corner,” Verstappen explained. “Back then, a lot of weird things did happen with the car.

“That's why you could never really run it to the limit, because you didn't know where the limit was, or suddenly the limit had shifted. That [change] has made it a lot better in the last few race weekends, just knowing a bit more where the limit is and having a more predictable balance.”

Team principal Laurent Mekies also dismissed the suggestion that Red Bull had already anticipated the huge progress in Baku and had been able to use it to convince Verstappen to put pen to paper.

“The short answer is no. We were not waiting for a magic upgrade that was supposed to bring us to the performance,” the Frenchman clarified.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Laurent Mekies, Red Bull Racing Team Principal Photo by: Joe Portlock / Getty Images

“We knew that we had upgrades coming and we also knew that Baku would be the last one of this year. It was continuing the trend of the development of the car, and as I said earlier, at the time we actually felt that we would probably struggle to close those final three tenths.

“So it was certainly not an argument of convincing [Max] at the time of the discussions.”

Mekies stressed that Verstappen's contract extension was instead based on the longer term and on his confidence that Red Bull can continue to provide him with competitive machinery in the future.

In that respect, the Baku upgrade was not so much used to convince him, but is seen internally more as an example of what is possible when all the pieces of the puzzle fall into place.

“I think more globally, we knew that the dynamic was very strong in Pierre [Wache]'s team and in Ben [Hodgkinson]'s team, in terms of what we felt was still the potential of the car package, both on the chassis side and on the PU side,” Mekies continued.

“And yes, this is the sort of discussion we had with Max. It’s not about the Baku package or any other package, but about the underlying factors and where we felt the long-term opportunities were. But no, nothing specifically about the Baku package.”

As for those long-term opportunities, both Mekies and Verstappen continue to stress that the current situation is still not good enough. Red Bull is not there yet and still needs to address several underlying weaknesses.

With the current chassis and the limitations of the budget cap, that will no longer be possible in 2026, which is why Verstappen has repeatedly emphasised that further changes will be needed for the 2027 car if Red Bull is to compete consistently at the front again.

Sports.title: Colapinto urges fans to stop online abuse: “You’re not helping me or my future”
Sports.content:
Franco Colapinto has vocally asked Argentinian fans to stop online abuse after several incidents in the last couple of months.

Following the Zandvoort, Madrid and Baku races, hateful comments were directed at FIA stewards, Pierre Gasly and his family, and Lando Norris, among others. This has been a recurring theme in the 2026 Formula 1 season, prompting Alpine to regularly release statements to try and combat the vituperation.

Colapinto had previously been coy when it came to taking a stand on this matter; in Baku he meekly labelled the behaviour as “not nice to see”, and after causing the Turn 1 pile-up in Azerbaijan, he nuanced the situation.

“I think we miss that it doesn't come only from Argentinians,” Colapinto then said. “It comes a lot from them, I fully agree, [but] it doesn't just come from them. They are extremely passionate and they support me a lot. It's bad. They are bad many times.

“But it comes from all the world and from many other fanbases. I don't know if we are not seeing it. I get loads of it. No one ever talks about it.”

On Thursday, the Argentine went on to make his strongest statement to date in a bid to curb his fanbase’s frenzy – he directly told his fans that they ‘sometimes went too far’ and ‘were not helping him or his future’.

“Hello everyone, there’s something very important that I’ve needed to talk to you about for some time,” Colapinto said in a Spanish-language video posted on Instagram. “I probably should have spoken to all of you sooner, but this is something that needs to be addressed, something we need to change and improve.

Franco Colapinto, Alpine Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

“I will always be grateful, and I genuinely feel incredibly fortunate, to have had you all supporting me from the very beginning.

“I’m grateful for all the support you give me, for how you help me achieve results, and for how you constantly push me to aim higher. You help me and the team achieve our results, race after race, day after day, as we train and try to improve. And I’m genuinely grateful for all of that.

“I know it makes you incredibly proud when things go well for me, when I score points for myself and the team. And I have always been very grateful for that support.

“But sometimes, we go too far. Instead of supporting me, we end up criticising people and attacking other drivers, other colleagues, my team-mates, my mechanics, my engineers – people I work with every single day.

“I know you think you’re defending me, but you’re actually doing the opposite. You’re not helping me or my future.”

Colapinto’s immediate future is secure, with the 23-year-old having clinched a new Alpine deal for the 2027 season back in August. He currently lies 12th in the 2026 standings with 27 points to his name, while team-mate Gasly is 10th on 41 points.

Sports.title: Who will win this year’s ultimate F1 dream ticket? You decide…
Sports.content:
After hundreds of applications for the ultimate prize in grand prix racing, the Heineken x F1 Season Ticket is down to six finalists – and F1 fans can now vote to decide who wins.

The candidates – from the UK, New Zealand, Singapore, Czechia and the USA – have all put their pitches forward for the adventure of a lifetime, which will see one of them get free travel, accommodation and passes for every single F1 race next season.

The competition challenged F1 fans around the world to share their passion for the sport and explain why they, more than anyone, deserve to be gifted an unforgettable season of racing, experiencing unique events, connecting with fans and watching the action first hand.

The initiative was designed by Heineken to showcase the connections that can be formed through a shared passion for the sport, demonstrating that ‘Fans Have More Friends.’

F1 fan Brandon Burgess was the first recipient of the golden ticket and has been posting his stories to almost 150,000 followers on his social channels this season. His journey has now almost run its course – and now it is time to choose the next ‘star’ to take over his mantle.

Global shortlist

The list of entries demonstrates the sport’s global fanbase and the massive reach of the competition – and the final six all have a unique story to tell, with a different reason why they deserve that special prize.

Start action Photo by: Clive Rose / Getty Images

Callum, from Scotland, used to pretend to be Michael Schumacher in front of the TV when he was a toddler. He’s a keen film photographer and says: “I’d love to take you behind the scenes of the F1 season ticket and show you the people and places of F1 on film.”

New Zealander, Dale, says he wants to discover the “F1 world” behind every race, exploring the unique people, cultures and fans. “I want to meet the people who make it special and bring everyone along for the ride,” he says.

Lukas, who lives in Czechia, says winning the prize would “finally be some peace for my sofa” and promises fans they can “be the team boss” by choosing challenges for him to take part in each race weekend, sharing the results as the season goes on.

India, from the UK, describes herself as a “completely ordinary fan” looking to make next year “extraordinary” – and also asked other fans to set her fun challenges for each race, saying that winning would “bring together my two passions of F1 and seeing the world.”

Joy, whose home race in Singapore took place earlier this month, wants to use the opportunity to experience “the excitement and sportsmanship” of F1 around the world and to have a chance to “share the same passion” with those around her.

Jose, from the USA, is a fan not just of the racing but also of the strategy, technology and teamwork behind F1. He visited his home race in Las Vegas last year and said: “Travelling to every race in the 2027 would honestly be a dream come true.”

Singapore GP Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

Picking a winner

The opportunity to travel to every grand prix opens up unprecedented access to the sport and its fans. The current ticket holder Burgess has shown just how to get the best out of the experience this season and he was on the judging panel that picked the shortlist.

Speaking before the competition began, he said: “The key thing I'll be looking for is the passion for F1, because you have to be a true fan to make the most of this opportunity. It’s going to be hard to give it up and there’s quite a lot of pressure choosing who’s next.”

The competition was open to fans aged 25 or over, with entrants asked to name their favourite team and driver and select who they would take to a future race from a list of options provided by F1 and Heineken.

Fifty entrants were then selected at random and invited to submit a 90-second video on why they should become the next ticket holder – and the final six videos are now available to watch, so fans can determine who should win the adventure of a lifetime.

Sports.title: Camara over Ocon - did Haas make the correct call for F1 2027?
Sports.content:
Rafael Camara has been announced as a Formula 1 driver for the 2027 season and he will serve as Esteban Ocon’s replacement at Haas.

It will see the 21-year-old Brazilian make his F1 debut after such a rapid rise through the junior formulae.

Camara won the 2024 Formula Regional European Championship and the 2025 Formula 3 title, following that up by currently leading the Formula 2 standings by seven points.

But he is still such a raw talent as opposed to the experience and race-winning know-how of Ocon, who has endured a tough time since joining Haas at the start of 2025.

So has the American outfit made the right move? Our writers have their say.

Raw speed makes Camara a great pick

Rafael Camara, Invicta Racing Photo by: Dom Gibbons / Formula 1 via Getty Images

As the saying goes, you can make a quick driver reliable, but you can’t make a reliable driver quick.

Camara is one of the fastest drivers from the past decade in junior formulae; his qualifying record speaks for him. He took seven poles, more than anyone, on his way to the 2024 Formula Regional European Championship title; his 2025 F3 record was five poles out of nine, which is unprecedented in the current era. You’d have to go back to Luca Ghiotto’s identical feat, in the 2015 GP3 season, to find similar performance. And yet, in perhaps the most competitive title fight ever at that level, Ghiotto had narrowly lost out to Ocon in the title race.

Fast-forward 11 years, and Ocon is losing his Haas seat to Camara. Are the Frenchman’s results this season representative of his actual performance? Probably not, with the VF-26’s infamous inconsistency issue plaguing him for a long time. But it perhaps took a toll on the atmosphere within the team as frustration grew, and in that case, making a change made sense – especially with someone like Camara available.

The Brazilian has it all: backing from Haas supplier Ferrari – just like expected future Haas team-mate Oliver Bearman – obvious pace and potential back-to-back titles in FREC, F3 and F2. The Invicta racer currently leads the standings in F1’s feeder series, with five pole positions out of 13. Nobody else has taken more than two.

Of course, there have been mistakes, like his lock-up into retirement as he fought title rival Nikola Tsolov for victory in Monaco, but Camara has still taken consistent points finishes and commanding feature race wins.

Haas will miss Ocon’s experience, but Bearman can grow into the team leader role, and the decision makes sense to prepare for the future.

- Ben Vinel

Why remove a grand prix winner for a rookie?

Ocon after winning the 2021 Hungarian GP Photo by: Dan Istitene / Getty Images

Ocon was quite frank about it: he doesn't deserve this shit, he said, to be precise. And to be just as frank, I see no reason to disagree with him.

Yes, the numbers usually don't lie. And Ocon, despite being the more experienced driver, with every right to be considered a team leader, has scored fewer points so far than Bearman.

But is that really a case of him underdelivering?

Ayao Komatsu has admitted there have been issues with the car's inconsistency, and if you believe Ocon, he's only had a handful of races in which he's been able to have a proper go at it. And the last few rounds certainly suggest that, even if he's not better than Bearman, he's at least on a par with him.

Throughout its history, Haas has benefited greatly from having drivers with a wealth of experience. The likes of Romain Grosjean and Kevin Magnussen helped develop it into a credible team – and it has also failed spectacularly with rookies in the past. The choice to go with Mick Schumacher and Nikita Mazepin back in the day was a matter of survival, given the financial backing both brought. But does Haas really need to go for a rookie driver now? There's no reason to believe so.

So it appears that the Brazilian has been chosen by Haas on sporting grounds, but I can't see how he can be better right now than a proven race winner. Unless there's simply too much pressure from Ferrari to take on another junior from its Academy, I can't see Camara scoring more points for the team straight away than Ocon, with all his experience.

Ocon is still fast and reliable when the car works as it should. So why make the change? Especially if it's for another driver who can be taken away whenever Ferrari needs him.

How can you build your future around drivers who are basically on loan from a bigger team? I thought the Ocon and Bearman combination made perfect sense in that regard, as the Frenchman was the team's own driver. Now Haas gives more of an impression of becoming a Ferrari junior team rather than an independent outfit.

All of that, of course, becomes irrelevant if Komatsu has seen something absolutely special from Camara during these TPC tests – and given how Bearman has turned out, you'd argue Ayao knows what he's doing.

But still, there's a feeling that Ocon has been hard done by the team – which has almost used its underperforming car as an excuse to get rid of him.

- Oleg Karpov

This is the chance for Haas to sign a potential generational talent

Rafael Camara, Invicta Racing Photo by: Dom Gibbons / Formula 1 via Getty Images

Over recent rounds it’s been hard to feel anything but sympathy for Ocon, watching him deliver such outlandish statements in a clear desperate plea to stay on the grid. Would he have been saying such things if he weren’t up against it? No. It was clearly a tactic from him to remind people of what he’s done in the past, knowing the jury was very much out.

But like it or not, a lot of what he said was actually true. Ocon did cap off a solid junior career by winning GP3 - beating Max Verstappen in European F3 in the process - and more than held his own for a decade in F1.

His very impressive first full season in 2017 mustn’t be forgotten, scoring points in every round bar two for Force India, nor should the fact that he came very close to a career-changing move to Mercedes during its dominant years. There’s also his win at Hungary, 2021, as well as the fact that he’s one of only two drivers - Jenson Button the other - to outscore Fernando Alonso in a season as team-mates - 92 to 81 in 2022.

It is hoped that the above facts are what Ocon will be remembered for, and not his two seasons with Haas. Similarly, Daniel Ricciardo should mostly be remembered for everything but his decline at the end.

Yet there is another fact - or opinion - that mustn’t be ignored: it is time for Ocon to leave. Although results have improved of late, how much of that is down to the 30-year-old knowing he has a point to prove and a job on the line? Haas just isn’t going to get much better with the Frenchman behind the wheel, but it just might with such an exciting youngster in Camara.

Oleg talks about age and experience, but the 2026 champion-in-waiting - Kimi Antonelli - started the season as a teenager. So is that really as important in this day and age? Camara is also the same age as Bearman, and his junior record speaks for itself.

If he becomes F2 champion, he will join Charles Leclerc, George Russell, Oscar Piastri and fellow Brazilian Gabriel Bortoleto to win that and F3 as rookies. Camara will also become the only driver to win those two and FREC in consecutive seasons.

These are all the statistics of a future frontrunner and when one considers the 21-year-old’s speed as outlined by Ben, he is already F1-level. There’s no reason to believe he won’t be fighting for wins and titles in 10 years time. A chance for Haas to sign such a driver may not arise again, so this is an opportunity it must pounce on, and fair play for doing so.

- Ed Hardy

Sports.title: Camara to make F1 debut as Ocon's replacement at Haas in 2027
Sports.content:
Formula 2 championship leader Rafael Camara will make his Formula 1 debut for Haas in 2027 and is expected to line up alongside Oliver Bearman.

The 21-year-old Brazilian is replacing Esteban Ocon who will leave the American outfit at the end of 2026 after two disappointing seasons, his departure being confirmed on 30 September.

Camara has enjoyed a rapid rise through the junior ranks by winning the 2024 Formula Regional European Championship title and 2025 F3 crown, both done in dominant fashion.

So if he clinches the F2 championship for Invicta - he currently leads Nikola Tsolov by seven points - he will become the only driver to have won FRECA, F3 and F2 in consecutive seasons.

“I’m very happy to be joining TGR Haas F1 Team as a Formula 1 driver,” said Camara, who has signed a “multi-year” deal.

“It’s an important step in my career and I want to thank Gene Haas and Ayao Komatsu for the trust they have placed in me.

Oliver Bearman, Haas F1 Team, Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Mark Thompson / Getty Images

“I’m also very grateful to the Scuderia Ferrari Driver Academy for their support and for everything they have contributed to my development over the years, as well as to my family for always being there throughout this journey.

“Now my focus is on preparing myself in the best possible way for this new challenge. There will be a lot to learn, and I’m looking forward to working closely with the team, understanding the car and continuing to develop as a driver.”

Although Haas took its time in confirming this decision, it was entirely expected that Camara would be given the seat and triumph over the likes of reigning F2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli and reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa.

All three have taken part in TPC (Testing of Previous Cars) programmes for Haas, the most notable being a three-day test at Portimao in August as part of a plan to evaluate all candidates.

What also would have helped Camara's cause is him being a Ferrari academy graduate - like Bearman - and the Scuderia has a strong relationship with Haas, selling it many car parts like the power unit.

Team boss Ayao Komatsu said: “I’m really excited to sign such a young, amazing talent like Rafael Camara.

Ayao Komatsu, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

“I don’t need to tell everyone about his achievements in the junior formulas, it’s been very impressive, and in his rookie season in Formula 2, the speed he’s shown in some very difficult moments, like qualifying in Monaco and Montreal – that all goes to show the potential Rafa has.

“He showed when we had him drive in our TPC programme in Portugal that he could handle himself very well with not a huge amount of time to learn the car, he showed us more than just raw speed.

“Rafa managed to create an environment to get the best out of himself, it was very impressive and certainly the laps he completed were special.

“We’re all excited about this opportunity and really committed as TGR Haas F1 Team to nurture this talent and provide a place where he can flourish.

“We want to create an environment where he’s comfortable and supported, where he can really excel in his capabilities.”

This news means there are now just three seats theoretically left available for 2027, two coming at Racing Bulls, but it is expected to retain Liam Lawson and impressive rookie Arvid Lindblad.

The other is the seat alongside Camara, though it is an open secret that that’ll be taken up by Bearman, 21, who has highly impressed since joining as a rookie last year.
