World.title: What Indonesia and Hungary can learn from their young people
World.content:
The month of October stands as a historic monument to youth-driven political transformation. Decades and oceans apart, young visionaries in both Indonesia and Hungary seized this specific month to radically alter their nations’ trajectories. In 1928, Indonesian youth laid the groundwork for independence during an anti-colonial congress in Batavia. Twenty-eight years later, in 1956, Hungarian students took to the streets of Budapest to spark a revolution against Soviet tyranny. The events had different aims, but both show how a younger generation can challenge the status quo and help define what comes next.

Two moments, two histories

On 23 October 1956, university students took to the streets of Budapest demanding political reform, freedom of expression and the withdrawal of Soviet troops. What began as a student demonstration grew into a nationwide revolution. The uprising was eventually suppressed, but the courage of those who stood up for freedom remains central to Hungary’s modern history.

Indonesia’s story unfolded under different circumstances. On 27 and 28 October 1928, representatives of youth organisations gathered in Batavia, now Jakarta, for the Second Youth Congress. Coming from different regional, ethnic and religious backgrounds, they declared their commitment to one motherland, Indonesia; one nation, the Indonesian nation; and Indonesian as the language of unity. The declaration became known as Sumpah Pemuda, or the Youth Pledge.

Key figures of the First and Second Youth Congress

Unity without giving up diversity

Indonesia was still under Dutch colonial rule, and independence would be proclaimed seventeen years later, in 1945. The pledge expressed a conviction that would help sustain the independence movement and did not erase regional identities or local cultures. Instead, it set out a shared national identity that could bring together young people from different regions, ethnic groups, religions and language communities. Thus, it strengthened the idea that diversity did not have to stand in the way of unity.

First Youth Congress

The movement had been building for years. The founding of Boedi Oetomo in 1908, the First Youth Congress in 1926 and the growth of youth organisations helped create links across the archipelago. At the 1928 Second Youth congress, participants included members of groups such as Jong Java, Jong Sumatranen Bond and Jong Celebes. They came from different backgrounds, and they agreed that these differences could coexist within a shared national identity. During the congress, composer Wage Rudolf Supratman played Indonesia Raya on the violin; the song later became Indonesia’s national anthem.

Second Youth Congress

If you missed it: Indonesian Independence Day in Budapest brings a taste of the archipelago to Hungary

What these histories mean for young people today

The Hungarian Revolution and the Indonesian Youth Pledge should not be treated as equivalent events. In 1956, Hungarian students challenged political repression and demanded freedom. In 1928, Indonesian youth sought to build a common national identity under colonial rule. Their political circumstances and immediate goals were different. The connection lies in the role young people played; they refused to leave questions about their countries’ futures to others.

That message still resonates. Young people today face questions about education, jobs, the environment and their place in society. Remembering the October anniversaries means more than looking back; it also means giving young people opportunities to speak, take part in decisions and turn ideas into action.

Javanese youth delegation (Jong Java)

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Bringing Indonesian and Hungarian young people closer

The connection between Indonesia and Hungary can also grow through everyday encounters between their people. Scholarships and cultural programmes provide a practical starting point. Through Darmasiswa, Hungarians can explore Indonesian language and culture, while Stipendium Hungaricum offers Indonesian students opportunities to pursue higher education in Hungary.

People-to-people ties take shape beyond scholarship announcements. They grow when students share a classroom, work on an assignment, learn a new language or explain a custom to a friend. An Indonesian student adjusting to a Budapest winter and a Hungarian student learning to order food in Indonesian may seem like small moments, but such experiences can replace assumptions with understanding.

The Embassy of Indonesia in Budapest supports these connections through cooperation with universities, Indonesian-language classes and cultural activities. Experiences with gamelan music and traditional Indonesian dance can introduce Hungarian participants to parts of Indonesia that they may not encounter through tourism or news coverage alone. More opportunities for students and communities to meet can help make the relationship between the two countries tangible in daily life.

Illustration.

Remembering the past, creating the future

With Hungary’s 23 October commemoration coming just five days before Indonesia’s Youth Pledge Day, the calendar offers a timely invitation for people in both countries to learn about each other’s history. The two anniversaries do not tell the same story, but they offer a shared starting point for conversations about courage, identity and participation.

The legacy of the young people of 1956 and 1928 is not only something to commemorate but also to show what can happen when young people believe that their voices matter. By investing in education, cultural exchange and joint projects, Indonesia and Hungary can help a new generation build friendships, and these connections offer a practical way to turn respect for the past into cooperation for the future.

World.title: Using private health insurance with direct billing in Budapest
World.content:
International private health insurance can be reassuring until you actually need to use it outside your home country. For foreigners living in Budapest, business travelers, and tourists, one of the first practical questions when arranging private medical care is: Will I have to pay the bill myself?

Collaborative content

The answer depends on both the insurance policy and the healthcare provider. In some cases, direct billing to health insurance in Budapest allows the clinic and insurer to handle eligible medical costs between them. Instead of paying the full amount upfront and submitting a claim later, you may only need to deal with costs that are not covered by your policy.

Direct billing can considerably simplify getting medical care abroad. However, international private health insurance or travel insurance doesn’t automatically mean you can use direct billing. In other cases, you will need to pay out of pocket and submit a reimbursement claim later.

How can you use your private health insurance at a clinic in Budapest?

There are two common ways to use private health insurance for medical treatment in Budapest, Hungary.

With the traditional reimbursement model, the patient pays for the treatment in Budapest and receives an invoice and supporting documents from the clinic. You then submit these to the insurance company, which reimburses eligible expenses according to the policy terms.

Direct billing simplifies reimbursement: the healthcare provider submits the required claim information directly to the insurer, which then pays for covered services, if the arrangement is available.

Direct billing to health insurance can remove a significant administrative burden for an international patient already navigating an unfamiliar healthcare system and language in Hungary.

Can direct billing to insurance be processed with travel insurance?

Travelers visiting Budapest may also use direct billing, but under special conditions. Coverage usually applies to eligible illnesses or injuries that occur or begin while you are outside your home country and within the policy’s validity period. The clinic may require a guarantee of payment from the patient before billing the insurance company directly.

For this reason, travelers should contact their insurer or ask the clinic to check the arrangement before assuming the insurer will settle the visit directly.

When direct billing is unavailable, the usual alternative is to pay upfront and request reimbursement afterward. Keeping the invoice, medical documentation and any forms requested by the insurer is therefore important.

Check your insurance policy before choosing a clinic in Budapest

When you need medical care unexpectedly, insurance administration is unlikely to be a priority. Spending a few minutes checking your policy details before booking a visit can make the process much easier.

Geographical coverage: Check whether your insurance covers treatment in Budapest, Hungary.

Check whether your insurance covers treatment in Budapest, Hungary. Direct billing: Check whether the healthcare provider you plan to visit can bill your insurer directly, or whether you need to pay upfront and claim reimbursement.

Check whether the healthcare provider you plan to visit can bill your insurer directly, or whether you need to pay upfront and claim reimbursement. Specific treatment coverage: Confirm that your consultation, examination, or treatment is covered, and whether a referral is needed to see a specialist.

There may be additional conditions. Some insurers require pre-authorization before particular medical services. You may also need a referral before seeing a specialist, even if the clinic doesn’t require one. The clinic may ask for a guarantee of payment (GOP), which confirms the insurer will cover eligible costs.

Also, check your deductible or co-payment rate or amount, and be aware of any exclusions. Direct billing only changes how the clinic settles eligible costs; it does not expand your insurance policy’s coverage.

Have your insurance card ready, as you may need to show it at your first appointment. The policy information can also help the clinic verify the necessary details before booking.

Checklist for direct billing to health insurance: things to do before booking an appointment Source: FirstMed Budapest

Remember that direct billing is not the same as receiving treatment free of charge. Any deductible, co-payment, or excluded service remains the patient’s responsibility. If the insurance company ultimately refuses a claim, the patient may also be responsible for the medical costs.

Having your insurance card and your insurer’s contact information readily available can help you quickly determine your options in an unexpected situation.

How direct billing to health insurance works at a private clinic in Budapest

Direct billing procedures vary between private healthcare providers in Budapest and insurance companies, but the process usually begins before the appointment.

At FirstMed, an English-speaking private clinic in Budapest, patients provide their insurance information when arranging their first visit so the clinic can check whether direct billing can be organized. FirstMed works with more than 130 private health insurance providers, although arrangements may sometimes also be possible with insurers outside its existing network, explains Ilana Varga, FirstMed’s insurance manager.

The patient brings their insurance card to the first visit and completes the required payment guarantee documentation. Depending on the insurer, a claim form may also need to be signed. Once direct billing is confirmed, the clinic handles the relevant claim documents and payment arrangements with the insurer.

If direct billing cannot be arranged, the alternative is generally to pay for the treatment and submit a reimbursement claim yourself. In this situation, international patients should ask whether the healthcare provider can issue invoices and supporting documents in English and in a format suitable for their insurer.

Understanding your insurance policy is key

Private health insurance can make accessing medical care in Budapest easier, particularly for international residents and visitors who prefer English-speaking healthcare. But the practical experience depends heavily on knowing how the individual policy works.

Checking direct billing eligibility, coverage limits, referrals, pre-authorization requirements and out-of-pocket costs before an appointment can help avoid unexpected bills and unnecessary paperwork.

Frequently asked questions about using private health insurance in Budapest

Do I always have to pay first when visiting a private doctor in Budapest? No. If your insurance policy allows direct billing and the healthcare provider can arrange it with your insurer, they may settle eligible costs directly. Otherwise, you will generally need to pay the clinic and claim reimbursement afterward. Does having international health insurance guarantee direct billing? No. Direct billing depends on your individual policy terms and the arrangements between your insurer and the healthcare provider. It is best to confirm this before treatment whenever possible. What if the Budapest clinic does not normally work with my insurer? It is worth asking before assuming that direct billing is unavailable. In some cases, an insurer may issue a guarantee of payment that lets the clinic arrange direct settlement even without an established relationship. If that isn’t possible, your policy may still cover reimbursement after payment. Can tourists use travel insurance for direct billing at a private clinic? Sometimes. The policy must allow direct billing, and the insurer may need to provide a guarantee of payment. Coverage also depends on the circumstances of the illness or injury and the policy’s terms and validity period. What documents should I ask for if I need to claim reimbursement? Ask your healthcare provider for an invoice and any medical or claim documentation your insurer requires. Foreigners staying in Budapest may also want to confirm in advance that these documents can be provided in English and in a format their insurance company accepts.

For a more detailed explanation of the process and how FirstMed handles it, read the full guide to direct billing to health insurance in Budapest.

Remember, insurance coverage and direct billing eligibility depend on the terms and conditions of the individual insurance policy. Confirm your coverage and any authorization requirements with your insurer.

World.title: Hungary needs an AI workforce plan before anxiety becomes resistance
World.content:
Artificial intelligence no longer feels like a distant policy discussion. It is beginning to shape how companies hire, train, automate and reorganise work. The latest IMF message from Bangkok adds urgency to this trend: AI investment is supporting growth, but it is also likely to disrupt labour markets.

Written by A.S. Alhebsi / Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi – Author and Researcher specializing in Security, Heritage, Risk Management, and Control Room Operations

That should matter in Hungary, where the economy depends heavily on manufacturing, supplier networks and a workforce expected to adapt quickly to changing industrial demand. If AI enters these sectors without a credible workforce plan, productivity gains could arrive alongside deeper uncertainty.

The UAE’s recent emphasis on digital skills and secure digital public infrastructure is relevant because it highlights a simple but often neglected truth. Technological transition is not managed by software alone. It is managed by institutions that prepare people for new expectations before anxiety hardens into resistance.

Hungary’s risk is not necessarily immediate job collapse. It is a slower erosion of confidence. Workers may wonder whether routine administrative, planning or support roles still offer a future. Younger employees may worry that entry-level opportunities will shrink. Employers may underestimate how much clarity people need when job design begins to change.

If you missed it – Exclusive interview: What is business education for in the age of AI?

This matters because labour-market transition is partly psychological. Employees who feel ignored or kept in the dark are less likely to embrace new systems. Public debate then turns suspicious, even when some technologies could genuinely improve competitiveness.

Hungary therefore needs a practical AI workforce plan.

That means identifying which sectors face the earliest task disruption, aligning retraining with actual job redesign, and ensuring that employers treat communication as part of implementation. Vocational systems and universities should not merely discuss AI; they should translate it into applicable competencies.

There is also a broader regional dimension. Central European economies compete for investment partly on the basis of skills and reliability. Countries that manage the human side of AI better may become more attractive places to build higher-value operations. Those that neglect it may discover that social unease becomes an economic cost.

The best AI strategy is not the loudest. It is the one that keeps productivity rising while preserving public confidence that the future of work has not been written without the people who still need work.

World.title: Micro Budapest: a free website turns 40 of Kolodko’s mini statues into a treasure hunt
World.content:
A new website invites locals and visitors to track down 40 of the tiny, mostly bronze figures that sculptor Mihály Kolodko has placed around Budapest.

Searching is part of the fun. Each entry on Micro Budapest therefore gives only an approximate address, enough to bring you to the right place and leave the figure for you to discover. If you still cannot find it, help is one tap away: the exact GPS coordinates open the spot in OpenStreetMap.

Visitors can browse by district or by theme, from “Hungarian Childhood” and “Politics & History” to “Curious & Touching”, open a map of the 40 selected figures, and use “My Location” to see which one is nearest. Micro Budapest is free to use and available in Hungarian, English, German, French, Greek, Italian and Spanish.

Every location was checked on the spot rather than copied from existing lists. The site also offers a background story for each statue. Kolodko rarely explains his works himself, so these stories are Micro Budapest’s own: independently researched from newspaper articles and Hungarian sources, and the team’s view of what each figure means, not an official explanation.

Photo: Kolodko Art / Facebook Photo: DNH Photo: DNH Photo: DNH Photo: DNH Photo: DNH

Most of the statues appear unannounced, and they can be stolen, moved or altered at any time. A news section reports new figures and losses, and three statues are currently marked as missing on the map. The site asks visitors to report anything they notice.

Micro Budapest is a curated selection, not a complete list, and has no connection to the artist.

Website: microbudapest.com

World.title: Hungary Weekly Briefing: Magyar–Zelensky talks, EU funding breakthrough and Hungary’s changing political landscape
World.content:
Hungary’s political and diplomatic landscape continues to evolve rapidly. This week brought important developments in relations with Ukraine, a potential breakthrough over billions of euros in frozen EU funds, and fresh debates over migration, economic policy and the country’s international partnerships.

The latest Hungary Weekly Briefing on Substack brings together the key stories of the week, with analysis and context for international readers, expats, investors and everyone following developments in Hungary.

On the economic front, Hungary has moved closer to unlocking EUR 4.2 billion in previously frozen EU funding, potentially opening the door to renewed Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe opportunities for Hungarian universities.

The briefing also examines the Hungarian government’s migration policy, a major EU court ruling concerning the release of convicted people smugglers, and new polling showing Tisza’s continued political lead despite criticism of its economic performance.

World.title: Sharjah International Book Fair 2026 to bring together 2,673 publishers and exhibitors from 124 countries for 1,500 events – photos
World.content:
The 45th Sharjah International Book Fair (SIBF 2026) will take place from November 4-15 at Expo Centre Sharjah under the theme ‘Made of Stories’, bringing together 2,673 publishers and exhibitors from 124 countries. This year’s edition will also host 106 writers, artists and intellectuals from 25 countries, with 1,500 cultural and artistic events, and welcome Oman as Guest of Honour, presenting a programme celebrating its literature, heritage, writers and artists.

The details were announced at a press conference held by the Sharjah Book Authority (SBA) at its headquarters in Sharjah. The Authority unveiled the dates of the Thriller Festival and Sharjah International Library Conference, and new visitor experiences, including ‘Poets’ Corner’, where visitors’ stories are transformed into poems in Arabic and English, and ‘Future Hands District’, an interactive educational city designed to introduce children to different professions.

Photo: SIBF

Stories that shape generations

In his keynote, H.E. Ahmed bin Rakkad Al Ameri, CEO of SBA, said: “For 45 years, SIBF has brought together readers, writers, publishers and creative minds from around the world. This year’s theme, ‘Made of Stories’, celebrates how the stories we read, hear and pass down through generations shape our memories, identity and understanding of the world, and how we create stories of our own to leave for future generations.”

H.E. Ahmed bin Rakkad Al Ameri, CEO of SBA. Photo: SIBF

He added: “The journey of SIBF is part of the wider cultural vision established by His Highness Sheikh Dr. Sultan bin Mohammed Al Qasimi, Supreme Council Member and Ruler of Sharjah, who made books and knowledge the foundation for human development and a bridge connecting cultures and peoples.”

“Today, under the guidance of Her Highness Sheikha Bodour bint Sultan Al Qasimi, Chairperson of SBA, we continue to advance this vision, strengthening the fair’s status as a global publishing platform and expanding opportunities for publishers and creative professionals to collaborate and reach new readers and markets,” he concluded.

Celebrating Omani culture

Discussing the Guest of Honour participation, H.E. Ahmed bin Saud bin Nasser Al Rawahi, Assistant Director General for Knowledge and Cultural Development at Oman’s Ministry of Culture, Sports and Youth, and Director of the Muscat International Book Fair said: “We see this celebration as a tribute to Oman and its culture, and an opportunity to strengthen the longstanding ties between our countries and peoples. Oman’s selection as Guest of Honour builds on a shared history and close relations rooted in brotherhood and neighbourliness.”

Hungarian embassy opened in Oman

He added: “Our participation will introduce visitors to Oman’s history, heritage and cultural achievements while encouraging dialogue and exchange between Oman and Sharjah. The programme includes literary and intellectual discussions, poetry evenings, historical and cultural events, and workshops for children and young people.”

Media coverage of the fair

Salem Ali Hamad Al Ghaithi, Director of the Sharjah Broadcasting Authority, outlined the fair’s media coverage plan, including special programmes and interviews with writers and intellectuals on Sharjah TV, Al Sharqiya TV, Al Wousta TV and Sharjah Sports TV. Coverage will also include more than 20 hours of live broadcasting on Plus Radio, major events streamed on the Maraya platform and round-the-clock updates across digital platforms.

Salem Ali Hamad Al Ghaithi, Director of the Sharjah Broadcasting Authority. Photo: SIBF

A partnership supporting knowledge and culture

Saood Ibrahim Mohammed Saleh, Vice President of Government Sales (Dubai and Northern Emirates) at Etisalat, said: “As Etisalat marks its 50th anniversary, we take pride in our longstanding sponsorship of this major cultural event. We see this strategic partnership as a national and cultural responsibility, rooted in our belief that investing in people and knowledge is as important as investing in digital and technological infrastructure. We remain committed to using the latest innovations and digital solutions to support publishers, authors and readers.”

Saood Ibrahim Mohammed Saleh, Vice President of Government Sales (Dubai and Northern Emirates) at Etisalat. Photo: SIBF

Support for culture and community development

For his part, Mohamed Hachicho, General Director of Equiti’s Sharjah Branch, the fair’s Financial Services Partner, said: “We are proud to partner with the Sharjah Book Authority and sponsor the fair, supporting culture, knowledge and the community. Sharjah holds a special place for us because of its vision for culture and education as foundations of community development. As we expand our presence in the emirate, we aim to be an active community partner, recognising the power of knowledge to empower people, create opportunities and build a better future.”

Mohamed Hachicho, General Director of Equiti’s Sharjah Branch, the fair’s Financial Services Partner. Photo: SIBF

Bringing stories to life

Khoula Al Mujaini, General Coordinator of SIBF, outlined the fair’s cultural and artistic programme, explaining how this year’s theme shapes the activities and experiences offered to visitors.

She said: “Stories have been part of our lives since childhood, shaping our memories and how we understand ourselves and the world. We also create stories through what we write, share and leave behind. This idea inspired the theme of the 45th edition and runs throughout its books, discussions and activities, giving every visitor the chance to discover a new story, experience a different chapter or begin one of their own.”

Khoula Al Mujaini, General Coordinator of SIBF. Photo: SIBF

Expanding opportunities for publishers

Mansour Al Hassani, Director of Publishing Services at SBA, outlined the professional programme accompanying the fair and the opportunities it offers publishers to develop their businesses, exchange expertise, and expand rights trading and translation activities across international markets.

He said: “The Sharjah International Book Fair’s programme brings together publishers and book industry professionals from around the world, giving them opportunities to discuss developments in publishing markets, develop their skills, and build new business relationships and partnerships.”

Mansour Al Hassani, Director of Publishing Services at SBA. Photo: SIBF

Participating publishers

SIBF 2026 will welcome 2,673 publishers, including 1,151 Arab and 1,122 international publishers, showcasing titles in multiple languages across literature, science, children’s books and other fields.

Cultural events and guest speakers

SIBF 2026 will feature 1,500 cultural, creative and artistic events, bringing together 106 guests from 25 countries. The programme includes panel discussions, literary talks, workshops, theatrical performances and interactive activities for children and adults.

Writers, poets, intellectuals and researchers from the UAE, the Arab world and beyond will explore topics spanning literature, poetry, literary criticism, history, science, technology and contemporary social and cultural issues.

Emirati and Arab speakers

SIBF 2026 will welcome Emirati writers, thinkers, poets and artists, including Dr. Sultan Al Ameemi, Ali Abu Al Reesh, Dr. Habib Ghuloom, Dr. Shihab Ghanem, Dr. Ahmed Al Khoori, Fathiya Al Nimr, Dubai Abulhoul, Aisha Sultan and Nasser Al Dhaheri.

Photo: SIBF

Arab guests will include Moroccan academic and researcher Dr. Said Yaktine, a specialist in narratology, literary theory and digital literature; Lebanese actor, writer and director Rafiq Ali Ahmad; and Lebanese novelist and journalist Najwa Barakat.

The programme will also feature Sudanese novelist Dr. Amir Tag Elsir, Kuwaiti novelist Saud Alsanousi, and Syrian-Canadian author Zoulfa Katouh.

International authors and academics

SIBF 2026 will welcome international writers, researchers and creative figures, including V.D. Satheesan, currently serving as the 13th Chief Minister of Kerala. He will join American writer, artist and translator Daisy Rockwell; American-Canadian novelist and journalist John Vaillant; Chinese novelist and screenwriter Liu Zhenyun; and Filipino historian Ambeth R. Ocampo.

The programme will also feature Nigerian author Nnedi Okorafor; British novelist Clare Mackintosh; and Indian actress, writer and content creator Shenaz Treasurywala.

Other participants include Australian writer and designer Peter Gould; South African actress and producer Salamina Mosese; Singaporean poet Natalie Wang; German novelist Daniela Tully; and Thailand’s Rewat Panpipat

Workshops and creative activities

SIBF 2026 will also feature two specialised courses requiring advance registration. German novelist Daniela Tully will lead a course on narrative voice, character development, dialogue, editing and the publishing process. Meanwhile, Egyptian actor and writer Khaled El Sawy will present ‘Acting Studio: From Training to the Stage’, focusing on performance techniques, character development and improvisation.

Theatrical and family performances

The 12-day cultural extravaganza will present three productions requiring advance booking, beginning on November 7 with the exclusive premiere of the musical ‘When Memories Sing’. The show will revisit childhood songs and familiar voices remembered across generations.

On November 8, Abdullah Annan will present ‘Impossible or Science?!’, an interactive family show combining optical illusions and scientific experiments. Children and families will be invited to participate, vote and learn the scientific explanations behind seemingly impossible acts.

The outdoor stage at Expo Centre Sharjah will then host ‘Waterland’ on November 14 and 15, a theatrical production featuring Hussein Al Mahdi, Shaila Sabt, Ghorour Safar, Mohammed Al Musallam, Ahmed bin Hussein, Shamlan Al Omairi, Amani Al Dobb, Areej Al Attar, Najla Al Baloushi, Wahaj Al Anzi, Raghad Mohammed and Ahmed bin Jalal.

Thriller Festival returns November 7-10

SIBF 2026 will host the fifth edition of the ‘Thriller Festival’ from November 7-10, in collaboration with Capital Crime London and Thriller Festival New York. The event will bring together more than 12 specialists, including crime, mystery and thriller writers, literary agents and screenwriters.

Featured guests include British novelist and former police officer Clare Mackintosh; American author Karen Dionne, whose novel The Marsh King’s Daughter was adapted for film; and British writer and journalist Elizabeth Moore, known for her psychological thriller The Man on the Middle Floor.

They will be joined by Vaseem Khan, author of the Baby Ganesh Agency and Malabar House series; British novelist Abir Mukherjee, author of the Wyndham & Banerjee detective series; and British writer David Fennell, whose crime fiction includes the Sleeper and Grace Archer series.

Arab participants include Egyptian novelist Noha Dawoud, Emirati writer and director Ibrahim Al Marzouqi, and Emirati author Adel Al Sumaiti.

The festival will also welcome Emirati novelist Mohammed Ali Al Hammadi, Emirati writer Alia Nasser Al Zaabi, and Syrian novelist and journalist Islam Abu Shukair.

Cookery Corner

The Cookery Corner will bring together Arab and international chefs for live cooking demonstrations, introducing visitors to ingredients, flavours and techniques from different culinary traditions.

Participating chefs include Mohammad Orfali from Syria, Salam Daqqaq from Palestine, Jad Youssef from Lebanon, Kausar Raja from Pakistan and the UK, and Marina Georgallides from Greece and the UK.

They will be joined by Xavier Bramble from the Caribbean and the UK; Nitisha Patel, Romy Gill and Monisha Bharadwaj from India and the UK; and Sulaiman Al Kindi and Samira Al Aghbariya from Oman.

Oman’s Guest of Honour programme

Oman will be the Guest of Honour at SIBF 2026, with 50 participants, including 41 writers and poets. Its programme will explore the country’s history, heritage and cultural identity, alongside developments in Omani literature, poetry and the arts. Visitors will also be introduced to Omani cuisine, with activities for children and young people.

The agenda will include 15 cultural sessions, six children’s workshops and 20 artistic performances, including daily musical and traditional folk performances. Two additional artistic presentations and two cookery sessions will also be held.

Participating writers and poets include novelist Zahran Al Qasmi, Dr. Mohammed Al Yahyai, poet Hassan Al Matrooshi, winner of the Al Muallaqa Prize for Classical Arabic Poetry, Dr. Abdulaziz Al Omairi, winner of the Al Burda Award for Nabati Poetry, Dr. Mahmoud bin Mohammed Al Rahbi, and writer and storyteller Ahmed bin Nasser Al Rashdi.

Publishers’ Training Programme

SIBF 2026’s professional events will begin on October 31 with the Publishers’ Training Programme, organised by SBA in collaboration with New York University (NYU). The programme will bring together more than 200 publishers from 17 countries to develop their professional skills and understanding of changes in the global publishing industry.

Sessions will cover developments in the global audiobook market, video and social media marketing strategies, international translation rights markets, and the exchange of content and cultural assets between markets.

The 16th Sharjah Publishers Conference

The 16th Sharjah Publishers Conference will take place from November 1-3, bringing together publishers and book industry professionals. Nine countries will participate for the first time, including Angola, Aruba, Belarus, Burundi, Cambodia, Cape Verde, Myanmar, Trinidad and Tobago, and Niger.

Held under the theme ‘Publishing in an Accelerating Age’, the conference will feature more than 30 sessions and workshops covering artificial intelligence, developments in the audiobook market, publishing rights trading, children’s books and the growing role of comics in publishing.

Participants will also be able to apply for the Sharjah Translation Grant, which supports translating books between Arabic and other languages.

Sharjah International Library Conference

The Sharjah International Library Conference will take place from November 7-9, organised by SBA in partnership with the American Library Association (ALA). It will bring together more than 400 librarians, information professionals and library staff from academic, public, school, government and private institutions.

Discussions will cover guided and independent reading using the Destiny Discover platform; the contribution of partnerships, public policy and community leadership to building stronger communities; and ways to develop school libraries through student leadership.

Visitor services and transport

SBA is coordinating with the Sharjah Roads and Transport Authority to identify additional parking areas and arrange transport services to and from the fair. Details will be announced in the coming days.

Official partners and sponsors

SIBF 2026’s partners and sponsors include Etisalat as Official Telecommunications Partner, SAAS as Development Partner, Trends Group as Knowledge Partner, Sharjah Broadcasting Authority as Official Media Partner, Expo Centre Sharjah as Strategic Partner, Bank of Sharjah as Banking Partner, Equiti as Financial Services Partner, and Omeir Travel Agency and National Paints as Partners.

SIBF 2025 dominates global publishing scene with record rights deals and 1.4 million visitors

World.title: Hungary’s farmers need forecasts they can use, not just admire
World.content:
A sophisticated model has limited value to a farmer if the warning arrives too late or cannot be translated into a workable choice. Water resilience begins at the point where scientific confidence meets the practical calendar of planting, irrigation and transport.

Written by Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi (A.S. Alhebsi), Author and Researcher specializing in Security, Heritage, Risk Management, and Control Room Operations

On 9 October 2026, the Emirates News Agency reported that the UAE Research Program for Rain Enhancement Science had taken part in the Meteorological Technology World Expo and the World Meteorological Organization’s TECO conference in Amsterdam on 5–8 October. Its meetings concerned radar, remote sensing, forecasting, hydrological models and scientific cooperation, including discussions with the Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute. That is evidence of research engagement, not proof that rain-enhancement technology can end water scarcity.

Hungary’s agricultural and industrial users face water risks that differ from the Gulf, but its researchers and businesses can still draw lessons from the UAE’s interest in atmospheric observation and hydrological modelling. The scientific relationship should be measured through actionable data, not a shared slogan.

I would encourage universities, farm associations and water authorities to test forecast products against the decisions people actually make. A useful pilot with UAE counterparts could compare communication methods and quantify false alarms as well as missed warnings.

A weather forecast should not end on a screen. It should end with someone better prepared.

If you missed it: Hungary’s agriculture faces major crisis: Less than 3% of arable land is irrigated

For a Hungarian farmer, a climate model is not simply an academic achievement. It may influence irrigation planning, planting dates, crop choice and conversations with buyers. When forecasts change, decisions may need to change too. That makes clarity about uncertainty an economic necessity rather than a technical footnote.

The Emirates’ participation in the Amsterdam meetings is relevant because it draws attention to observation technologies and hydrological modelling. Yet science becomes useful only when its products are tested and communicated in language that working farms can act upon. An impressive radar image cannot substitute for a clear explanation of what the evidence does and does not show.

Hungary and the UAE face different water pressures, which makes methodological exchange valuable if it is conducted carefully. Researchers could compare how measurement uncertainty affects decisions in arid and temperate environments and whether warning formats help operators avoid costly delays. Any such work should be explicitly described as a proposal, not an existing collaboration.

I would like to see field-level evaluation take priority over promotional claims. Does an early warning change a farm decision? Does it reduce avoidable water use? Do users understand how quickly a forecast might change? These outcomes reveal whether investment in data is producing resilience.

Rain-enhancement research deserves scientific scrutiny, but it does not replace irrigation efficiency or maintenance. My argument is for a practical partnership between forecasters and the people whose livelihoods depend on them.

As we wrote before, Hungarian agriculture, as we know it, is nearing the end – but researchers already have a plan

World.title: Tougher Security Response Won’t Solve Albania’s Growing Crisis: Experts
World.content:
For three days, streets in central Tirana have been taken over by university students and high-school pupils who have boycotted classes to protest against the government.

Demonstrators throwing Molotov cocktails and stones have clashed with police, who have attempted to disperse them using tear gas, rubber batons and water cannon. The unrest has spread to other cities, including Shkodra, Durres and Korca.

The main demand of the protests is the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Since coming to power in 2013, Rama has become increasingly powerful as Prime Minister, while other democratic institutions have weakened, analysts argue. This is why the anger expressed at the protests has been directed at him personally.

The young participants have also voiced demands for better-quality education, improved living conditions and greater job opportunities.

World.title: Serbia Channels Public Funds to Pro-Vucic Diaspora Groups
World.content:
In Serbia itself, the Directorate regularly funnels money to local organisations that claim to support the Serb diaspora in the region.

The Izrazajnost association, for example, received a total of 23,800 euros in 2023-2024 for two projects promoting the use of Cyrillic.

Izrazajnost is led by actor Milan Bosiljcic, who in 2023 was among a host of public figures who put their signatures to a statement of support for the SNS.

In 2024, the Directorate awarded 9,400 euros to an association co-founded by Bosiljcic’s daughter, Sara, called Jeremija, for the purposes of a language camp. The association’s first project, which was not funded by the Directorate, was conducted in cooperation with Solidarité Kosovo, an organisation founded by SNS member Arnaud Gouillon, who was head of the Directorate at the time.

Since 2023, the Belgrade Centre for Education and Youth Development, CEROB, has received almost 34,000 euros from the Directorate for diaspora youth camps.

In late 2023, the Centre for Investigative Journalism of Serbia, CINS, reported that SNS activists tasked with canvassing voters for their support were being paid in cash at CEROB’s Belgrade office.

A year later, CEROB representative Ognjen Kocevic was appointed by the Serbian government to the Managing Board of the Institute for the Evaluation of Education Quality.

The Directorate also awarded two grants totalling 13,600 euros to the Association of Students of Republika Srpska in Serbia.

During local elections in 2024 in Serbia’s second city of Novi Sad, members of the association were caught on camera working in an SNS call centre at the Novi Sad Fairgrounds, where party operatives used voter records to track turnout.

Last year, the Directorate gave 8,500 euros to the Association of War Veterans of Serb Lands 1990–1999, for summer youth camps. The association’s leader, Zeljko Vukelic, previously sparked public outrage for sending children aged 11 to 15 to military training camps in Russia in 2017, where children were taught to handle guns and hand grenades.

None of the associations mentioned above responded to requests for comment.

Political scientist Dusko Radosavljevic said the direction of funding reflects the SNS roots in the ultranationalist Serbian Radical Party, which Vucic was a key part of through the bloody collapse of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, right up until 2008 when he broke away and formed the SNS.

“It must not be overlooked that this regime has, from its inception, carried a distinct ideological marker – a far-right stance,” Radosavljevic said.

“This is a regime rooted in the Serbian Radical Party, one of the most abhorrent political creations in Serbia. It exerts a malignant influence fueled by disputes with neighbours, nationalism, and support for war crimes.”

World.title: Week in Review: Bad Deals and Scandals
World.content:
Less than two weeks before parliamentary elections in Serbia, the public got a rare glimpse inside the workings of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party machine. In an exclusive interview for BIRN, Momcilo Marjanovic, an insider, revealed the workings of the party’s “security” machine.

Marjanovic discusses the ins and outs of vote buying, how party thugs are deployed to intimidate voters and protesters, or defend party offices, as well as how provocateurs are planted inside opposition protests. He also describes how public funds are used to pay for this special apparatus.

World.title: Croatian Football Fans’ Pro-Nazi Chants Prompt Arrests
World.content:
Torcida fan group march before match on Thursday. Photo: Torcida Split/Facebook

Police in Split have arrested several people after members of Torcida, a group of hardcore supporters of Hajduk Split football club, marched through the city chanting antisemitic slogans, including “Trample, trample the Jews,” “Auschwitz, Auschwitz,” and “Rise, Adolf”, referencing Adolf Hitler.

The incidents are being investigated for hate speech. Further arrests are expected on Friday. All those detained are members of Torcida and already known to the police. An investigating judge will decide whether to order pre-trial detention.

The chants occurred a few hours before Hajduk’s match against Dutch club Ajax – a club seen as having a longstanding Jewish connection.

The incident has been condemned by the Croatian government, the mayor of Split, political parties and members of the public.

“We strongly condemn the unacceptable chants glorifying the Nazi regime,” the government stated on its X profile. “Such shameful behaviour represents a negation of sport and the democratic values ​​that modern Croatia upholds,” the post added.

Torcida fans are known for expressing extremist views.

A series of incidents occurred before the Conference League match, when Hajduk chanted fans marched in a column led by a VW Golf Mk1 with a coffin on its roof, on which the word “Ajax” was written.

The Israeli embassy in Zagreb also condemned the incidents.

The embassy was “deeply shocked by the grave antisemitic incident that occurred yesterday in Split and condemns it in the strongest possible terms,” ​​a statement provided to the news agency Hina said.

“We are deeply grateful to the Government of the Republic of Croatia and to Sara Lustig, Special Advisor to the Prime Minister on Holocaust Issues, for their swift response and clear condemnation of this event,” it added, expressing confidence that “authorities will act quickly and decisively regarding this matter”.

“Such incidents should be unequivocally and decisively condemned by all competent authorities at every level,” it continued.

Croatian President Zoran Milanovic said verbal condemnation was not enough.

“Words of condemnation, such as those we hear from the government, are no longer sufficient; measures and sanctions are necessary to demonstrate that there is no place in Croatia for the glorification of Nazism and Ustasha ideology,” Milanovic said in a press release, referencing Croatia’s World War II fascist movement.

The game itself was halted for 12 minutes during the second half after Hajduk fans let off various pyrotechnic devices, including flares and powerful firecrackers.

Hajduk could face a heavy fine from UEFA. Following the match, Hajduk issued an official apology.

“When situations like today’s occur, we are obligated to apologise,” it stated. The club also apologised to the management and players of Ajax, who witnessed scenes “by which we do not wish to be remembered in Europe”. It did not mention the specific events before the match or the Nazi chants.

The match ended with a 2-1 victory for Hajduk.

World.title: Albania PM Defiant as Protests Spread to Provincial Cities
World.content:
Prime Minister Edi Rama blamed the opposition and “foreign actors” on Friday for the escalation of violence during student protests in Tirana, describing the continuing unrest as an attempt to hinder Albania’s progress toward the European Union.

Speaking from a kiosk that had been burned down during the protests, Rama tried to suggest that students weren’t the ones leading the violence that has accompanied demonstrations in recent days, while accusing his political opponents of exploiting the discontent of young people for their own ends.

World.title: Serbia’s ‘Captured’ TV Screens All Tell the Same Story
World.content:
Serbia approaches October 25 elections with a deeply polarized and uneven national media ecosystem. The media environment is characterized by systemic political influence, instrumentalization, government control, the independent regulator’s paralysis and heightened security risks for independent journalists and media outlets.

These worrying trends have greatly affected the pre-election media space, which has been defined by extreme structural asymmetry. Meanwhile, traditional television, dominated by heavy regime influence and a lack of critical voices, remains the main vehicle for political communication and voter mobilization.

Traditional TV is watched in Serbia for five hours daily on average, and is the main source of political information for the older population. On the other side, websites and social networks offer diverse views and are the main source of information for people aged 15 to 30.

Paradoxically, despite more than 2,500 registered media outlets, Serbia has been placed in a group of high-risk countries concerning media pluralism because of severe deficits in political independence of the media and lack of overall market plurality, according to the Media Pluralism Monitor 2026.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Polish Man Charged With Plotting to Kill PM, Suspected Saboteurs Arrested
World.content:
Czech Army chief warns of possible Russian attack; PM still has conflicts of interest

The chief of the general staff of the Czech Army, Miroslav Hlavac, this week warned that Russia could test the cohesion of NATO by launching a partial attack against one of its members. “I want to emphasise that we are ready and we will defend the Czech Republic with what we have,” he said in an interview with the Czech News Agency. “And I say this with all the force and responsibility for the army of the Czech Republic, also warning that the country’s response to a potential foreign attack did not only rely on Czechia’s military capabilities but also on the response from the entire state apparatus, defence industry and society. “State preparedness is a never-ending process. You will never be 100 per cent prepared. It is important that the state, and any state, not just the Czech Republic, has its security system prepared in such a way that it is able to respond to the threat and subsequently mitigate and address the consequences of the crisis,” Hlavac insisted.

“Based on the assessment of the information provided by the Czech national authorities, the Commission has concluded that [Czech Prime Minister Andrej] Babis’s situation constitutes a conflict of interest,” Elizabeth Werner, head of the European Commission’s directorate general for agriculture and rural development, was quoted as saying this week by Transparency International Czechia as part of DG Agri’s response to the Czech NGO’s previous complaint. Czech and foreign anti-corruption watchdogs have for months warned that the Czech PM’s steps to distance himself from his business interests – particularly the transfer of his shares of Agrofert into a trust fund back in February – in reality did nothing to mitigate the risks and ultimately did not resolve his conflicts of interest. Babis, meanwhile, insists the EU Commission’s evaluation is “nonsense”. Talking about his former agro-chemical empire, Babis insisted: “I did much more than I had to do. If I had followed the rules for conflicts of interest with European commissioners, I would have just reported the conflict and walked out the door… I will never get [Agrofert] back and I don’t receive any profit from it.”

It was an intense week of closed-door talks as parties from across the political spectrum launched negotiations following last weekend’s municipal elections. Less than a week after the ballot, the future leadership and coalition formats appear clearer in about half of Czechia’s 13 regional cities. Having emerged first in six of the country’s larger cities, Babis’s ruling ANO party has so far been able to reach an agreement with other partners in two of them – Karlovy Vary and Pilsen. On the contrary, ANO is likely to end up in the opposition in Czechia’s two largest cities, Brno where several parties have already entered coalition talks, as well as in the capital Prague where the centre-right and victorious STAN movement promised “to present the framework of cooperation” for the future municipal leadership by next week. Post-election talks remain largely open in the cities of Ostrava, Pardubice, Jihlava, Zlin and Ceske Budejovice.

World.title: The Krk Cave With Stories of Smugglers, Treasures & Bears
World.content:
October the 18th, 2026 – There’s a mysterious Krk cave that carries strange stories of smugglers, treasure and even cave bears…

The underground world deep beneath Croatia is home to an incredibly rich and fascinating world, and the Cerovačke and Baraćeve caves, the Blue Cave on Biševo and Manita peć in Paklenica National Park are just some of the caves you should visit at least once in a lifetime. Putni kofer writes that the island of Krk also has its own magical cave. It’s called Biserujka and is located not far from Slivanjska Bay and near the small village of Rudine in the north-eastern part of the island. This underground beauty is rich in impressive stalactites, stalagmites and speleothem columns, and an interesting story of pirate treasure is also associated with it.

THE CAVE TAKES ON BROWN, GREY AND REDDISH COLOURS BECAUSE OF MINERALS

It is also known as Vitezić Cave or Slivanjska Jama, and the name Biserujka, at least according to legend, is owed to the treasure that was once hidden in it. It supposedly belonged to local pirates, and after it was found it was moved to an unknown place. Where did it end up? According to tradition, only “Ive Gospodin” knows that, whose house stands at the entrance to the village of Rudine. Biserujka is not a huge cave. It is only 110 metres long, and from the entrance to the bottom its depth is 13 metres. It stretches relatively shallowly beneath the surface, yet it abounds in diverse cave decorations. They can be brown, grey and reddish, and their colour is given by various minerals, especially iron and manganese oxides.

The overburden of Biserujka is thin and nowhere exceeds six to eight metres. During rainy periods water penetrates into its interior: it passes through the limestone and dissolves calcium compounds that gradually deposit in the cave and form speleothems. How slow the entire process is is sufficiently illustrated by the fact that for a layer only one millimetre thick it takes from 10 to 30 years. Visiting the cave is very simple and requires no speleological experience or special equipment. From a stone cottage you descend by stairs into a small hall called the Balcony, from which you pass through the Window, the narrowest part of the arranged path. The path then leads into the Great Hall richly covered with speleothems, the Hall with Bridges and the Cypress Hall, in which the speleothem columns resemble a petrified cypress forest. The final part is so close to the surface that it contains soil and plant roots.

graffiti through the ages can still be seen within the cave

In the deeper part of Biserujka the temperature of the ground and air is around 15 degrees, while the relative humidity is around 95 percent. The lowest point of the cave is 30 metres above sea level. The first record of Biserujka dates from 1834 and is connected with the arrest of a smuggler from Senj who was allegedly hiding in it.

In around 1850, its entrance was closed with a door, which was the first time in Croatia that such a method of protecting a cave was applied. It was arranged for tourist visits in 1913, when the stone cottage and stairs were built. The long history of visiting is also witnessed by numerous graffiti. Many have been removed in the meantime, but some have been preserved as a trace of the past, among them the oldest from 1859.

Biserujka also has interesting inhabitants: 28 species of organisms have so far been discovered in it, among them six stenoendemics, i.e. narrow endemics of the Kvarner area. Bones of a cave bear about 16,000 years old have also been found in the cave. That animal lived there at the end of the Ice Age, when due to the lower sea level Krk was connected to the neighbouring mainland. The cave is connected by an educational walking path to the bay of Slivanjska. The walk takes about 30 minutes, and the path passes through a typical karst landscape, past dry-stone walls and rocky pastures lashed by the bora, all the way to the bay with a small harbour and a sandy beach. The ticket for Biserujka costs €7 for adults, €5 for children from three to 12 years old, while children under three pay nothing. During the winter months a visit is possible by prior arrangement.

World.title: New Catamaran Line to Pučišća and Postira Begins on 1st of November
World.content:
October the 18th, 2026 – A new catamaran line will begin sailing to Pučišća and Postira starts as of the 1st of November, claiming it will reach Split in 70 minutes.

After a months-long procedure and administrative wrangling, the new state high-speed line Pučišća – Postira – Omiš – Split is expected to begin regular service on Sunday, November the 1st 2026. Morski reports that this significantly changes the everyday life of numerous islanders for whom a trip to Split on the mainland previously meant travelling by road via Supetar and then by ferry to the mainland.

The new line number 9605 will be operated by the catamaran Tropic, owned by Krilo Fast Ferries. The vessel was built in 2022 and can carry 332 passengers. This is a year-round state line, so it is not just a “summer line”, but a concrete benefit for the residents of the island of Brač.

The sailing schedule is still being finalised; it is known that the catamaran would depart daily from Pučišća at 06:15, stop in Postira and then continue across the channel to the mainland to reach the Port of Split. The journey would take about one hour and ten minutes. The return departure from Split is planned for 16:15, while Omiš, a little further south along the coastline, would be included in the sailing on Saturdays and Sundays.

Despite the great satisfaction felt as a result of this in the island communities of Pučišća and Postira, the question of including Povlja in the new catamaran connection remains unresolved. Several models were considered and were on the table, specifically seasonal stops and a smaller number of weekly departures during winter, just enough for the islanders. Support was given by the mayor of Selca Ivan Marjanović, and even by people in the County and at state level, but Povlja were left “empty-handed”, i.e. they were not included in the new state line, which after numerous announcements is quite disappointmenting.

World.title: Varaždinske Toplice Thermal Water Was Healing People 2,000 Years Ago
World.content:
October the 18th, 2026 – Varaždinske Toplice is known for its thermal water, but not everyone realises just how far back its popularity stretches, having healed people 2,000 years ago.

Spring thermal water has a beneficial effect on rheumatic ailments, the skin, relaxation… We know that today, but it was also known by the innovative Roman conquerors 2,000 years ago. Less than an hour’s drive from Zagreb lies a place whose healing warm water, with a temperature reaching 58 degrees, was used by the Romans, who built temples, pools and baths right there. Putni kofer writes that an entire complex dedicated to that healing water. Varaždinske Toplice, which is still popular today, is home to some fascinating archaeological heritage that has just received new confirmation of its value.

The Archaeological Zone of Varaždinske Toplice recently received the temporary status of a cultural asset, which, according to the explanation of the Ministry of Culture, it will hold until a decision is made establishing the status of a permanent cultural asset or for a maximum of six years.

“Thermal water began attracting the first human groups back during the Palaeolithic era, as evidenced by finds from the large tufa cave 5 Gradišće on the western side of Toplička gora, while finds from the Neolithic and Bronze Age tell us about the continuity of settlement in the wider area of today’s settlement. In the 3rd century BC, the Pannonian Iasi lived here, after whom the Romans named this place Aquae Iasae. The Roman settlement of Aquae Iasae was inhabited from the 1st to the 4th century, and at that time Toplice was a significant health, ritual, cultural and even economic centre of Upper Pannonia,” it is stated, among other things, in the explanation of the protection decision.

THE ROMANS BUILT TEMPLES, POOLS AND A LUXURIOUS BATH COMPLEX AROUND THE SPRING

The warm springs therefore attracted the population way back during prehistory. Over time, one of the important ancient spa centres on the territory of present-day Croatia arose around them. The thermal sulphurous water, which emerges to the surface at a temperature of as much as 58 degrees Celsius, was so highly valued that the Romans built an entire complex of public buildings around it. The spring is still active today: the water emerges at the same place and supplies the Special Hospital for Medical Rehabilitation Varaždinske Toplice. The phenomenon that attracted people several thousand years ago lives on today.

Today’s archaeological park is home to the impressive remains of an expansive Roman complex that developed from the 1st to the 4th century. Systematic research, which began back in 1953, has uncovered the remains of ancient buildings on an area of approximately 6,000 square metres. There were baths with pools, a forum surrounded by porticoes, temples dedicated to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, and a monumental pool that encompassed the spring itself. Parts of walls two to three metres high, floors, stone thresholds, frescoes and systems for the supply and drainage of water have also been preserved.

THE ORIGINAL ROMAN POOL IN WHICH THE WATER WAS COOLED BEFORE USE

Particularly fascinating is the original Roman pool measuring approximately 8 by 13.5 metres. It was built of large stone blocks, and water flowed from it through special channels towards the baths. The Romans also had to solve a very practical problem: the water that emerges at 58 degrees is too hot for direct bathing. The large pool helped cool it, while an elaborate system of channels enabled the controlled use of the precious spring.

17,000 COINS THAT THE ROMANS THREW FOR LUCK WERE FOUND AT THE SITE

For the Romans thermal water was not only a natural resource. They believed that the springs also had supernatural power, so the area around them was a place of worship of various deities, especially nymphs whom they associated with water and healing. During research at the site around 17,000 Roman coins were found that people from the 1st to the 4th century threw into the sacred spring as votive offerings. Numerous altars, reliefs, inscriptions and sculptures of deities were also found.

THE REMAINS OF THE ROMAN SETTLEMENT CAN TODAY BE VIEWED IN THE PARK AND IN THE MUSEUM

During its long history, Aquae Iasae was not spared wars and destruction. At the beginning of the 4th century the complex suffered during Gothic invasions, but its importance was so great that the Roman emperor Constantine the Great ordered its reconstruction. After the collapse of the ancient world many buildings disappeared under layers of earth, but the spring continued to be used. It is precisely the thermal water, or rather the deposition of tufa, that is responsible for the exceptional preservation of parts of the Roman complex.

Today, the remains of the former settlement can be viewed in the Archaeological Park Aquae Iasae, located in the town’s spa park. The park itself was landscaped as early as 1820, and its history is another reminder of the centuries-long connection of the town with thermal water. In addition to the archaeological site it is worth visiting the Local History Museum in the Old Town, where valuable finds from the Roman period are exhibited. In this way time for relaxation in Varaždinske Toplice can be combined with exploration and incredible historical stories.

World.title: Changes for Croatian Wolt Users Ordering Alcoholic or Energy Drinks
World.content:
October the 18th, 2026 – Significant changes have arrived for Croatian Wolt users who want to order alcoholic or energy drinks using the platform.

The delivery platform Wolt has introduced mandatory age verification for all of the service’s users in Croatia who order alcoholic and energy drinks via its app or website. As they reported in a notice to users, the new rules are being introduced in order to comply with new legal regulations in Croatia, and adulthood will no longer be able to be confirmed simply by ticking a box, but exclusively by connecting to the state mGrađani system. Index reports that Wolt emphasises that the check is quick and secure and that through this process the platform receives only the information whether the buyer meets the age requirement of 18 years, without insight into other personal data.

how does it work?

Age verification is carried out at the last step before completing the order itself. The user selects the option “Confirm your age”, after which Wolt redirects them to the mGrađani app. If the order is made via a computer, a QR code appears on the screen that needs to be scanned with a mobile phone. If ordering directly from a mobile phone via the Wolt app, the system automatically offers to open the mGrađani app. After the user logs in with their credentials and clicks on authorisation, the system sends confirmation to Wolt, and the buyer returns to the basket and completes the payment.

without an oib or mGrađani, alcohol and energy drinks can’t be ordered

Wolt notes that those who do not have the mGrađani app installed or do not complete the verification process will not be able to complete an order that contains alcohol or energy drinks at all. They also stress that for a successful check it is necessary to have an OIB, and they advise users who encounter technical difficulties to check whether they have updated both the mGrađani app and the Wolt app itself on their mobile phone.

World.title: German Newspaper: Greed for Profit Threatening Croatian Tourism
World.content:
October the 17th, 2026 – The well known German newspaper Die Welt has accused the country of greed, claiming it is threatening Croatian tourism.

The German newspaper Die Welt has published a somewhat accusative text about this year’s tourist season in Croatia. The paper warns that the short-term desire for higher earnings could endanger the country’s most important economic branch. DW has reported that the author of the article, Volker Corsten, describes his own impressions from the area between Zadar and Split and from the Adriatic islands. He points out that the beaches during the summer of 2026 were apparently “noticeably emptier than in previous years”, that there were “no usual traffic jams on the coastal roads”, and that even in August, the peak of the season, “one could walk through the old town centres of Zadar and Šibenik without large crowds”. We’re not sure how true that is.

ice cream, aperol and grilled squid…

What are the reasons for this claim, the author of the Berlin newspaper asks. At the same time he emphasises that it was by no means the climate, which he describes as almost ideal. The sea was, he notes, exceptionally clean and of a pleasant temperature, and the weather conditions were sunny and without extreme heat. “Everything was, as always, excellent – as long as nothing is consumed, nothing is wanted on the beach, and one does not look at the bill for accommodation and visits to restaurants.”

According to Die Welt, the problem begins precisely at the moment when tourists look at the bills, i.e. the prices – for accommodation, restaurants and other tourist facilities. The German newspaper cites prices in Zadar as an example. In the most visited tourist parts of the city a scoop of ice cream costs at least three euros, while in side streets it can still be found for around two euros, Die Welt writes. It adds that an Aperol Spritz, depending on the location of the hospitality establishment, costs between nine and eleven euros.

The German media outlet also notes that the price of one of the most popular Dalmatian dishes, grilled squid, in 2026 in many taverns has risen to around 25 euros, while “a year earlier it amounted to around 20 euros”. As a symbol of the price increase the newspaper highlights the example of pancakes at a kiosk on a beach near Šibenik: “Before the introduction of the euro in 2023 they cost seven kuna, or around one euro. After the switch to the euro the price rose to two euros, and this year to as much as five euros!”

prices have risen, but quality allegedly hasn’t

Referring to data from the Croatian Bureau of Statistics, Die Welt states that prices in tourism between 2015 and 2024 rose by 70 percent. At the same time it recalls that the current inflation rate in Croatia is 4.4 percent, while on the coast, according to the author’s assessment, the rise in prices is even more pronounced. Although the Croatian Ministry of Tourism officially claims that the number of officially registered overnight stays in July was slightly higher than a year earlier, the author of the text recalls numerous reports about empty beaches and hotels: “Anyone who compares those claims (of the Ministry of Tourism – ed.) with their own impressions thinks of Potemkin villages.”

a criticism of croatia’s tourism strategy

The German newspaper recalls that the Croatian authorities want to develop a more sustainable and higher-quality form of tourism, with Mallorca often mentioned as a model. However, according to the author’s assessment, when it comes to prices Croatia has already set off down that path, but the quality of infrastructure, hotels, private accommodation, gastronomy and service still lags behind the level of prices demanded from guests: “Almost fifty years of socialist Yugoslavia cannot be erased so quickly.”

World.title: Light and Dark “Rings” Appear Along the Northern Coast of Palagruža
World.content:
October the 17th, 2026 – Strange light and dark rings have appeared along the northern coast of Palagruža, resulting in all kinds of suspicions from those who saw them…

Unusual light and dark rings have appeared on the surface of the sea, arranged in almost regular oval circles that stretch in large arcs and are clearly visible from a great distance. Morski reports that this phenomenon has aroused the curiosity of autumn visitors to Palagruža who wondered what exactly was going on. Dalmacija danas sought the answer from the people who spend the most time on Palagruža and know the peculiarities of the local sea well, the lighthouse keepers.

They explained to them that this is a natural phenomenon connected with sea currents, which occasionally meet in that area and, as they picturesquely described it, “break”. The sea currents interact with each other, create vortex movements and areas of different current speeds.

In certain places where surface waters approach or diverge, zones of different roughness of the sea surface can form. Under certain lighting these are seen as lighter or darker stripes, arcs and other shapes, which explains the interesting “mystery” from Palagruža that nobody would be ridiculed for thinking aliens were coming!

World.title: Is Germany Pressuring Croatia Over Montenegro EU Entry?
World.content:
October the 17th, 2026 – According to a Euronews report, Germany is strongly pressuring Croatia over the Montenegro EU entry issue, but Andrej Plenković claims otherwise.

The German Government is allegedly intensifying its pressure on Croatia to resolve the open issues with Montenegro so that there is no standstill in its accession to the European Union, but the PM claims that isn’t what’s occurring. Index reports that Berlin has allegedly actively become involved in resolving the problem and is demanding a constructive approach from Zagreb, which four officials directly familiar with the situation claimed for Euronews.

This week, Croatia sent Podgorica a list of eight disputed points that it wants resolved before the conclusion of accession negotiations. Because of this, Germany is striving to ensure that the enlargement process continues without slowing down, as a blockade of Montenegro, which is considered the most advanced candidate, could jeopardise the entire process.

Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković stated on Thursday ahead of the European Council summit in Brussels that there are issues that have been pointed out to Montenegro for years. “In the last two years there has been no progress at all,” Plenković said, adding that Croatia has been “extremely constructive” in the negotiations.

war crimes and historical issues

The disputes mainly relate to the legacy of the wars of the 1990s, which includes property claims and unresolved border issues. These problems endanger Montenegro’s goal of becoming the 28th EU member by 2028. The Croatian side emphasises that the investigation of war crimes and compensation for victims are conditions that Podgorica must fulfil in order to conclude the negotiations. At the same time Zagreb faces accusations that it activated the disputes at the last moment in order to increase pressure on Podgorica. Croatia, for its part, replies that these are long-standing problems and that its demands are of a symbolic nature.

diplomatic engagement and criticism

The European Commission has also become involved in the talks in recent weeks, and several member states are trying to prevent bilateral issues from stopping the process. France wants to avoid problems with enlargement because of its internal political situation, while Luxembourg criticises the practice of using the accession process to resolve mutual disputes.

Although several governments are talking to Croatia, the strongest pressure is coming from Berlin. Germany recently also offered mediation, but that offer has not yet been realised. The government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz wants to act as an impartial mediator out of fear that bilateral disputes could jeopardise the entire enlargement process. Croatia’s position has also met with public criticism, including that of the EU High Representative for Foreign Policy Kaja Kallas. On the margins of the summit she stated that bilateral issues must not block the accession process.

the geopolitical angle

EU officials fear that the mood towards enlargement could change if Montenegro’s entry is not completed soon. Next year elections will be held in several key member states, including France, where polls are led by Marine Le Pen, known for her scepticism towards further expansion of the Union.

Montenegro’s accession is taking place in a context in which Brussels is using the enlargement policy to strengthen ties with neighbouring countries because of tensions with Russia. Since Montenegro is first in line for membership, a standstill due to bilateral issues could also negatively affect the other candidates – Albania, Moldova, and especially Ukraine, whose accession is linked to future peace negotiations with Moscow. Montenegro would at the same time be the first country to enter the bloc according to the new enlargement methodology. This year Podgorica is chairing the Berlin Process, an initiative for regional cooperation in the Western Balkans, and is closely cooperating with the German government. In that context Germany is also advocating new models of enlargement, such as the status of “associated candidate” for Ukraine. Germany therefore considers that, given Podgorica’s efforts and the geopolitical situation, it is crucial to make a breakthrough in Montenegro’s accession so that the enlargement process does not come to a halt.
