The Sheikh-ul-Islam stressed that “religion is separate from the state, and school is separate from religion”. He also accused certain “internal and external forces” of politicising the issue and trying to turn citizens against the state.

Araz Aliyev sees Pashazade’s statement as evidence that the authorities made the decision hastily:

“If the decision had been carefully considered and prepared over many years, the authorities should have consulted someone. It appears they made the decision in haste.”

For more on the legal aspects of the hijab ban, protests at schools and detentions, see JAMnews’ earlier report.

How will relations develop?

None of the experts interviewed expects Azerbaijan and Turkey to break off their alliance. However, they all believe the chill between the two countries will persist for some time.

Araz Aliyev believes the tensions will remain at the political level and gradually ease:

“Turkey needs Azerbaijan, while Azerbaijan needs Turkey even more in terms of national security, the economy and defence. Companies close to the leadership in both countries may face pressure from one another, but I do not believe their alliance will be threatened. After some time, we will hear declarations of brotherhood again.”

He notes that the two countries have weathered similar crises in the past. In particular, tensions in the late 2000s, when Turkey and Armenia were discussing protocols to normalise relations, led to Turkish flags being taken down in Baku. Aliyev believes the summit of the Organisation of Turkic States, which is expected to take place in Turkey at the end of the month, could indicate the direction in which relations between Baku and Ankara will develop.

Gergerlioğlu also does not expect Erdoğan to distance himself from Baku solely over the hijab issue. He says Ankara places much greater importance on revenue from the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, Turkey’s ambition to play a leading role in the “Turkic world” and the support of its nationalist-conservative electorate.

“Behind closed doors, they will probably say politely: ‘Wouldn’t it have been better not to introduce such a ban?’ However, if Aliyev begins openly supporting Israel, Turkey will also start signalling its discontent with the relationship more openly.”

The MP also points to declining electoral support for the ruling party. He claims that some voters dissatisfied with the AKP’s “two-faced” policy towards Israel backed the New Welfare Party in the last election. In his view, the hijab issue could deepen this discontent further.

Javid Agha reaches a similar conclusion. He believes that no matter how often Erdoğan repeats the slogan “one nation, two states”, he will have to take into account the views of the religious-conservative electorate that forms the foundation of his political support and adjust his position accordingly.

Fidan’s statements in Baku also offer insight into this diplomatic strategy. Ankara does not deny that problems exist, but seeks to move discussions about them out of the public arena and into closed-door diplomatic channels. So far, however, there are no signs that Baku intends to make concessions either on the hijab issue or on its relations with Israel.

Strained relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 19, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 19. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day Second Karabakh War ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation.

Trend presents the chronicle of the 23-rd day of the second Karabakh war:

- President Ilham Aliyev has received a delegation led by the Speaker of the Turkish Grand National Assembly Mustafa Sentop.

- President Ilham Aliyev gave a video interview to the Russian TASS news agency.

- President Ilham Aliyev shared a publication on Twitter about Armenia's heavy artillery shelling of settlements in violation of the humanitarian ceasefire.

- President Ilham Aliyev congratulated Chief of the State Border Service of Azerbaijan, Colonel General Elchin Guliyev on raising the Azerbaijani flag on the Khudafarin bridge.

- President Ilham Aliyev shared a publication on Twitter about the liberation of several villages in the Jabrayil district.

- The Armenian military equipment and weapons were destroyed. The list of the destroyed equipment has been announced.

- A high-ranking official of an Armenian Armed Forces battalion was killed.

- As a result of the shelling of the Tartar district by the Armenian Armed Forces, the owner of the house was seriously injured.

- Armenia shelled Azerbaijani positions on the state border.

- The Azerbaijani army has seized a certain amount of military equipment abandoned by Armenian troops.

- Armenians opened fire on the film crew of the Azerbaijani AzTV channel in Aghdam, injuring one journalist.

- The Defense Ministry of Azerbaijan has released a video of a war trophies seized from Armenian troops in the direction of Jabrayil and Fuzuli.

World.title: Azerbaijani judokas conclude the Asian Open Cup with 14 medals (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 18. The Asian Open Cup in judo has concluded in the Kazakh city of Aktau.

On the second day of the competition, Azerbaijani judokas won one gold, one silver and four bronze medals.

Sudaba Aghayeva (70 kg), having defeated all her opponents, claimed the gold medal. Madina Kaisynova (+78 kg) finished the tournament with a silver medal.

The bronze medals went to Janpolad Aliyev and Elmar Gasimov (both in the 100 kg category), Subhan Akhundov (+100 kg) and Alina Kugaeva (70 kg).

On the first day of the competition, silver medals were won by Nazir Talibov (66 kg), Kamran Suleymanov (73 kg), Farida Mirzoyeva (52 kg) and Ulviya Bayramova (57 kg). Rashad Yelkiyev (66 kg), Nariman Mirzoyev and Rufat Shovletov (both 73 kg), as well as Gulnara Bayramova (57 kg), claimed bronze medals.

Thus, Azerbaijani judokas concluded the two-day Asian Open Cup with a total of 14 medals, including one gold, five silver and eight bronze.

World.title: Exposure of Iranian agents in Germany: another provocation set to tune of Azerbaijani national anthem (VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 18. Another action by the anti-Azerbaijani network in Germany has ended in fiasco. This small-scale demonstration, supposedly aimed at protesting against “issues in Azerbaijan,” particularly the unified school uniform policy, has exposed yet another blatant provocation by foreign intelligence services, especially the Iranian network.

Video footage circulated following the demonstration clearly shows that the overwhelming majority of its organizers and participants are not Azerbaijani citizens, but foreign nationals and individuals who closely cooperate with foreign intelligence services. The Iranian national flags, as well as portraits of Iran’s religious leaders visible in the footage, provide a clear indication of the ideological center behind the event and who is pulling the strings.

Although the National Anthem of the Republic of Azerbaijan was played in the background, the Iranian flags raised at the event and the composition of the participants demonstrate that this rally has nothing to do with Azerbaijan. The Azerbaijani national anthem being played in the shadow of Iranian flags is also an obvious act of political manipulation by the rally’s organizers and a blatant sign of disrespect for our country’s national symbols.

The extremely small number of participants, the overwhelming majority of whom are representatives of foreign countries, demonstrates the failure of this provocative attempt and once again exposes the true face of the anti-Azerbaijani network in Europe.

We present footage from the “show” organized by foreign agents of influence in Germany.

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 18. The parliamentary delegation of Azerbaijan led by Speaker of the Milli Majlis Sahiba Gafarova arrived in the Kyrgyz Republic on a visit on 18 October.

This was stated by Azerbaijani Parliament.

Speaker Sahiba Gafarova and the delegation were welcomed at the Manas International Airport of the city of Bishkek by Deputy Speaker of the Joğorqu Kenesh (parliament) of Kyrgyzstan Yildiz Taalaybek ghizi, Ambassador of Azerbaijan to Kyrgyzstan Latif Gandilov, TURKPA Secretary General Ramil Hasan and other officials.

The Speaker of the Milli Majlis will hold a number of meetings and take part in the 15th plenary session of the TURKPA in the frameworks of the visit.

World.title: 'Very dangerous' unapproved peptide explosion hits NSW hospitals
World.content:
A surge in hospitalisations related to the use of unapproved peptides promoted as "wellness" products has prompted a warning from NSW health authorities.

New data from NSW Health shows 1,180 people turned up to hospital emergency departments across the state between July last year and September this year seeking medical treatment after taking unapproved peptides.

Monthly hospital presentations increased from just 5 in July 2025 to almost 220 last month.

Peptides are short chains of amino acids that make up proteins in our bodies and there are a number of peptide-based medicines that are approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA).

But unregulated peptides have exploded in popularity on social media, with promises of weight loss, aging reversal and muscle growth.

Health Minister Ryan Park said such unapproved peptides could have serious side effects, including liver and kidney damage, allergic reactions, severe vomiting and other complications.

"People present to the emergency departments quite unwell and people need treatment, so this is not minor," he said.

"People can get very unwell, very quickly as a result of these products.

'Very dangerous'

There is concern about websites selling peptides. (Four Corners)

NSW Health said products that were not approved may contain peptides, including BPC-157, GHK-Cu, TB-500, retatrutide and CJC-1295.

Mr Park said people should not buy or use unapproved products, particularly those promoted through social media and online retailers.

"This is very, very dangerous," he said.

"I think it'll be a topic for conversation with health ministers over the next few months, simply because of the scale of increase of use across the community and the potential harms that it has on individuals."

People are being urged to talk with their usual doctor about their health goals and only use approved peptide products that have been prescribed by a qualified health practitioner in Australia.

Those already using an unprescribed peptide product are being urged to speak with a health professional before taking the next dose to ensure it is a registered medicine.

"If you haven't had a product prescribed by a GP and you haven't had it issued at a pharmacy, please don't use it," Mr Park said.

World.title: 'Shared language of horror' uniting Aussie and Indonesian filmmakers
World.content:
Indonesian filmmaker Ivan Mosqueda does not hesitate when you ask him about his favourite Australian horror movie.

"Talk to Me," Mr Mosqueda said.

He is not alone.

The 2022 hit by Australian brothers Michael and Danny Philippou, which made $92 million from a $4.5 million budget, has inspired a generation of creators.

A social media-captured seance becomes a conduit between the living and the dead in this debut horror. (Supplied: A24)

Mr Mosqueda is part of a group hoping to leverage the momentum of the Australian horror genre in a filmmaking program between Indonesian and regional Queensland universities.

University of Southern Queensland (UniSQ) lecturer Katherine Putnam said a "shared language of fear" had broken down language barriers among the group of filmmakers.

Katherine Putnam says the horror genre can bring different cultures together. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

"Fear is universal," Dr Putnam said.

"The thing about horror is that it is a highly popular genre in Indonesia. It's also a highly popular genre in Australia, especially with youth."

The team spent a week filming short horror movies in Indonesia before calling action in Toowoomba, west of Brisbane.

Director of photography Juan Satiadarma said he enjoyed visiting Australian Maccas. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

The language of horror

While Mick Taylor, the sadistic outback butcher from Wolf Creek, still haunts many Australians on road trips, Dr Putnam said the face of the domestic horror industry was changing.

"As a genre, it goes beyond the gore to the primal emotions and themes about our world and how it operates," Dr Putnam said.

The program is operating on a tight $60,000 budget, funded by UniSQ and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

Dr Putnam hoped it would lead to more creative partnerships between Australia and Indonesia and ease the reliance on financing from the United States.

The regional Australian and Indonesian filmmakers after filming in Pittsworth. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Mr Mosqueda said it was interesting to contrast the similarities and differences between Australian and Indonesian horror.

"Back in Indonesia, religion still has a big part, so the horror comes from traditional beliefs," he said.

Meanwhile, Mr Mosqueda said different species of insects that showed up on set in Toowoomba were a shock.

A scene from regional Australian filmmaker Soren Jocumsen's The Long Road Home. (Supplied: Soren Jocumsen)

"Whereas in Australia, the scary part could be the wilderness because Australia is big and there is lots of empty space."

'Regional with benefits'

For the three Australian filmmakers involved in the program from Cairns, Mackay, and the Sunshine Coast, it was a rare chance for creatives outside of Brisbane to receive funding.

"It's been a whirlwind, bit of a fever dream to be honest," Sunshine Coast-based filmmaker Amy Parry said.

She said filmmakers outside of metro cities were banding together, inspired by the Phillippou brothers' YouTuber-to-box-office success.

Sunshine Coast-based filmmaker Amy Parry directing a horror short film in Pittsworth. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

"We've got a great little collective of filmmakers [on the Sunshine Coast], and of course we can travel to Brisbane and the Gold Coast," Ms Parry said.

But Ms Parry said she was concerned regional filmmakers will be the first to suffer as the state government cut at least $13 million in annual funding to Screen Queensland for the next two years.

The organisation had been involved with Baz Luhrmann's Elvis, Marvel's Thor: Ragnarok, and Bluey.

"It would just be great for the government to also find value in the huge industry that is here and bringing so much money into the state."

World.title: Trump endorses 'great warrior' Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has written a glowing endorsement of the Israeli prime minister just months after labelling him "crazy" and days after suggesting he does not trust him.

In a lengthy post on his Truth Social platform, Mr Trump urged Israelis to vote for Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party in their upcoming election, now just over a week away.

He labelled the Israeli prime minister a "Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace", pointing to the decision the pair took to launch their war against Iran on February 28.

Negotiations to end that conflict have been stalled for months, despite Mr Trump's repeated insistence Iran has been defeated.

"If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote.

"Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.

Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu have dinner at the White House in 2025. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

"Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived!"

He said Mr Netanyahu was the partner the US was "demanding of Israel, a Country for which it has done so much".

"Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel," Mr Trump said.

Benjamin Netanyahu's social media posts says Israel's enemies want him to lose the election while its friends want him to win. (Supplied: Benjamin Netanyahu)

Mr Netanyahu seized upon the endorsement, posting an image on social media showing Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, Iran's reclusive Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani along with the caption: "Israel's enemies want Netanyahu to lose."

It was accompanied by an image of the Israeli prime minister and Mr Trump, and the caption: "A friend of Israel wants Netanyahu to win."

Trump changes tune

In June, the US president unleashed an expletive-laden tirade against Mr Netanyahu as he effectively accused him of trying to undermine the prospects of a deal with Iran.

During a fiery phone call, after the Israeli prime minister ordered strikes on central Beirut against Iranian-backed Hezbollah, Mr Trump said Mr Netanyahu was "f***ing crazy" and said he would be in jail had it not been for his efforts to protect him.

Mr Netanyahu is subject to an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court (ICC) for alleged war crimes — something the US has condemned the court for pursuing, issuing sanctions against its officials in response.

The Israeli prime minister is also embroiled in a long-running corruption case at home, which is still before the local courts.

Mr Trump has previously urged Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon the prime minister, which he has to this point refused to do.

On Friday, during an interview with US network Newsmax, Mr Trump talked up the success of his relationship with Mr Netanyahu.

But when expressly asked whether he trusted the man, he replied: "I don't trust anybody in the world of politics."

Netanyahu vying for re-election

Mr Netanyahu is facing the challenge of his political life in the upcoming October 27 election, with polling suggesting his Likud party could be the second largest in the Israeli Knesset, behind challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party.

'Everything Netanyahu is not': The 'straight' shooter looking to rule Israel Israel's upcoming election could be one of the most consequential in the country's history, with Netanyahu's own former military chief the favourite to oust the prime minister from office.

However, he could retain the prime ministership after such a result, given the need for complicated coalition negotiations to establish a working majority and secure power.

The relationship between the US and Israel, and their leaders, has been a focus of campaigning during the election, with some of Mr Netanyahu's opponents accusing him of weakening the ties with Israel's closest ally.

Reports emerged earlier this month that the Trump administration had encouraged Israel to launch unilateral attacks against Iran, shattering the relative calm that had persisted for months, because the US president did not want to return to all-out war before the US midterm elections in November.

Mr Netanyahu is Israel's longest serving prime minister.

World.title: Brighton winger's long-range goal conjures decades-old memories of Beckham
World.content:
A remarkable Diego Gomez goal from halfway has put an exclamation mark on Brighton's 5-0 English Premier League win over Crystal Palace.



The result marked another statement victory in a campaign that has already seen the south-coast team overwhelm Arsenal 3-0.



But it was Gomez, hitting it like Beckham, who stole the spotlight.

Collecting the ball near the halfway line, the Brighton midfielder advanced just inside Crystal Palace's half and launched a 50-metre shot over stranded goalkeeper Walter Benitez and into the net for a spectacular goal in the seventh minute of the EPL match at Amex Stadium on Sunday.

The Paraguay international's shot revived memories of a strike from a similar range from David Beckham when playing for Manchester United against Wimbledon on the opening day of the 1996-97 Premier League season.

It remains one of English soccer's most famous goals and thrust Beckham into the global spotlight.

Gomez's goal put Brighton 2-0 ahead against its biggest rival — and the team went 3-0 up three minutes later before running out a 5-0 winner.

Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler said Gomez tried a similar effort in the 2-0 win at Sunderland last weekend.

"There the wind wasn't perfect for this try," Hurzeler said. "Now the wind was better for him.

"I'm really happy that he gets this reward for all of the effort he's putting into the club, into his own development, and into the team."

Brighton's big win leaves it third on the EPL table behind Manchester City and Arsenal.

The side has scored a league-high 23 goals in seven games and has the best goal difference.

AP

World.title: Magnitude-2.8 earthquake rattles shelves, wakes Barossa residents up
World.content:
Barossa Valley residents have awoken to the rumble of a magnitude-2.8 earthquake overnight.

The earthquake was recorded at 2:26am on Monday, with nearly 250 reports were received by Geoscience Australia.

The quake was located at Stone Well, on the outskirts of Tanunda, about 55 kilometres north-east of Adelaide.

Geoscience Australia seismologist Tania Page told 891 ABC Adelaide an earthquake of this size would cause "maybe two or three seconds of shaking".

"Most of the reports are around Tanunda and Nuriootpa," Ms Page said.

"People are reporting rattling shelves, a lot of noise, so earthquakes of this size tend to just sound like a thunder, or a truck going past, or a smaller explosion even."

Mark, a resident of Nuriootpa, described the tremor as "pretty powerful, it was very bass-like".

"At first I thought it was thunder," he said.

"It woke me up straight away, and my little cat who sleeps on the end of our bed, she was up for a while.

"I reckon it was about three seconds, maybe more."

According to Geoscience Australia, earthquakes with magnitudes of less than 3.5 "seldom cause damage".

World.title: Man charged with attacking woman with iron bar has case shelved indefinitely
World.content:
A man accused of hitting a woman with a metal bar five times could potentially avoid facing justice indefinitely after telling a judge he had just $12 to his name and could not afford a lawyer.

The young father is among a growing number of people charged with serious crimes in the Northern Territory successfully applying for their cases to be stayed under a recently revived High Court ruling.

The man, who the ABC has chosen not to name, faced the Darwin Local Court last week where he represented himself because he had been denied a legal aid lawyer.

He told Judge Ben O'Loughlin he was "on the bones of me backside", earning less than $400 a fortnight through JobSeeker, and suffering from medical issues while caring for three young children.

The impasse has left many people unable to secure a lawyer. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

The court heard the man had received a rejection letter from Legal Aid NT (LANT) which has implemented sweeping cutbacks and stopped taking on new criminal cases due to an ongoing funding stoush with the NT government.

The impasse has left people who cannot afford representation, including children, unable to secure a lawyer and some victims waiting up to a year for their cases to be heard.

In granting the man's stay application, Judge O'Loughlin said the thing most likely to change the outcome in future was "Legal Aid changing their attitude".

More LANT service cuts flagged

Earlier this month, LANT director Catherine Voumard imposed deeper cuts at the government-funded service.

In an internal email leaked to the ABC, Ms Voumard told staff that after reviewing "pressures" at the Darwin Local Court, duty lawyers would only assist defendants who weren't in custody in "exceptional circumstances", or those who have a mental illness or language barrier, from October 1.

The decision comes just a few months after federal Attorney-General Michelle Rowland wrote to the NT government warning it was expected to adequately fund legal services under the National Access to Justice Partnership, and failing to do so risked breaching international human rights obligations.

Marie-Clare Boothby says the government is continuing negotiations with LANT. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

NT Attorney-General Marie-Clare Boothby has maintained the organisation has more money than ever after the NT government increased baseline funding by $5.5 million as part of a multi-year agreement.

But on Friday, a spokesperson for Ms Boothby's department confirmed funding was being withheld because LANT had not signed the agreement.

They said LANT had been allocated $13 million in 2026-27, but only $3.4 million had been released, "with the remainder subject to the execution of a funding agreement".

The government did not respond to questions from the ABC about the terms of the offer and LANT did not respond to any of the ABC's questions.

Child sex case 'indefinitely delayed'

NT Criminal Lawyers Association president Beth Wild said the funding crisis was no longer just affecting defendants without representation, but now "undermining the entire justice system".

Beth Wild says cases involving serious violence and sexual offending are affected. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Ms Wild said the impact spanned from relatively minor offences to domestic violence and serious sexual offence cases in the Supreme Court.

"In at least one case involving an alleged child sex offence, proceedings have been indefinitely delayed because the matter cannot progress until the funding crisis is resolved," Ms Wild said.

Territory Criminal Lawyers principal Clancy Dane said the situation was "horrifying for victims".

"For victims it will be deeply disturbing knowing that their perpetrator is living their life in the community," he said.

"The time is long overdue for both the Attorney-General and the LANT director to explain in precise detail why they have been unable to work together to restore legal aid services, and critically, what they say is needed for full services to be restored."

Clancy Dane says Ms Boothby and LANT owe Territorians an explanation. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

In other cases before the Darwin Local Court this week, prosecutors scrutinised defendants' bank statements and personal circumstances to ensure they were genuinely unable to afford a lawyer.

In the case of the father granted a stay, prosecutor Melinda Listing said he should start saving to "represent himself in the future".

NT Supreme Court clears way for potential wave of adjournments The Northern Territory Supreme Court has cleared the way for criminal defendants refused legal aid on funding grounds to have their cases adjourned indefinitely.

In another case involving a man from the Tiwi Islands receiving JobSeeker, which was adjourned, prosecutor Jeremy Banwell questioned unexplained transactions amounting to up to almost $1,000 moving in and out of his account.

"The Crown's ultimate position is, an individual may well have the capacity to afford legal representation, were they to adjust their spending habits," he said.

Ms Boothby said the government was continuing negotiations with LANT to finalise a funding agreement and would crack down on misuse of the service.

"Taxpayers will no longer foot the bill for alleged offenders who can genuinely afford a lawyer," she said.

World.title: Oyster farmers cautious ahead of summer as algal bloom recovery continues
World.content:
Oyster growers are cautiously navigating the aftermath of South Australia's harmful algal bloom, nearly 12 months after some harvesting regions reopened.

Simon and Meagan Turner operate out of one of the state's largest growing regions north-west of Adelaide at Franklin Harbour on the Eyre Peninsula.

The area was closed for four months last year, reopening in November.

Oyster farming has been in Simon Turner's family for nearly 40 years. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Charlotte Martin)

Now, oysters are healthy and a sense of normalcy is finally returning.

"Dolphins, benthic feeders, they're all coming back in force and that's a fairly good indicator that the bay is coming back," Mr Turner said.

Less stock in the water

Recovery is moving at different speeds across the coastline, but there is one constant across the board: decreased stock.

With closed harvesting areas and an uncertain future this time last year, growers did not input young oysters when they usually would.

"It's probably now that we're going to feel the effects of the algal bloom, as far as production goes … because oysters take about 12 to 15 months to grow," Mr Turner said.

For the Turners, it has resulted in about 40 per cent less stock on hand than normal.

Despite the challenges ahead, the Turner family is optimistic after the future. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Charlotte Martin)

Government support helped shelter the business from major financial losses amidst the worst of the bloom, and since reopening it has been "an extremely good year financially".

"But we're going to seriously feel it now because we just don't have the product in the water," Mr Turner said.

"I think most people will go, well, the bloom started then and it finished then, so we're back on track and off we go. It just doesn't work like that."

Confidence is returning to the oyster industry after last year's algal bloom. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Charlotte Martin)

Tale of two peninsulas

Across the Spencer Gulf at Stansbury, Steve Bowley has not put new stock in for at least 18 months.

Mr Bowley said an increase in barnacles and dead weed stock has damaged his water infrastructure, while he estimated a $400,000 decline in business value and an increase in mortalities.

"Out of every five dozen [oysters], I reckon I'm getting one dozen that are dead … I certainly haven't seen that in 20-odd years," Mr Bowley said.

Oysters at Steve Bowley's Stansbury leases are dying at a much higher rate than normal. (ABC North & West SA: Clem Stanley)

"I think what we're seeing is that as the oysters are stressed by the lack of oxygen in the water and these other things, lack of water flow from the barnacle and the weed, then it's the weak ones that die."

Before the bloom, he had been hoping to sell the business and retire.

"Can I get my money back? I don't think I can. I think our business is largely worthless now," Mr Bowley said.

Steve Bowley is seeing more barnacles than ever before at his Stansbury lease. (ABC North & West SA: Clem Stanley)

Waiting for what summer brings

With summer fast approaching and no way of knowing if the harmful algal bloom will return, all eyes are on the water.

"It's kind of hanging over us a bit like the Sword of Damocles in that we're waiting [to see] if the water temperature rises and then it blooms again, what the impact of that is going to be," Mr Bowley said.

"It's discouraging, to say the least."

Despite the uncertainty, South Australian Oyster Growers' Association chair Peter Treloar said the industry felt "relieved".

Peter Treloar says growers are "confident and relieved". (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Charlotte Martin)

"There's always ups and downs in the industry, but for the most part there's confidence, there's production occurring, and growers are looking forward to making sales ahead of Christmas," he said.

Like the rest of the state, the Turner family is just happy to be back in the water.

"I believe the ocean flows through our veins as a family … and during the algal bloom it was quite a load mentally to see that taken away from us," Ms Turner said.

"It just feels like a moment where we can finally breathe."

World.title: Hearings NSW Police wanted secret begin today. This is what to expect
World.content:
The state's police watchdog is set to hold rare public hearings into the actions of law enforcement during a February protest of Israel President Isaac Herzog's visit to Sydney.

The Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (LECC) will today open a series of public and private hearings examining the actions of NSW Police.

The watchdog has previously said the incident received the most public complaints of police misconduct in the commission's history.

What is LECC examining?

The use of pepper spray by police officers at the rally will be examined. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

Under the name Operation Makalu, the LECC will examine alleged acts of misconduct by NSW Police officers responding to a protest at Town Hall in February.

The hearings were sparked by more than 800 public complaints, 556 of which were made to the commission and 267 directly to NSW Police.

Eight days after the protest, the LECC first announced it was investigating the police operation, specifically the use of force by responding officers.

In May, the LECC said it had reviewed more than 450 items submitted to it, conducted interviews with witnesses and reviewed more than 1,000 hours of CCTV footage from the scene.

The commission is also looking at the police force's planning for the protest, officers' use of pepper spray and how its use was documented on the night.

What happened at Town Hall?

Thousands turned out to the protest in February, which police deemed unlawful. (ABC News)

The protest took place after NSW Police were given additional powers ahead of Mr Herzog's visit to Sydney on February 9.

The rally organised by the Palestine Action Group (PAG) came despite police issuing a restriction on demonstrations in the CBD as part of wide-ranging powers granted in the wake of the Bondi Beach terror attack.

The Public Assembly Restriction issued by NSW Police made the planned gathering unlawful.

The location of the protest, Town Hall, was inside the exclusion zone declared by police, who offered to have the rally moved to Hyde Park, an offer the group rejected.

Police estimated 6,000 people gathered at Town Hall for what organisers said would be a peaceful rally.

Palestine Action Group's Josh Lees with police at the demonstration in February. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

Tourism Minister Steve Kamper also made a "major event" declaration, allowing police to close off access to a major event area and directing people to leave.

Those powers allowed police to manage crowd safety and maintain separation between groups to avoid confrontation in the CBD.

Around the same time as the protest at Town Hall, a vigil to mark the Bondi Beach terror attacks attended by Mr Herzog was being held at nearby Darling Harbour, a few kilometres away.

Images from the Town Hall rally of the violent clashes between police and protesters were followed the next day by NSW Premier Chris Minns defending officers against accusations of police brutality.

NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon also said officers "did what they needed to do" after an "angry and aggressive" group of demonstrators twice marched on police.

How will it work?

Police described the crowd as violent, when defending actions of officers. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

Originally set for September 29, the hearings were delayed due to procedural issues between the LECC and NSW Police.

Beginning on Monday, the commission will hold private hearings for five weeks examining whether any NSW Police officers committed misconduct at Town Hall on February 9.

Similar to Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) hearings, the examinations will open with an address from a counsel assisting the LECC inquiry on Monday before shutting its doors to the public.

After the five-week block of private hearings, the commission will then hold open hearings with evidence from "senior commissioned officers".

Body-cam footage from Town Hall protest emerges New police body-cam footage from the February Town Hall protest has captured police boasting about punching protesters.

According to a notice published by the watchdog last week, officers below the rank of inspector will be granted pseudonym orders to protect their identities when giving evidence to the inquiry.

NSW Police submitted to the inquiry that examinations held in public would have a negative impact on officer mental health, community relations and social cohesion.

"The NSW Police Force acknowledges the decision by the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission to hold private hearings as part of Operation Makalu," a police spokesperson said.

"NSWPF awaits the findings of the operation."

The commission will have to deliver a final report to be tabled in parliament after the hearings, though no date has been confirmed.

World.title: Delays up to an hour hit Brisbane rail commuters
World.content:

Rail commuters have been caught in delays stretching as long as an hour, after a signalling issue blocked half of the available lines at Eagle Junction.

Queensland Rail discovered the issue shortly after 6.30am.

About 40 minutes later Translink warned all northern lines except Ferny Grove were experiencing delays, including the Airport, Caboolture, Doomben, Redcliffe Peninsula, Shorncliffe, and Sunshine Coast lines.

By 7.30am, Queensland Rail said the delays could be as long as 60 minutes.

Engineers were on-site correcting the fault, which left two of four tracks closed, but the rail authority could not provide an estimate of when the services would run as usual.

The delays affected trains travelling north and south through the major rail station.

A man has been charged after allegedly threatening to shoot three people with a sawn-off shotgun during a confrontation over a stolen van in Dulwich Hill on Friday, before setting fire to the vehicle and fleeing on foot.

An hours-long lockdown began in the inner west suburb after 10.20am on Friday, when Jake Kermode, 32, was allegedly confronted over a stolen van taken from a nearby suburb days earlier.

Kermode allegedly set fire to the van, near an apartment complex at Williams Parade and Constitution Road in Dulwich Hill, and waved the shotgun at three witnesses, before fleeing on foot with the weapon.

Police had shut down the area as they combed Dulwich Hill for the gunman on Friday. James Brickwood

Nearby businesses, cafes and schools were put into lockdown on Friday as tactical police, along with the police helicopter, combed nearby streets for the alleged gunman. The lockdown was lifted about 3pm that day.

World.title: Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber break silence over death of son Presley: ‘Beyond heartbroken’
World.content:
CultureCelebrityVale Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber break silence over death of son Presley: ‘Beyond heartbroken’ Chris Hook October 19, 2026 — 7:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Supermodel Cindy Crawford and American businessman Rande Gerber have publicly addressed the death of their son Presley Gerber for the first time with a tribute published on Crawford’s Instagram account. Presley’s sister Kaia Gerber also signed off on the statement and posted her own separate message via her own account. Presley, a 27-year-old model and mental health advocate died at a rehabilitation facility on September 20. The death is being investigated as a suspected overdose but no official cause of death has yet been revealed. Gerber pictured with his younger sister Kaia Gerber, mum Cindy Crawford and dad Rande Gerber. Photo by Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images “We are beyond heartbroken to lose our beloved son and brother. We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years,” the statement, posted early Monday morning (AEDT) read. “He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever. We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability.



“We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain. Til we meet again our sweet boy. We love you forever, Mom, Dad and Kaia,” the tribute finished. Separately Kaia, a 25-year-old actor recently seen in the Disney+ TV series The Shards, based on Bret Easton Ellis’s novel, posted her own long tribute with video of the two siblings dancing together when they were young children, along with a picture of the pair on a beach. “Prez, I don’t have the words, and maybe the tiny mercy is that we didn’t need them all along. Words fail and words subtract and words summarize and words always lack truth. And how naive of me to believe that language could transcend grief,” Kaia Gerber wrote.



“You know how much I loved being your sister. It has always been, and will forever be, my favourite thing about myself. I came into this world with a white-knuckle grip around you. I had more love for you than I knew what to do with. And now that it has nowhere obvious to go, I’m certain it’s going to swallow me whole.” Kaia Gerber and Presley Gerber in 2018. Getty Presley went into cardiac arrest before his death, a leaked 911 audio recording obtained by People said. Santa Monica Police Department said in a statement to the outlet that Presley was found dead upon arrival. “[Santa Monica Police Detectives] are investigating the death as a suspected overdose,” police said. “At this time, there is no indication of foul play. The official cause and manner of death will be determined by the Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner. The investigation remains ongoing.” Presley began modelling as a teenager and was signed by the agency IMG Models at 15. He had been open about his mental health struggles, including depression and substance abuse, before becoming an advocate.



In 2019, Presley was charged with drink-driving, and late sentenced to three years’ probation and ordered to do two days of community service and complete a DUI program, per The Hollywood Reporter. He began an Instagram series called Mental Health Mondays in 2023, where he talked openly about his mental health, before it finished in 2025. World.title: Australia news LIVE: Greens senator claims rumours weaponised against him, denies being on leave from party; Riots, looting in France as more than half a million protesters take to streets
World.content:
Trade Minister Don Farrell has urged the Coalition to back the Australia-EU free trade agreement, saying that failing to do so would be “an act of economic self-harm”, as Nationals leader Matt Canavan rejects the proposal before shadow cabinet came to a position on it.

“I am deeply concerned that the Nationals - and let’s face it, there’s only four of them in the Senate - [are] trying to pull … the Liberal Party, into a position of opposing our new EU free trade agreement, and so I ask the Liberals [need] to really deeply consider whether they want to be in a position to oppose a free trade agreement,” Farrell told ABC Radio National this morning.

“[Opposition Leader] Angus Taylor, in his maiden speech, said he supported free trade. Most of the Liberals that I speak to, either in the Senate or in the lower house tell me that the party supports free trade, and so what we’re saying to Mr Taylor is stand up to Mr Canavan on this occasion because to defeat a new free trade agreement with the Europeans would be an act of economic self-harm for Australia”.

Trade Minister Don Farrell. Alex Ellinghausen

Canavan and his Nationals colleagues have said the free-trade agreement the government has struck with the European Union is worse than no trade agreement, and should be scrapped entirely. Liberal colleagues speaking to various media outlets on condition of anonymity have said the deal is better than the current trade settings.

Last week Canavan penned an opinion piece in The Australian newspaper that said the deal “exposes Australian jobs to unfair trade, it would weaken Australia’s sovereignty on climate change policy and it does not even provide meaningful access for Australian goods to European markets”.

Farrell said this morning that the Europeans had made “very significant concessions” in striking the deal, and if the government was forced to renegotiate the agreement a worse outcome might occur for Australia.

World.title: ‘Long reads’ and ‘frothy fun’ in store as Sydney Festival 2027 unveiled
World.content:
CultureTheatreSydney Festival ‘Long reads’ and ‘frothy fun’ in store as Sydney Festival 2027 unveiled Michaela Boland October 19, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The 2027 Sydney Festival will include a nod to wellness culture with an outdoor installation of old cars transformed into saunas, cold plunges and spas, free for public use. If that is a sentence you never expected to read, that makes two of us. Sydney Festival Director Kris Nelson in one of the old cars that will be turned into a spa experience during the festival in Barangaroo. Janie Barrett Upon reflection the waynapuni pools public bathhouse, to be created by industrial designer Benjamin Paul, working with First Nations teenagers, and installed in Barangaroo Reserve from January 7 to 25, is quintessentially Sydney Festival. Since it began, Sydney’s annual arts jamboree has demonstrated a knack for reflecting our city back to us and public bathing is certainly having a moment.



At the first Sydney Festival in 1977, during the craft era, Haymarket was transformed into a bustling arts and crafts market. Nelson says ‘long reads’ are important, but fun party nights are also a big part of festival programming. Janie Barrett A decade later, 14 bands were on the line-up for an overnight Twelve-Hour Rockathon at Sydney Entertainment Centre, and who can forget Festival First Night from 2008-2012, which drew 250,000 people to the centre of Sydney during the GFC, when we all really needed a party. Artistic director Kris Nelson’s second Sydney Festival boasts a huge contemporary dance program, Dance Reflections, backed by high-end French jewellery house Van Cleef & Arpels and the return of First Nations-led multi-arts strand Blak Out. Among the highlights outside of these programs is a new show from comedian Hannah Gadsby, American clown Spencer Novich and free dance event, The Party, at the Cutaway.



Nelson frames his programming style through the prism of summer beach reading. “It’s equal parts fluff, pulp and big heavy reads, and there’s something about that in a summer program that I want,” he says. “I want a frothy fun party or a great gig night, as much as I want something that is like the long read.” Fulfilling that slot is Irish company Dead Centre, which will transform Ukrainian poet Ilya Kaminsky’s poetry into a contemporary drama wherein a soldier shoots a deaf boy who can’t hear his orders, the next day, the townspeople are deaf. “It’s heavy and it’s beautiful. It’s an allegory, a protest,” Nelson says.



The Ballet du Grand Théâtre de Genève will bring choreographer Rachid Ouramdane’s Outsider to Sydney Festival 2027. Gregory Batardon It is also the closest the 2027 program comes to engaging with the current febrile geopolitical climate. “Lots of people in the program are touched by what’s happening in the world, it’s a program that’s engaged in our times,” Nelson says. Dance Reflections is an ongoing international festival overseen by former New York City Ballet dancer Serge Laurent, who gathers some of the world’s premier dance troupes into curated programs staged in varying combinations since 2022 in nine cities, from London to Shanghai. The 10th iteration in Sydney will present a physical theatre smorgasbord of 13 different shows at venues across Sydney and a dozen dance workshops at Sydney Dance Company.



France’s Rachid Ouramdane has devised an aerial work wherein 20 dancers and four extreme sports athletes will be suspended by tightropes and thrown through space at the Cutaway Barangaroo. Famed choreographer Anne Teresa de Keersmaeker and Morocco’s Radouan Mriziga will collaborate on Together at Carriageworks, a reimagining of Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons. A decade after her death, Trisha Brown’s company will perform Roof Piece at the Art Gallery NSW. The world premiere of Ngurragabu, a major new work exploring an environmental apocalypse from Australia’s pan-national First Nations dance company Marrugeku has been included in the program. Marrugeku’s ensemble of First Nations, Filipino and Melanesian dancers will perform within a monumental mangrove forest being devised by visual artist Abdul-Rahman Abdullah.



Up Late with Bianca Hunt will consist of conversations with artists and cultural leaders. Arts festivals at their best showcase incredible international artists alongside new Australian works, inspiring audiences and artists and seeding potential ongoing collaborations. Laurent is non-committal about Marrugeku being included in future international Dance Reflections programs. “With artists you have to know each other, it’s a story each time,” he says. His curatorial approach is to provide a platform for artists from different backgrounds. Budjerah will be performing Donny Hathaway songs at the Metro Theatre for Black and Blues. Paul Harris



“Dance Reflections is a way to bring together very diverse artists [with] a very strong common point. They are researchers trying to find their own voice, so it’s quite eclectic, but in fact very consistent.” Marrugeku’s artistic co-director Dalisa Pigram has a similar approach to choreography. “We have nine artists spanning regions of maritime knowledge, including the Melanesian and Torres Straits, Singapore and East Indonesia and on the mainland Bardi Jawi and Nyaru knowledges within the region of the Kimberley.” Ancient saltwater knowledge systems have a lot to offer us as we contemplate melting ice caps and increased precipitation, she says. “I’m not a choreographer at the front asking people to move in certain ways, we have an approach that’s inspired by what moves the dancer,” she says.



MO’JU will be channelling the music of Bill Withers for Black and Blues. Justin McManus First Nations programming head Aidan Rowlingson has expanded the festival’s established Blak Out program to include a music series, Black and Blues. “I love the [concept of] First Nations musicians taking on their favourite soul blues artists at the Metro Theatre,” Nelson says. ARIA Award-winner Budjerah will channel Donny Hathaway, Wiradyuri/Filipinx artist MO’JU will conjure the music of Bill Withers and Etta James will be celebrated by Jamaican/Arrernte artist SOLCHLD. “Expect a sense of familiarity and discovery,” Nelson says.



Emily in Sydney will present another opportunity to see one of our most recognisable artists anew. The curated exhibition of paintings by Emily Kame Kngwarreye, drawn largely from private Sydney collections, will be on at S. H. Ervin Gallery. Up Late with Bianca Hunt at Belvoir St Theatre will consist of conversations with artists and cultural leaders. Wiradjuri Yuin actor Angeline Penrith will return for the third year with Redfern Renaissance, a series of performance readings and discussions about the revolutionaries and activism of Redfern’s National Black Theatre in the 1970s. Sydney Festival runs from January 7–25, 2027. Tickets go on sale Thursday, October 22 at sydneyfestival.org.au, with 10,000 prime seats available from $49 or less across all ticketed shows.

World.title: Spender and Chalmers’ reform adviser back GST change to offset tax cuts
World.content:
PoliticsFederalFederal budget Spender and Chalmers’ reform adviser back GST change to offset tax cuts Paul Sakkal October 19, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A leading member of Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ economic advisory panel and MP Allegra Spender have separately raised the alarm on high levels of state and federal spending and called for a GST hike to pay for tax cuts for workers. The Grattan Institute, an influential independent think-tank, has come out in favour of a tax mix switch at a time of near-record tax and spending levels under the Albanese government. Federal ministers and backbenchers have become concerned about inflation and productivity in recent weeks as tension has emerged between Chalmers and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers in question time last Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen In a report to be released on Monday, Grattan chief executive Aruna Sathanapally urges politicians to raise the GST from 10 to 15 per cent and expand it to include all types of food, raising $76 billion per year. The think tank says $33 billion should be used to cut income taxes for lower- and middle-income workers while $25 billion should be put to boosting JobSeeker, pensions and rent assistance. Sathanapally, who Chalmers picked for his economic reform roundtable last year, called for fiscal rules to force profligate state governments to curb spending as the RBA threatens more rate rises to reduce demand that is partly fuelled by government spending.



“There are no easy paths back to budget sustainability. But with smarter spending decisions and a tax system that raises sufficient revenue to care for our ageing population, both current and future generations can be better off,” Sathanapally said, adding that lower-income families would be left about $8000 a year better off under the proposed changes. Related Article Political leadership In a funk: How economic pain is straining the PM and treasurer’s relationship The institute says state government spending has grown even more quickly than the Commonwealth’s. Federal spending has still grown “substantially”, its report states, but Australia’s credit rating has remained steady while Queensland, Victoria, Tasmania and the ACT have all experienced rating downgrades. The think tank’s intervention in the economic debate adds to recent calls for tax reform from former Coalition ministers Josh Frydenberg and Mathias Cormann, both of whom argue for change to the GST, and Labor figures Bill Kelty, Paul Keating and Lachlan Harris. Albanese and Chalmers have been under internal and external pressure to address Australia’s economic problems. Their political headache was exacerbated by an own goal on credit card surcharges, which lead to the tax office refusing to accept credit card payments.



Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino admitted on Sunday that ministers knew the ATO might stop accepting credit cards as far back as July. Before Mulino’s comments in an interview on ABC’s Insiders, the government only emphasised its knowledge about the ATO’s final decision, which it learned in September. “In July, the government became aware that the ATO was looking at options,” Mulino said. Wentworth MP Allegra Spender. Alex Ellinghausen Only about 5 per cent of taxpayers pay bills via credit card, but the move has added to arguments from the business lobby that Labor is not in touch with the concerns of business owners. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson seized on Mulino failing to rule out 60 or 70 per cent tax rates for small businesses who use trusts and pay into a “bucket company”. These firms will be incentivised to rearrange their structure.



On the proposal for fiscal rules, Wilson said: “They are like a diet and we know Labor can’t kick their spending addiction.” Spender, a tax reform advocate who was also on Chalmers’ reform panel last year, said fiscal rules were needed at the federal level, going beyond the Grattan Institute’s call for restrictions at state level. Rules that would cap expenditure and tax were proposed by former Treasury secretary Ken Henry in last year’s roundtable, but Chalmers has argued against arbitrary caps. “The government should adopt stronger fiscal rules, particularly to manage expenditure. Spending has grown too fast particularly for a high-inflation environment and we’re not bringing it back quick enough,” Spender said. “The GST should be on the table, as must better resource taxation, digital taxes and a shift from stamp duty to land taxes.”



Related Article Letters Difficult times aren’t a sign of schism at the top of the ALP ACCI chief executive Andrew McKellar also supported fiscal rules in that meeting, and said on Sunday they were necessary. Frydenberg, the former Coalition treasurer mulling a return to politics, called for debate on the GST last week but was quickly slapped down by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor. Australia’s income tax rates are relatively high by international standards and the highest rate kicks in at relatively low-income threshold. Many tax experts say that income taxes reduce the incentive to work, whereas people notice less if the GST creates slightly higher prices, creating fewer distortions and a more efficient system. The Grattan report says that the Commonwealth should use the higher GST take to cut back on the ballooning level of grant funding to the states in education and health, which are often subject to political dispute and compromise.



Under Grattan’s proposals, a low-income single-parent family who rents would pay nearly $80 more in GST per week but receive $202 in extra welfare and receive a $27 income tax cut, leaving them $150 a week better off. A higher-income working family would pay about $162 more in tax because they consume more and pay more GST. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Rail commuters have been caught in delays stretching as long as an hour, after a signalling issue blocked half of the available lines at Eagle Junction.

Queensland Rail discovered the issue shortly after 6.30am.

About 40 minutes later Translink warned all northern lines except Ferny Grove were experiencing delays, including the Airport, Caboolture, Doomben, Redcliffe Peninsula, Shorncliffe, and Sunshine Coast lines.

By 7.30am, Queensland Rail said the delays could be as long as 60 minutes.

Engineers were on-site correcting the fault, which left two of four tracks closed, but the rail authority could not provide an estimate of when the services would run as usual.

The delays affected trains travelling north and south through the major rail station.

An hours-long lockdown began in the inner west suburb after 10.20am on Friday, when Jake Kermode, 32, was allegedly confronted over a stolen van taken from a nearby suburb days earlier.

Kermode allegedly set fire to the van, near an apartment complex at Williams Parade and Constitution Road in Dulwich Hill, and waved the shotgun at three witnesses, before fleeing on foot with the weapon.

Police had shut down the area as they combed Dulwich Hill for the gunman on Friday. James Brickwood

Nearby businesses, cafes and schools were put into lockdown on Friday as tactical police, along with the police helicopter, combed nearby streets for the alleged gunman. The lockdown was lifted about 3pm that day.

World.title: Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber break silence over death of son Presley: ‘Beyond heartbroken’
World.content:
CultureCelebrityVale Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber break silence over death of son Presley: ‘Beyond heartbroken’ Chris Hook October 19, 2026 — 7:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Supermodel Cindy Crawford and American businessman Rande Gerber have publicly addressed the death of their son Presley Gerber for the first time with a tribute published on Crawford’s Instagram account. Presley’s sister Kaia Gerber also signed off on the statement and posted her own separate message via her own account. Presley, a 27-year-old model and mental health advocate died at a rehabilitation facility on September 20. The death is being investigated as a suspected overdose but no official cause of death has yet been revealed. Gerber pictured with his younger sister Kaia Gerber, mum Cindy Crawford and dad Rande Gerber. Photo by Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images “We are beyond heartbroken to lose our beloved son and brother. We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years,” the statement, posted early Monday morning (AEDT) read. “He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever. We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability.



“We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain. Til we meet again our sweet boy. We love you forever, Mom, Dad and Kaia,” the tribute finished. Separately Kaia, a 25-year-old actor recently seen in the Disney+ TV series The Shards, based on Bret Easton Ellis’s novel, posted her own long tribute with video of the two siblings dancing together when they were young children, along with a picture of the pair on a beach. “Prez, I don’t have the words, and maybe the tiny mercy is that we didn’t need them all along. Words fail and words subtract and words summarize and words always lack truth. And how naive of me to believe that language could transcend grief,” Kaia Gerber wrote.



“You know how much I loved being your sister. It has always been, and will forever be, my favourite thing about myself. I came into this world with a white-knuckle grip around you. I had more love for you than I knew what to do with. And now that it has nowhere obvious to go, I’m certain it’s going to swallow me whole.” Kaia Gerber and Presley Gerber in 2018. Getty Presley went into cardiac arrest before his death, a leaked 911 audio recording obtained by People said. Santa Monica Police Department said in a statement to the outlet that Presley was found dead upon arrival. “[Santa Monica Police Detectives] are investigating the death as a suspected overdose,” police said. “At this time, there is no indication of foul play. The official cause and manner of death will be determined by the Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner. The investigation remains ongoing.” Presley began modelling as a teenager and was signed by the agency IMG Models at 15. He had been open about his mental health struggles, including depression and substance abuse, before becoming an advocate.



In 2019, Presley was charged with drink-driving, and late sentenced to three years’ probation and ordered to do two days of community service and complete a DUI program, per The Hollywood Reporter. He began an Instagram series called Mental Health Mondays in 2023, where he talked openly about his mental health, before it finished in 2025. Presley’s sister Kaia Gerber referred to the Instagram series in an interview withVogue magazine in August in which described the impact of her brother’s battle with addiction. “When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone,” she said. “I think that’s also why I started to self-​identify as the easy [child] and never wanted to ask for help. Because it felt like too much to have two children who were needing.” But Presley’s openness was particularly challenging, she said.



“My parents for most of our lives were very, very private and didn’t share anything – and now we have this absolute teacher, my brother, who says, ‘I’m gonna be very human for everyone’,” she said. “There’s only so much you can hide from the world. And trying to put a lid on something just makes the person feel like you’re ashamed of them.” Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Wiradjuri Yuin actor Angeline Penrith will return for the third year with Redfern Renaissance, a series of performance readings and discussions about the revolutionaries and activism of Redfern’s National Black Theatre in the 1970s. Sydney Festival runs from January 7–25, 2027. Tickets go on sale Thursday, October 22 at sydneyfestival.org.au, with 10,000 prime seats available from $49 or less across all ticketed shows.

World.title: Spender and Chalmers’ reform adviser back GST change to offset tax cuts
World.content:
PoliticsFederalFederal budget Spender and Chalmers’ reform adviser back GST change to offset tax cuts Paul Sakkal October 19, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A leading member of Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ economic advisory panel and MP Allegra Spender have separately raised the alarm on high levels of state and federal spending and called for a GST hike to pay for tax cuts for workers. The Grattan Institute, an influential independent think-tank, has come out in favour of a tax mix switch at a time of near-record tax and spending levels under the Albanese government. Federal ministers and backbenchers have become concerned about inflation and productivity in recent weeks as tension has emerged between Chalmers and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers in question time last Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen In a report to be released on Monday, Grattan chief executive Aruna Sathanapally urges politicians to raise the GST from 10 to 15 per cent and expand it to include all types of food, raising $76 billion per year. The think tank says $33 billion should be used to cut income taxes for lower- and middle-income workers while $25 billion should be put to boosting JobSeeker, pensions and rent assistance. Sathanapally, who Chalmers picked for his economic reform roundtable last year, called for fiscal rules to force profligate state governments to curb spending as the RBA threatens more rate rises to reduce demand that is partly fuelled by government spending.



“There are no easy paths back to budget sustainability. But with smarter spending decisions and a tax system that raises sufficient revenue to care for our ageing population, both current and future generations can be better off,” Sathanapally said, adding that lower-income families would be left about $8000 a year better off under the proposed changes. Related Article Political leadership In a funk: How economic pain is straining the PM and treasurer’s relationship The institute says state government spending has grown even more quickly than the Commonwealth’s. Federal spending has still grown “substantially”, its report states, but Australia’s credit rating has remained steady while Queensland, Victoria, Tasmania and the ACT have all experienced rating downgrades. The think tank’s intervention in the economic debate adds to recent calls for tax reform from former Coalition ministers Josh Frydenberg and Mathias Cormann, both of whom argue for change to the GST, and Labor figures Bill Kelty, Paul Keating and Lachlan Harris. Albanese and Chalmers have been under internal and external pressure to address Australia’s economic problems. Their political headache was exacerbated by an own goal on credit card surcharges, which lead to the tax office refusing to accept credit card payments.



Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino admitted on Sunday that ministers knew the ATO might stop accepting credit cards as far back as July. Before Mulino’s comments in an interview on ABC’s Insiders, the government only emphasised its knowledge about the ATO’s final decision, which it learned in September. “In July, the government became aware that the ATO was looking at options,” Mulino said. Wentworth MP Allegra Spender. Alex Ellinghausen Only about 5 per cent of taxpayers pay bills via credit card, but the move has added to arguments from the business lobby that Labor is not in touch with the concerns of business owners. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson seized on Mulino failing to rule out 60 or 70 per cent tax rates for small businesses who use trusts and pay into a “bucket company”. These firms will be incentivised to rearrange their structure.



On the proposal for fiscal rules, Wilson said: “They are like a diet and we know Labor can’t kick their spending addiction.” Spender, a tax reform advocate who was also on Chalmers’ reform panel last year, said fiscal rules were needed at the federal level, going beyond the Grattan Institute’s call for restrictions at state level. Rules that would cap expenditure and tax were proposed by former Treasury secretary Ken Henry in last year’s roundtable, but Chalmers has argued against arbitrary caps. “The government should adopt stronger fiscal rules, particularly to manage expenditure. Spending has grown too fast particularly for a high-inflation environment and we’re not bringing it back quick enough,” Spender said. “The GST should be on the table, as must better resource taxation, digital taxes and a shift from stamp duty to land taxes.”



Related Article Letters Difficult times aren’t a sign of schism at the top of the ALP ACCI chief executive Andrew McKellar also supported fiscal rules in that meeting, and said on Sunday they were necessary. Frydenberg, the former Coalition treasurer mulling a return to politics, called for debate on the GST last week but was quickly slapped down by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor. Australia’s income tax rates are relatively high by international standards and the highest rate kicks in at relatively low-income threshold. Many tax experts say that income taxes reduce the incentive to work, whereas people notice less if the GST creates slightly higher prices, creating fewer distortions and a more efficient system. The Grattan report says that the Commonwealth should use the higher GST take to cut back on the ballooning level of grant funding to the states in education and health, which are often subject to political dispute and compromise.



Under Grattan’s proposals, a low-income single-parent family who rents would pay nearly $80 more in GST per week but receive $202 in extra welfare and receive a $27 income tax cut, leaving them $150 a week better off. A higher-income working family would pay about $162 more in tax because they consume more and pay more GST. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Labour pledges social media ban for under-16s within 100 days
World.content:
Watch a livestream of the announcement below.

Labour is pledging to implement the under-16 social media ban in its first 100 days and set up an online watchdog that can fine technology giants that break new rules.

If back in government Labour says it will give people more control of their internet feed by platforms to allow users to choose between an algorithm-driven feed or posts only from accounts people follow.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6401779896112

The new rules would mean users could switch between those feeds at any time.

There would also be a new 'Digital Duty of Care' law that would require platforms to "identify risks and protect Kiwis from harmful content and addictive designs".

Any breaches of these new rules would be assessed by a new independent online regulator, which would have powers to "enforce safety standards, investigate harmful practices and take action against companies that break the rules'.

The new duty of care law would cover stronger protections for under-18s against harmful content, bullying and design features that encourage excessive use or damage self-esteem, the party says.

It would also have "stronger protections against deepfake abuse, including non-consensual sexual images, and powers to take down harmful nudify apps and sites".

Lastly the new law would cover reponsibilities for companies and make platforms identify risks, detail what they're doing to keep people safe and fix the problems when things go wrong.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins says big technology companies have too much power when it comes to New Zealanders' online experience. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

The government introduced a bill to ban social media for under-16s in August but it did not have support from National's coalition partners New Zealand First or Act.

It was introduced so close to Parliament rising for the election that National's Christopher Luxon and Erica Stanford said it would not get its first reading this term.

Labour said it would support the bill at first reading to allow it to go to select committee but the Leader of the House Louise Upston made clear it would not go before the House as there wasn't enough time.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins says big technology companies have too much power when it comes to New Zealanders' online experience.

"Social media is part of everyday life. It helps us stay connected, share ideas and keep in touch with the people we care about."

"At the same time, scams are becoming more sophisticated, fake images and videos are harder to spot, and a lot of parents are worried about what their children are seeing," he said.

"Parents shouldn't have to take on big tech on their own."

Labour science, technology and innovation spokesperson Reuben Davidson said legislation implementing the social media ban would be passed in the first 100 days, "and we'll make it stronger at select committee with new privacy protections too".

World.title: Backroads to the Beehive: Coal, politics and division on the West Coast
World.content:
With less than three weeks until Election Day, RNZ's South Island Correspondent Tim Brown and camera operator Louis Dunham have toured Te Waipounamu to hear the good, the bad, and the ugly from the places and people where the political spotlight does not usually shine. They take readers on a journey from the Backroads to the Beehive, starting with the West Coast.

The West Coast's wild ancient forests and vast mineral wealth gave rise to the country's labour movement.

Key figures from Blackball's 1908 miners strike later served in the first Labour government and the West Coast has been a stronghold for the Labour Party since the 1920s, with the region's miners and workers its garrison.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406945480112

The social and economic upheaval of the 1980s rearranged traditional alliances and the coast is now deeply divided.

National has won previously unwinnable West Coast seats three times since 1990, with Maureen Pugh most recently toppling Damien O'Connor by just over a thousand votes in 2023.

National has won the party vote in West Coast-Tasman at every election this century, apart from 2020's Labour landslide.

Moana mechanic David Larkin says it is not hard to figure out why.

Audio player for " RNZ hits the road for Backroads to the Beehive " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2010548%2Fbackroads-to-the-beehive-coal-politics-and-division-on-the-west-coast

RNZ hits the road for Backroads to the Beehive Morning Report Download MP3 7m

"The values of the Labour Party now are nothing like the Labour Party that formed here. Those values have all gone," he says.

Just down the road in Ruru, fisherman Allan Rooney says he was Labour supporter until the party lost its way in the 1980s.

"It's a party of people that have never had a frickin' job. Look at 'em," he says during a break from weed-whacking his lush green lawns.

Pugh is stepping down in November and Labour stalwart O'Connor is instead running in the Otago and South Canterbury electorate of Waitaki after 33 years representing the coast.

Katie Milne, a West Coast dairy farmer and former Federated Farmers president, is standing for National and Rory Paterson, a North Canterbury-based teacher, is representing Labour.

Rooney is dismissive of Labour's chances.

Ruru fisherman Allan Rooney used to support Labour but now supports New Zealand First and Act. RNZ / Louis Dunham

"They didn't go so well last election. The guy that's standing here doesn't even friggin' live here but he's thinking about moving here if he gets in," he says.

Rooney is also dismissive of Chris Hipkins, only offering a husky chortle when asked for an opinion about the Labour leader. But he is no fan of National leader Christopher Luxon either and plans to back the coalition's minor parties.

"Back to reality is definitely Winston and looking ahead is David Seymour, right now," he says.

"If you'd asked me about ACT five or six years ago I would have started laughing but he has common sense policies."

The coast is full of contrasts.

'I'm not even religious but I get down on my knees and I pray that we get these clowns out of there'

Blackball local Matthew Howard - who prefers to be known as Mr Howard - does not see it that way.

"People have just got stupider and lost the point of why we had a Labour Party in the first place," he says dismissively when asked for an assessment of Labour's waning fortunes.

"We had to have a Labour Party so that we got decent working conditions, decent wages, people could have a decent home to live in and a decent life.

"The people in National and ACT, they don't want that for everybody. They only want that for a few."

Howard saves his most stinging criticism for New Zealand First.

"Winston is an old clown who should bugger off with his overfed mate," he says.

RNZ / Louis Dunham

Howard owns the land on which a large Labour hoarding sits overlooking Blackball's main road and is in no doubt about how he will vote.

"Two ticks Labour all the way down the line. Hopefully they'll save the country from this bunch of absolute clowns we've got destroying it at the moment," he says.

"I'm not even religious but I get down on my knees and I pray that we get these clowns out of there."

Jane Wells, who has lived in Blackball on-and-off for 50 years and formerly ran the pub Formerly The Blackball Hilton, also wants a change in government.

"The government that we've had for the last three years has been the most revolting government we've ever had," she says.

"Everything they say reminds me of the people that they think support them and that's the people with lots of money. They don't give a s*** about the people at the bottom."

As Wells gestures to her great-granddaughter playing on the verandah of her home, she says she wants a better future for New Zealand.

"For the sake of the world we have got to do more as far as the environment and climate change goes," she says.

"We have got to be careful. Canterbury's water - that used to be pure aquifers and it was the talk of the world. With all the dairying, it's just horrific now. It's got so much crap in it that it's dangerous."

Jane Wells and her partner Pat Kennedy have run and started businesses in Blackball. RNZ / Louis Dunham

'I don't feel there is a strong person out there that I could trust to look after my needs'

Young Blackball mother Marie Tippet says neither major party has left her feeling enthused about the election.
